231.text: This matches the term's established religious-zeal sense elsewhere in Paul (Rom 12:8; 2Cor 8:7); no divergence.

232.text: Innocence is the terminal state that grief, earnestness, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and punishment-readiness together, sharing the same party, produce and prove.

430.text: H4430 (king) is not itself an M-code characteristic acting on H0149 or H7109 -- he is the human party those two characteristics concern, not a characteristic in causal/tension relation with them.

436.text: The operation H5648 ('done') is carried out by those executing the decree; H4430 (king) is a party toward whom the consequence of that operation is directed, alongside his realm.

608.text: G4710 is exclusively nominal across all twelve of its occurrences (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-DSF forms), meaning the subgroup's noun-member consistently names diligence/zeal/haste as a possessable, giveable, or measurable quality (something one 'shows', 'has produced in you', 'puts into a heart', or is measured 'by') -- structurally opposite to G4709's pure manner-of-action adverbial function. This is the clearest grammatical-role divergence between the two subgroup members: G4710 names the THING, G4709 describes the HOW.

609.text: G4710's occurrence list shows a wider register-range than G4709's: it covers pure physical haste with no moral overtone (Mark 6:25, Herodias's daughter rushing to the king with a grim request; Luke 1:39, Mary's journey), alongside heavily moralized/evidentiary senses in the Pauline corpus (2Cor 7:11-12, 8:7-8; used as proof of sincerity of repentance or love) and paired-virtue senses (Rom 12:8, 12:11; Heb 6:11; 2Pet 1:5, chained with faith/virtue/knowledge). G4709's three occurrences, by contrast, are uniformly positive/earnest in register (pleading, searching, doing one's best) with no neutral-or-negative-context instance comparable to Mark 6:25's use for a request tied to John the Baptist's beheading -- showing G4710 tolerates a broader range of surrounding moral valence than G4709 does within this subgroup.

613.text: H0149 (Ezra.7.23, 'full') and H0629 share the same administrative-Aramaic sense of complete, exact execution of a decree, and both occur in Ezra's royal-correspondence chapters modifying verbs of official compliance (H5648 'done') rather than describing a person's disposition -- the two terms are functionally interchangeable as intensifiers of thoroughness within this register.

616.text: H0149's single occurrence (Ezra.7.23) is embedded in a wrath-avoidance clause ('lest his wrath be against the realm') absent from any H0629 occurrence -- where H0629's diligence-formula is consistently framed as positive compliance with a decree (payment, building, judgment, offering), H0149's 'full' compliance is framed negatively, as the condition that averts divine anger, a distinct rhetorical shading not shared by its sister term in this subgroup.

772.text: Both patterns occur. In 2Cor 7:11-12 and 8:7-8, earnestness FOLLOWS a prior belief/experience (godly grief, or Paul's estimation of the Corinthians) and becomes evidence for a further judgement about character. In Luke 7:4 earnestness accompanies a plea that itself is grounded in a preceding judgement ('he is worthy'). No verse shows earnestness itself producing a subsequent belief with no antecedent -- it functions consistently as accompanying or evidencing judgement rather than generating one from nothing.

780.text: In 2Cor 7:11, earnestness is one of a cluster of vividly named emotional responses (fear, longing, indignation) produced by godly grief -- here it functions as a felt, almost visceral moral urgency accompanying repentance, closer to transient intensified emotion than a fixed disposition, though it is offered as evidence of settled character change.

815.text: The characteristic co-occurs frequently with: fervency of spirit and service (Rom 12:11); faith, speech, knowledge, and love (2Cor 8:7); grief, fear, longing, indignation (2Cor 7:11); love proven genuine (2Cor 8:8); virtue and knowledge in a growth-chain (2Pet 1:5); hope (Heb 6:11); and care/heart (2Cor 8:16). It clusters especially with love, faith, and hope as an accompanying, evidencing quality.

817.text: In 2Cor 7:11 earnestness heads a sequence of responses produced by godly grief (grief precedes and produces earnestness, which is followed by further responses like indignation and fear); in 2Pet 1:5 effort/diligence precedes and initiates the addition of virtue to faith, beginning a developmental chain. The characteristic thus can both follow an antecedent cause (grief) and precede a subsequent development (virtue-chain).

818.text: Both causal and developmental relationships are shown: godly grief causally produces earnestness (2Cor 7:11), and earnestness/effort developmentally initiates a sequential chain of virtue-building (2Pet 1:5) -- the sequence is not merely correlational but shows genuine cause-then-effect and effort-then-growth structuring.

820.text: Yes, this characteristic is produced by godly grief, as shown explicitly in 2Cor 7:11 ('see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you').

821.text: The characteristic functions as a constituent element within larger virtue-lists or evidence-catalogues (2Cor 7:11's list of grief's fruits; 2Cor 8:7's list of Corinthian excellences) rather than being itself composed of other named characteristics as constituents -- it is a component contributing to a whole (proof of genuine repentance/love) rather than a compound built from other cluster members.

825.text: The characteristic (H0149/H0629) is a pure adverb of manner attached to administrative/legal verbs (paid, done, built, executed, bought/offered) and never to a verb of perceiving, believing, or concluding -- none of the occurrences reveal a person's perception, belief, or judgement; the domain is external compliance with a decree, not cognition.

826.text: Neither precedes nor follows a judgement or belief in any occurrence -- the characteristic modifies an act of execution (payment, building, judicial enforcement, offering) directly, with no cognitive act recorded before or after it in the same clause.

827.text: No orientation toward a future fullness of the person appears -- the terms describe the completeness of a single administrative act (payment, building, judgment, offering) already commanded, not a trajectory of growth or maturation in the one who acts.

828.text: The immediate response denoted (complete, prompt execution of a command) is consistent across every occurrence of both strongs -- payment 'in full without delay' (6.8), decree carried out 'with all diligence' (6.12, 7.21, 6.13), building progressing 'diligently' (5.8), purchase/offering 'with all diligence' (7.17), judgment executed 'strictly' (7.26), and compliance 'in full' (7.23) all show the same uniform thoroughness-response, varying only in the domain of the act, not in the quality of response.

831.text: The mechanism (adverbial intensification of manner attached to a verb of official action) is uniform across every context -- financial disbursement (6.8), decree-compliance formula (6.12, 7.21, 6.13), ongoing labor (5.8), judicial rigor (7.26), cultic purchase (7.17), and temple-provisioning compliance (7.23, H0149) -- the grammatical mechanism does not vary even though the domain of the commanded act does.

832.text: The evidence gives no signal either way as to created-design versus fallen-condition -- the terms belong to an administrative/legal register describing compliance with royal and divine decrees, not to a theological narration of human nature's origin or corruption; not determinable from this evidence.

833.text: No emotion-language or bodily-feeling language accompanies the characteristic in any occurrence -- it is presented as a manner-qualifier of official action (payment, building, judgment, offering), showing neither settled disposition nor transient emotional response; the register is administrative, not affective.

834.text: Consistent across every context -- no felt-quality or emotional coloring is ever attached; the term remains a flat administrative manner-adverb whether describing payment, building, decree-execution, or judgment.

835.text: The mode of operation shifts by domain even while the grammatical form stays constant: financial completeness (6.8, 'in full without delay'), decree-compliance formula (6.12, 7.21, 6.13, 'with all diligence'), ongoing constructional labor (5.8, 'diligently'), judicial severity (7.26, 'strictly'), cultic purchase/offering (7.17), and temple-provisioning fullness averting wrath (7.23, H0149) -- the constitutional level is always the external act, but the specific administrative domain varies context by context.

836.text: Yes -- the characteristic consistently operates through a communicative/decree-based mode: it qualifies compliance with an explicit royal or divine decree ('I make a decree... let it be done with all diligence,' 6.12; 'I make a decree... let it be done with all diligence,' 7.21; 'whatever is decreed... let it be done in full,' 7.23) -- the diligence/fullness is always the response to a spoken/written command, never a self-originated act.

837.text: The evidence names no inner condition (fear, love, faith) under which the diligence takes hold rightly -- it is presented as a simple external response to a decree backed by royal or divine authority, with the threat of wrath (7.23) or judicial penalty (7.26) as the only motivational context given; whether any inner disposition accompanies compliance is not stated and would need adjacent narrative to establish.

840.text: The characteristic operates identically across relational distance -- it governs compliance between king and subject-officials (Persian kings to treasurers/governors, 6.8, 6.12, 6.13, 7.21, 7.26) and between God and priestly officiants (7.17, 7.23), showing no difference in mode whether the bond is political/hierarchical or covenantal/religious; the manner of compliance is the same regardless of the relational bond's nature.

841.text: It crosses covenantal boundaries -- H0629/H0149 appear in decrees issued by pagan Persian kings (Darius, Artaxerxes) enforcing compliance both for civil/administrative matters (payment, building) and for the covenant people's temple worship (offerings, judgment under 'the law of your God'), showing the diligence-formula is a shared administrative idiom usable by non-covenant authority even when the object of compliance is covenantal (temple provisioning).

844.text: Where the characteristic moves toward God (Ezra.7.17, buying and offering sacrifices 'with all diligence' at the altar of God's house; Ezra.7.23, complying 'in full' with what God has decreed to avoid his wrath), the inner posture required is submissive exactness before divine authority -- treating God's decree with the same unhesitating completeness demanded of a royal command, differing only in that the consequence invoked is divine wrath rather than royal penalty.

845.text: The human-to-God direction (7.17, 7.23) shows a relationship of subordination under decree -- the person relates to God as a subject relates to a sovereign, owing exact and complete compliance to avoid wrath, a relationship framed in legal/administrative terms rather than intimate or covenantal-love terms.

846.text: No aspect of divine likeness is clearly instantiated -- the characteristic is administrative compliance directed toward God as sovereign decree-giver, not a shared attribute reflecting God's own nature (unlike, say, mercy or faithfulness); the evidence does not indicate God himself is 'diligent' in the same sense, so no likeness-aspect can be confidently named from this subgroup alone.

847.text: The characteristic reads as an exclusively creaturely administrative response -- it names how a subordinate party executes a superior's decree (whether royal or divine); nothing in the evidence attributes 'diligence' as an action or attribute of God himself, so it functions as a one-directional creaturely compliance-term rather than a shared quality.

849.text: No constitutional level (spirit/soul/body) is engaged by the evidence at all -- the terms describe external administrative acts (paying, building, executing, buying/offering) with no reference to inner faculties, so no body-link or depth/seat pattern can be drawn.

851.text: No movement across constitutional levels or from an external spirit is shown -- the characteristic moves entirely at the level of external administrative behavior, originating from a decree (spoken/written command) and terminating in an external act of compliance, with no mention of internal transmission through spirit, soul, or body. Record none for internal movement.

852.text: Where God is the reference point (7.23, whatever is decreed by the God of heaven), the basis is conditional/responsive -- full compliance is required precisely to avert God's wrath against the realm, framing the extension of diligence-worthy provision as a response demanded by, and contingent on, God's decree rather than an unconditional gift.

853.text: God's decree demanding full compliance 'lest his wrath be against the realm' (7.23) shows a disposition of jealous insistence on exact obedience regarding his house -- God is portrayed as one whose favor toward the realm depends on thorough compliance with what he has decreed for his temple, a disposition of conditional protection tied to reverent exactness.

859.text: No angelic ministry is mentioned in connection with the characteristic in any occurrence -- the mediating authority throughout is exclusively human/royal decree or divine decree, not angelic mediation.

860.text: The origin is consistently single across all contexts -- a decree issued by an authority (Persian king or God) always precedes and generates the demand for diligent/full compliance; the origin does not multiply or shift in kind, though the issuing authority alternates between king (6.8, 6.12, 6.13, 7.21, 7.26) and God (7.17, 7.23).

861.text: The characteristic engages no inner faculties (mind, will, emotion, conscience) at all across every occurrence -- its consistent non-engagement with any inward faculty indicates the characteristic's nature is purely behavioral-administrative, a manner-of-execution term rather than a faculty-based inner-being phenomenon.

862.text: The characteristic is best classified as a quality/manner of an act -- it describes HOW an action is performed (completely, exactly, without delay), not an act itself, nor a disposition, condition, or status of the person; it is an adverbial qualifier attached to acts of official compliance.

863.text: Simple in structure -- both H0629 and H0149 are single unanalyzed adverbs with no compound constituent elements; they intensify a verb directly without combining separate inner-being components.

865.text: The characteristic excludes at its edge any partiality, delay, or shortfall in carrying out the commanded task -- 'in full and without delay' (6.8) and 'full' compliance to avert wrath (7.23) both mark the boundary against half-measures or procrastination in execution.

866.text: The characteristic ends where mere willingness or intention begins without completed action -- it is not the decision to comply, nor the emotional zeal behind compliance, but strictly the exactness and completeness of the executed deed; it is not a disposition of the heart (no such language occurs) but the observable thoroughness of an outward act.

867.text: The characteristic consistently co-occurs with decree/authority vocabulary (H4430 king, H5648 done/executed) and with terms for royal or divine wrath/judgment (H7109 wrath in 7.23; judicial penalty terms in 7.26) -- these adjacent characteristics of authority and consequence appear in nearly every occurrence, showing the diligence-term is never isolated but always framed by a command-and-consequence structure.

868.text: The consistent co-occurrence with authority/decree and consequence terms shows this characteristic occupies a dependent, response-position in the inner-being landscape -- it never stands alone as a self-generated virtue but always as the required manner of answering a command, situating it structurally downstream of authority rather than upstream as a source of action.

869.text: The characteristic consistently follows a decree/command in sequence -- in every occurrence a decree is issued first ('I make a decree...', 'whatever is decreed...') and the diligence/fullness term describes the response that follows; the sequence is always command-then-compliance, never the reverse.

870.text: The command-then-compliance sequence is causal, not merely developmental or correlational -- the decree is explicitly the cause requiring the response (e.g., 7.23's 'lest his wrath be against the realm' makes compliance the necessary effect averting a stated consequence), showing a direct cause-and-required-effect relationship rather than a loose association.

871.text: The characteristic produces prospering/completed work as its outcome -- in Ezra.5.8, diligent labor is directly paired with 'prospers' (H6744), showing the mechanism whereby thorough execution issues in successful outcome; in 7.23, full compliance produces averted wrath, the negative-outcome mechanism.

872.text: The characteristic is produced by an issued decree/command -- it does not arise spontaneously but is generated as the required response to an authoritative order (royal decree in 6.12/6.13/7.21/7.26; divine decree in 7.17/7.23).

874.text: H0629 and H0149 most closely resemble each other within the same subgroup, both denoting exact/complete compliance with a decree; what distinguishes them is register and breadth -- H0629 spans financial, constructional, judicial, and cultic domains across seven occurrences, while H0149's single occurrence is narrowly tied to the wrath-avoidance clause of temple provisioning (per char_reading_observations' difference-inference).

875.text: The overlap between H0629 and H0149 is total in core meaning (both = complete/exact execution) but the boundary is rhetorical framing: H0629's occurrences are framed as positive compliance-formulas within routine administration, while H0149's sole occurrence is framed specifically as the condition averting divine wrath -- the boundary lies in consequence-framing (routine vs. wrath-preventive), not in denotation.

876.text: The distinction between H0629 and H0149 is one of degree/frequency and rhetorical emphasis, not kind, direction, or constitutional level -- both terms occupy the identical semantic and grammatical niche (adverb of manner intensifying compliance-verbs), differing only in how widely attested and how gravely-framed each occurrence is.

890.text: In Ps.76.10 the surface gloss 'praise' for H3034 diverges notably: the subject is 'the wrath of man,' meaning even hostile human anger is said to 'give praise/thanks' to God -- an ironic/forced usage where the verb's normal voluntary-gratitude sense is applied to an involuntary or even adversarial subject, showing God's sovereignty co-opting wrath itself into praise. This impact is distinct from Isa.12.1 and 2Chr.7.3 where the subject freely and willingly gives thanks.

891.text: In Isa.12.1 and 2Chr.7.3 the occurrence of H3034 sits squarely within the base Hiphil gloss 'give thanks/praise' with no notable divergence -- straightforward covenantal/liturgical thanksgiving directed to the Lord.

892.text: In Isa.12.1, thanksgiving (H3034) is directly bound to M02 (anger, H0599/H0639G) and M11/M81 (turning away, H7725I) and M11/M45 (comfort, H5162G): the thanksgiving is explicitly the response TO God's anger having turned and to his comforting action -- thanksgiving here functions as the verbal capstone/response completing the arc from divine anger through reversal to comfort. No prior context exists for this verse; this is the first pass.

894.text: In Ps.76.10, thanksgiving/praise (H3034) co-occurs with M02 (wrath, H2534, twice) -- here the relation is paradoxical: wrath itself is made an instrument that results in praise to God, showing this characteristic's capacity to be produced even from an antagonistic characteristic rather than only from benevolent ones. No prior context exists for this verse; this is the first pass.

1184.text: The verse's operation-tagged word is H7725I (turn away, role-T3), initiated by God's anger (subject) turning away from the speaker (object/beneficiary). H3034 itself (thanks) is not tagged role-T3 in this verse's role list (it carries only M49), so no D7.7.1 relation is recorded for H3034 as an operation-word; it is the responsive speech-act, not the operation.

1190.text: Isa.12.1 uses the Hiphil 'I will give thanks' in its standard sense of praising/thanking God directly in response to his reversed anger and comfort; this sits squarely within the base Hiphil gloss (to give thanks, laud, praise) with no notable divergence from the term's ordinary usage.

1199.text: Building on the prior finding (thanksgiving as capstone response to anger-turned-comfort): from thanksgiving's own vantage, this occurrence shows the characteristic functioning prospectively as well -- 'you will say... I will give thanks' -- meaning the thanksgiving is anticipated and rehearsed as the fitting future speech-act that will properly name and close the sequence of divine anger (M02) and comfort (M11/M45), underscoring that thanksgiving is the verbal seal that completes, not merely accompanies, the relational reversal.

1208.text: This occurrence renders H3034 as 'praise' (of God) but with an unusual subject -- 'the wrath of man' -- personified as the one who 'shall praise' God, meaning even hostile human passion is made to serve/testify to God's sovereignty. This is a notable divergence from the base gloss's typical human-subject-thanking-God pattern: here an abstract, antagonistic force is cast as the grammatical agent of praise, a paradox not seen in the other occurrences in this batch (Isa.12.1, 2Chr.7.3, etc.) where the human worshiper directly and willingly gives thanks.

1209.text: Building on the prior finding (wrath as instrument producing praise): from thanksgiving's own vantage, this shows the characteristic's remarkable scope -- it can be generated even by M02 (wrath) as raw material, meaning praise/thanksgiving here functions not merely as a response to benevolence but as the outcome God sovereignly extracts even from opposition, positioning thanksgiving as the ultimate telos to which even hostile forces are subordinated.

1587.text: In Isa.12.1 the Hiphil form 'I will give thanks' sits squarely within the base gloss of praise/thanksgiving directed at God for reversal of anger into comfort -- no divergent nuance beyond the standard Hiphil sense of giving thanks.

1589.text: In Ps.76.10 the Hiphil 'shall praise' carries a striking contextual nuance: the subject producing the praise is 'the wrath of man', an unusual and almost paradoxical subject for this verb which elsewhere is nearly always used of righteous or penitent human/divine praise; the impact here is that praise is depicted as forcibly extracted even from hostile human wrath, a notable divergence from its typical voluntary, devotional usage elsewhere (e.g. Isa.12.1, 2Chr.7.3).

1597.text: Building on the prior finding (thanksgiving as capstone response completing the arc of anger-turned-comfort): from thanksgiving's own vantage in Isa.12.1, the future tense framing ('you will say... I will give thanks') shows thanksgiving is rehearsed prospectively as the fitting verbal seal awaiting the full resolution of M02 (anger) into M11/M45 (comfort), making it dependent on and subsequent to those characteristics' resolution rather than co-equal or independent.

1599.text: Building on the prior finding (wrath as instrument producing praise): from thanksgiving's own vantage in Ps.76.10, the repetition of M02 (wrath) both as subject producing praise and as 'remnant of wrath' worn like a belt shows thanksgiving here is not merely triggered by wrath but actively subordinates and repurposes it -- wrath becomes raw material converted into the praise-characteristic's own output, illustrating thanksgiving's capacity to govern even hostile forces as tribute.

1600.text: In Isa.12.1 the role-T3 operation 'turned away' (H7725I) is directed by the Lord (party, T7/T10) as the initiator, moving away from the speaker (also tagged as recipient party via suffix); H3034 (thanksgiving) is itself the responsive speech-act anticipated once this operation completes, not itself the operation but its named consequence.

1602.text: In Ps.76.10 the wrath of man (party-adjacent, T8 'man') is the notional initiator of the praise directed toward 'you' (the Lord, addressee); the operation-tagged 'belt' (H2296, T3) is a separate action initiated by the Lord directed toward the remnant of wrath, distinct from the praise clause itself.

3200.text: Across this pass's occurrences the core Hiphil imperative/perfect/participle sense 'give thanks/praise' recurs as the dominant pattern in liturgical contexts: Isa.12.1, 2Chr.30.22, 2Chr.7.6, 2Chr.20.21, 2Chr.31.2, Ezra.3.11, Neh.12.24, Ps.109.30, Isa.12.4, Jer.33.11, Ps.7.17, 1Chr.16.4, 1Chr.29.13, Ps.35.18, Ps.118.21, Ps.52.9, Ps.107.8/15/21/31, Ps.100.4, Ps.136.1/2/3/26, Ps.33.2, 2Chr.5.13, 1Chr.16.7, Neh.12.46, Ps.138.4, Ps.138.1, 2Chr.7.3, 1Chr.23.30, 1Chr.25.3, Ps.142.7, Neh.11.17 -- all render the same basic act of vocal, often corporate/musical, thanksgiving directed at the Lord, frequently anchored by the refrain 'his steadfast love endures forever.'

3209.text: Across the verses the characteristic mostly follows a prior belief/perception (e.g. Isa.12.1 thanksgiving follows perceiving anger turned to comfort; Ps.28.7 thanksgiving follows trust/help already experienced; Lev.5.5 confession follows 'realizes his guilt'), but in some cases it also functions prospectively, rehearsing or anticipating a settled conviction (Isa.12.1's future tense 'I will give thanks'), so the pattern is both -- overwhelmingly following, occasionally anticipating.

3212.text: The immediate response is varied: in some verses it is instantaneous verbal outburst upon witnessing a divine act (2Chr.7.3, corporate falling and worship at the descent of glory), in others it is a settled, calm vow rehearsed ahead of time (Isa.12.1, future tense), and in still others it is wrenched from an unwilling/hostile subject (Ps.76.10, wrath praising) -- showing the immediate response is not uniform across contexts.

3221.text: The mode of operation varies by context: in temple/liturgical contexts it operates communally and musically (2Chr.5.13, with trumpets and cymbals); in personal-devotional contexts it operates as individual first-person speech (Ps.9.1, Ps.86.12); in penitential contexts it operates as a required, sometimes silent/ritual act laid upon an object (Lev.16.21, confession spoken over the scapegoat) -- direction also varies, being human-to-God in nearly all cases but occasionally human-to-human (Gen.49.8, brothers praising Judah) or even forced from an antagonistic source (Ps.76.10, wrath praising God).

3229.text: The relational scope includes the covenant community (Israel, Levites, kings), the wider nations/peoples (hoped-for or commanded to join), and even hostile or non-agentive subjects rhetorically co-opted (wrath of man, Ps.76.10); explicitly excluded are the dead/Sheol, who structurally cannot participate (Isa.38.18, Ps.6.5, Ps.30.9, Ps.88.10) -- the scope is maximal among the living but categorically bounded by death.

3238.text: The characteristic moves in sequence from a triggering perception or divine act (deliverance, glory witnessed, guilt realized) through the heart/inner disposition to outward vocal/bodily expression: e.g. Lev.5.5 'when he realizes his guilt... and confesses' shows perception-to-speech movement; Isa.12.1 shows divine action (anger turning, comfort given) preceding and producing the human speech-act of thanksgiving -- the movement is consistently from perceived reality, through the inner person, and out into speech, never the reverse.

3245.text: No occurrence in this subgroup shows adversarial spiritual activity specifically targeting or interfering with the act of thanksgiving/confession itself; the closest adjacent material (wrath of man in Ps.76.10) concerns human hostility being co-opted into producing praise, not an adversarial spirit resisting the characteristic.

3247.text: The origin of the characteristic's occasion is multiple and does change with context: it originates from personal deliverance/answered prayer (Ps.118.21), from witnessing a corporate theophany (2Chr.7.3), from realized guilt (Lev.5.5), from institutional appointment (1Chr.16.4), and even from being wrenched out of hostile wrath (Ps.76.10) -- the triggering origin is not single but varies by narrative context, though the responsive act itself (H3034) remains constant.

3259.text: Yes, this characteristic is itself produced by prior realities: by God's prior acts of deliverance, comfort, or steadfast love (Isa.12.1, Ps.28.7), by witnessing divine glory (2Chr.7.3), or by realization of guilt (Lev.5.5) -- praise/confession is consistently the produced/responsive term, not the originating one.

3376.text: In Zeph.2.3 all three occurrences of baqash sit squarely within the base gloss 'seek' (the Lord, righteousness, humility) with no surface divergence -- straightforward imperative use.

3377.text: In Esth.7.7 baqash surfaces as 'beg' rather than the more neutral 'seek' -- context (Haman pleading for his life before Esther) intensifies the base gloss into desperate supplication; this is a stronger nuance than the everyday 'seek' sense used elsewhere (e.g. 1Kgs.1.2's practical search for a young woman).

3378.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in Zeph.2.3 alongside baqash (the co-occurring M12 righteousness and M05 humility terms are the OBJECTS sought, not separate characteristics of the seeker in this verse's role tagging) -- baqash stands as the operative seeking-act relating to those pursued qualities.

3379.text: In Ezra.8.22 other M-codes are present (M07 shame, M23 power, M02 wrath) but none bears a direct dependency relation to the seeking-act itself within this verse's syntax; baqash names the condition under which God's hand is described as good.

3380.text: In Esth.7.7 other M-codes present (M08/M74 arose, M02 wrath, M47 life, M24/M58 harm) describe the king's rage and Haman's peril but do not structurally interact with the begging-act itself beyond providing its narrative motive.

3382.text: In Ezra.8.22, seeking (baqash) is directed by 'all who seek him' (worshippers, generic party) toward God (party H0430G), contrasted with those who forsake him -- the operation runs from human party toward the divine party as its object.

3383.text: In Zeph.2.3, the seeking operation is initiated by 'the humble of the land' (addressed party) and directed toward the Lord, and secondarily toward righteousness and humility as sought qualities.

3384.text: In Esth.7.7, the begging operation is initiated by Haman (party) and directed toward Queen Esther (party), seeking his life as the object at stake.

3400.text: In 2Kgs.22.13 and 2Chr.34.21 darash surfaces as 'inquire' matching the base gloss squarely (formal royal command to consult the Lord via a prophet) -- no notable divergence from typical usage.

3401.text: In 2Chr.25.15, other M-codes present (M02 anger, M43 prophet, M45 deliver) frame the narrative context (the Lord's anger, sending a prophet) but do not structurally modify the seeking-act itself; darash here names Amaziah's culpable act of seeking foreign gods, the object of divine anger.

3404.text: In 2Kgs.22.13, other M-codes present (M65 words, M41 obeyed) describe the covenant document and the fathers' disobedience; darash's own consultation-act is the king's response to that disobedience being uncovered, not structurally altered by those terms.

3405.text: In 2Chr.34.21, other M-codes present (M65 words, M74 kept) parallel 2Kgs.22.13's pattern; darash's consultation-act responds to the fathers' failure to keep the word, but the terms remain independently tagged rather than modifying the seeking-act.

3406.text: In 2Chr.25.15, the seeking operation is initiated by Amaziah (party) directed toward foreign gods (party/object), the very act that provokes the Lord's anger.

3407.text: In 2Kgs.22.13, the inquiring operation is initiated by the king's officials (commanded party) directed toward the Lord (party) concerning the newly found book.

3408.text: In 2Chr.34.21, the inquiring operation is initiated by the king's officials (commanded party) directed toward the Lord (party), parallel to 2Kgs.22.13.

3460.text: In Lev.10.16 the doubled construction ('diligently inquired') intensifies the base sense of investigation but does not shift its meaning beyond the term's ordinary procedural-inquiry sense; in Ps.77.2 the term sits within its standard devotional-seeking sense (seeking the Lord in trouble). Neither occurrence diverges from the base gloss.

3461.text: In Lev.10.16 the other M-code present is M56 (sin offering) and M02 (anger); H1875's inquiry is what triggers the discovery that the sin offering was mishandled, provoking the anger -- H1875 functions as the investigative act that surfaces the occasion for M02's anger, though it does not itself embody either characteristic.

3476.text: In Esth.2.21, 1Sam.24.9, Num.35.23, and 1Kgs.20.7 the surface sense shifts from the base gloss 'seek/desire' toward a conspiratorial/hostile sense 'to plot against, seek to harm/kill' -- a marked negative-valence divergence from the neutral-to-positive base gloss. By contrast in 2Chr.15.4 the surface sense aligns with the base devotional gloss (seeking God). This shows the same lexeme's stepGloss splits sharply by direction of the object across these occurrences.

3478.text: Esth.2.21: the operation-tagged word 'lay' (H7971K, role-T3) co-occurs with party-tagged 'hands' (H3027G) and 'King' (H4428G); the conspirators (Bigthan and Teresh, having 'sought'/H1245) initiate the operation of laying hands, directed at King Ahasuerus.

3481.text: In Esth.2.21, M02 (angry) precedes and motivates H1245's plotting-seeking; the anger of the eunuchs is the disposition, the seeking is the resultant hostile operation directed at the king -- H1245 supplies the active pursuit-phase that M02's anger sets in motion.

5370.text: Eccl 7:25's 'seek' (wisdom) is the standard intellectual-pursuit sense of baqash, well within its base gloss; no notable divergence.

5374.text: In Eccl 7:25, baqash (seeking wisdom) co-occurs with M16 (wisdom/folly terms), M43 (scheme/devices), M58 (wickedness), M66 (madness) and M15 (knowing). This characteristic's vantage: seeking is the METHOD by which the Preacher pursues and tests wisdom and folly — it is the investigative operation binding the other M-codes together as objects of inquiry rather than being one of them itself.

7073.text: Across this pass's 'inquire' surface-form cluster (1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.18.7, 2Kgs.22.13/2Chr.34.21, 2Kgs.3.11, 2Kgs.1.2/1.3/1.6/1.16, 2Kgs.8.8, 1Kgs.14.5, Ezek.20.3, 1Sam.28.7, Jer.10.21, Gen.25.22, Exod.18.15, Deut.12.30, 1Sam.9.9, 1Kgs.22.7/2Chr.18.6, 2Kgs.22.18/2Chr.34.26, Isa.8.19, Jer.37.7, 2Chr.32.31, Isa.19.3, Zeph.1.6, Isa.11.10, Ezek.20.1, 1Chr.21.30, Isa.9.13) the term consistently denotes formal consultation of a deity or authoritative source (the Lord, a prophet, an oracle, Baal-zebub, mediums/necromancers) for a verdict or answer -- the single largest and most cohesive sense-cluster in H1875's full occurrence set, matching this subgroup's core description of institutional/cultic resort to authority for guidance.

7076.text: The 'inquired'/'seeking'/'searched' occurrences in this pass show the root's outer boundary away from formal cultic consultation: Lev.10.16 (procedural cultic checking of a sacrifice), 2Sam.11.3 (mundane social inquiry about a woman's identity), Jer.38.4/2Chr.31.21 (civic/devotional 'seeking welfare' or 'seeking God' as ongoing disposition), Ps.109.10 (destitute foraging for food), Ezek.34.8 (pastoral searching for lost sheep), and Judg.6.29 (forensic investigation of who committed a deed) -- these occurrences share the base sense of careful, purposeful inquiry but apply it to secular, pastoral, or forensic objects rather than deity/oracle consultation, showing the root's flexibility extends the subgroup's core 'formal consultation' sense outward to any object warranting diligent investigation.

7094.text: Lev.10.16's 'diligently' renders the Qal infinitive absolute intensifying construction, showing darash used adverbially/idiomatically ('diligently inquired') to intensify the base investigative sense rather than introducing a new meaning -- an intensification-of-manner pattern paralleled by Deut.23.21's 'surely require'.

7273.text: In 2Chr.25.15 Amaziah's seeking of the gods of Edom reveals a mistaken belief that defeated foreign gods retain power worth consulting, a judgement the prophet exposes as irrational ('who did not deliver their own people').

7277.text: The immediate response to seeking is varied across contexts: it produces answer/deliverance (Ps.34.4), peace (2Chr.14.7), prospering (2Chr.26.5), being found (Jer.29.13), but also, when directed at illegitimate objects, provokes divine anger (2Chr.25.15) or judgment ('come to nothing', Amos.5.5). The response is consistently proportionate to the legitimacy of the object sought, not uniform in kind.

7287.text: Yes, darash regularly operates through speech: it is commanded imperatively ('Inquire first for the word of the Lord', 1Kgs.22.5; 'Seek the Lord and live', Amos.5.4/6/14), addressed as divine self-disclosure ('I will not be inquired of by you', Ezek.20.3), and enacted as spoken request to a prophet or oracle (2Kgs.22.13 'Go, inquire of the Lord for me'). The act of seeking is frequently voiced as command, plea, or reported speech rather than silent internal disposition alone.

10537.text: As accusative noun 'earnestness' (N-ASF), this occurrence names the intense exertion/attentiveness the Corinthians displayed as a direct effect of their godly grief.

10538.text: Here spoude denotes earnest application/diligence produced in the Corinthians -- not mere haste but eager effort applied toward making things right.

10539.text: As the first item in the list of effects 'produced' by godly grief, this earnestness is constitutionally the root/summary result from which the following items (eagerness, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, punishment) branch.

10540.text: Rooted in speudo 'to hasten/exert effort', spoude here operates as concentrated moral energy directed at correcting the situation the grief exposed.

10541.text: As an accusative singular feminine noun (N-ASF), it functions as the direct object of 'produced', naming a concrete result/quality generated in the hearers rather than an action itself.

10542.text: Within the range from mere 'haste' to 'zealous exertion/diligence', this occurrence sits at the diligence/earnestness end, heading a list of intensified responses to grief.

10543.text: This occurrence expresses a produced act/disposition -- earnestness that came about as a result, not a received or static condition.

10544.text: No structural opposite term for spoude (e.g. sloth/negligence) is present among related terms in this verse's list of effects.

10545.text: No person-type term (e.g. 'one who is diligent') for spoude appears among related terms in this verse.

10546.text: No supplication/seeking-term for spoude is present in this verse's list of related items.

10547.text: As a NT Greek term in Paul's own letter, spoude here carries its classical Greek sense of earnest effort intact; the NT context adds the specifically moral/repentance framing but doesn't alter the base meaning.

10548.text: Spoude is attested since Homer and classical prose (Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato) well before the NT; not a NT coinage.

10549.text: The passive infinitive form (V-APN, 'grief'/to-be-grieved) shows this term names the state of being pained/distressed that the letter caused in its readers.

10550.text: Here lupeo denotes being caused sorrow/distress -- specifically the 'godly grief' (kata theon) that Paul's earlier letter provoked, now shown bearing good fruit.

10551.text: As the qualified head-term ('godly grief'), it functions as the causal source from which the entire following chain of effects (earnestness, eagerness, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, punishment) is said to flow.

10552.text: Rooted in causing pain/vexation (lupe), the term here operates as an experienced, sorrow-inducing state rather than the act of inflicting it.

10553.text: Rendered here substantivally as 'grief' (an infinitive of result/aorist passive), the occurrence sits between the general 'cause sorrow' sense and the specific technical 2 Corinthians usage of 'grief that leads to repentance' -- both readings are supported by the surrounding qualifier 'godly'.

10554.text: The aorist passive infinitive form (V-APN) shows the grief as something undergone/received by the Corinthians, completed as a single past event whose effects are now being surveyed.

10555.text: Within the range from causing pain to being distressed, this occurrence sits at the 'being grieved/pained' pole, qualified as 'godly' to mark it as productive rather than destructive sorrow.

10556.text: This occurrence expresses a received condition -- grief that was experienced/undergone -- rather than a disposition or act performed by the subject.

10557.text: No structural opposite term (e.g. joy/comfort) for lupe/lupeo is present among related terms in this verse's list.

10558.text: No person-type term (e.g. 'a grieving person') is present among related terms in this verse.

10559.text: No supplication/seeking-term for grief is present among the related terms in this verse.

10560.text: As NT Greek, lupeo here is used within Paul's distinctly Christian theological framework (grief 'according to God' vs worldly grief), a nuance not present in classical usage of the verb for ordinary pain/vexation.

10561.text: Lupeo is attested from Hesiod and classical authors onward (Sophocles, Herodotus, Plato); not a NT coinage.

10562.text: As accusative noun (N-ASF), 'indignation' names a specific inner reaction of righteous vexation the Corinthians felt toward the wrong reported to them.

10563.text: Here aganaktesis denotes vexation/indignation -- a strong negative emotional response provoked by awareness of wrongdoing, listed among the fruits of godly grief.

10564.text: As one item in the rhetorical catalogue of effects, indignation is directional -- reacting against the offense itself, distinct from fear (directed at consequence) or longing (directed toward reconciliation).

10565.text: Root sense of vexation/physical-then-emotional irritation shows the term operating here as an intensified negative reaction against the wrong committed.

10566.text: This is the term's sole NT occurrence, but its sense here (vexation/indignation) matches ordinary classical usage (e.g. Thucydides' 'vexation'); no special divergence.

10567.text: As an accusative singular feminine noun, it functions as one of the parallel direct objects governed by 'what', naming a discrete emotional outcome rather than an ongoing action.

10568.text: Within the range from physical irritation to divine wrath, this occurrence sits at the human 'vexation at wrongdoing' point in the range, fitting the moral context of the letter.

10569.text: This occurrence expresses an act/reaction produced in the hearers -- indignation as one of the specific outcomes of the grief, not a settled disposition or received quality.

10570.text: No structural opposite term (e.g. complacency/apathy) for aganaktesis is present among the related terms listed in this verse.

10571.text: No person-type term for one who habitually feels indignation is present among related terms in this verse.

10572.text: No supplication/seeking-term for indignation is present among related terms in this verse.

10573.text: As a NT Greek hapax in Paul, the term carries over its classical secular sense of vexation without added theological freight of its own, though the surrounding context moralizes it as a righteous response.

10574.text: Aganaktesis is attested pre-NT in Plato and Thucydides ('vexation'); not a NT coinage, though this is its only NT occurrence.

10575.text: As accusative noun (N-ASM), 'fear' here names the trembling concern the Corinthians felt regarding the seriousness of the offense and its correction.

10576.text: Here phobos denotes trembling concern/apprehension -- a felt anxiety about consequences that motivated the Corinthians' corrective response, matching the sense used again in v.15.

10577.text: As one item among the produced reactions, fear here is directional -- oriented toward the seriousness of the matter and the possible relational rupture with Paul, driving urgency to make things right.

10578.text: Root sense tied to panic/dread shows the term operating here in its milder, moralized 'trembling concern' register rather than sheer terror.

10579.text: This occurrence's sense (trembling concern about the matter) matches its use in the very next verse (7:15) and other Pauline uses in this letter; no divergence.

10580.text: As an accusative singular masculine noun, it stands as one of the parallel objects in the list, naming a discrete emotional/moral outcome of the grief.

10581.text: Within the range from panic-terror to reverential awe, this occurrence sits at the 'trembling concern' point, appropriate to a moral/relational crisis rather than physical danger.

10582.text: This occurrence expresses a produced act/reaction -- fear as one specific outcome generated by the grief -- rather than an abiding disposition.

10583.text: No structural opposite term (e.g. boldness/confidence) for phobos is present among the related terms listed in this verse.

10584.text: No person-type term for a fearful/reverent person is present among related terms in this verse.

10585.text: No supplication/seeking-term for fear is present among related terms in this verse.

10586.text: As NT Greek, phobos here carries the same range attested in classical usage; the moral/relational Christian context specifies fear-of-consequence-for-sin rather than altering the base lexical sense.

10587.text: Phobos is attested from Homer onward across classical Greek literature; not a NT coinage.

10588.text: As accusative noun (N-ASF), 'longing' names an earnest desire/strong affection produced in the Corinthians -- toward renewed relationship with Paul.

10589.text: Here epipothesis denotes earnest desire/strong affection -- a yearning quality, paired with its cognate use in 7:7 describing the Corinthians' longing for Paul.

10590.text: As one produced effect in the list, longing is relationally directional -- oriented toward restored fellowship/reconciliation with Paul, distinct from indignation's orientation against the wrong itself.

10591.text: Root sense 'longing after' shows the term operating here as strong affectionate desire directed at restoring the relationship.

10592.text: This occurrence's sense (earnest longing/affection) matches its only other NT use at 7:7 in the same letter; no divergence.

10593.text: As an accusative singular feminine noun paralleling the other listed objects, it names a discrete affective outcome rather than a verbal action.

10594.text: Within a narrow semantic range essentially limited to 'earnest desire/longing', this occurrence sits centrally, showing the relational-affection sense of the term.

10595.text: This occurrence expresses a produced act/disposition -- a longing generated by the grief, oriented toward restoring the relationship, not a received condition.

10596.text: No structural opposite term (e.g. indifference/aversion) for epipothesis is present among related terms in this verse.

10597.text: No person-type term for one characterized by longing is present among related terms in this verse.

10598.text: No supplication/seeking-term distinct from the longing itself is present among related terms in this verse.

10599.text: As NT Greek, epipothesis appears only in this Pauline letter and carries no distinct OT/Hebrew background to weigh against; its sense is drawn directly from Paul's own usage.

10600.text: LSJ cites epipothesis only in NT (2 Cor 7:7, 7:11) and later authors (Aquila, Damascius); it has no earlier classical attestation, marking it as effectively a NT-period term.

10601.text: As accusative noun (N-ASM), 'zeal' names the fervent, ardent commitment the Corinthians displayed in support of Paul and against the wrong.

10602.text: Here zelos denotes ardent affection/enthusiasm in the good sense -- earnest concern for the right outcome, distinct from its bad-sense use elsewhere (jealousy/envy).

10603.text: As a produced effect near the climax of the list, zeal is directional -- fervent energy channeled toward vindicating Paul and resolving the offense, just before 'punishment' names the corrective outcome.

10604.text: Root sense of intense rivalry/fervour shows the term operating here as positive, ardent commitment rather than the jealousy/envy sense the same root can carry.

10605.text: Zelos can mean jealousy/envy in a bad sense elsewhere (Acts 13:45; Rom 13:13), but this occurrence's surface use as a positive fruit of godly grief renders it as commendable zeal/ardor, aligning with its good-sense use in Jn 2:17 and Rom 10:2 rather than the negative pole.

10606.text: As an accusative singular masculine noun in the list, it names a discrete produced quality/reaction, in parallel with the other objects governed by 'what'.

10607.text: Within a range spanning jealousy/rivalry to fervent zeal/enthusiasm, this occurrence sits at the positive fervent-commitment end, matching the good-sense usage seen in Jn 2:17.

10608.text: This occurrence expresses a produced act/disposition -- ardent zeal generated as a fruit of the grief, not a received or static quality.

10609.text: Zelos itself can function as its own structural opposite depending on sense (bad-sense jealousy vs good-sense ardor); here the positive pole is meant, standing against the jealousy/envy pole attested elsewhere for the same term.

10610.text: No distinct person-type term (e.g. 'zealot') for one who possesses zelos is present among related terms in this verse.

10611.text: No supplication/seeking-term for zeal is present among related terms in this verse.

10612.text: As NT Greek, zelos here draws on the classical eager-rivalry sense but is disambiguated by context toward the positive fervor sense rather than the jealousy sense also live in NT usage.

10613.text: Zelos is attested from Hesiod and classical Greek (Sophocles, Plato, Demosthenes) long before the NT; not a NT coinage.

10614.text: As accusative noun (N-ASF), 'punishment' names the readiness to see justice/retribution enacted against the wrongdoer, capping the list of produced effects.

10615.text: Here ekdikesis denotes vengeance/retributive justice/punishment -- the Corinthians' willingness to see the offender justly dealt with, matching its use elsewhere for vindication/retribution.

10616.text: As the final and most extreme item in the list, punishment is directional toward the offender -- the corrective, justice-restoring culmination of the whole chain of reactions.

10617.text: Root sense 'avenging/giving satisfaction' shows the term operating here as the community's readiness to see the matter set right through corrective justice.

10618.text: This occurrence's sense (retributive justice/punishment) matches its ordinary NT usage (Luke 21:22; Rom 12:19; 1 Pet 2:14); no divergence.

10619.text: As an accusative singular feminine noun, the final item in the parallel list of objects, it names the outcome-oriented disposition to see justice done rather than an action performed by the subject.

10620.text: Within a range from legal remedy/satisfaction to divine vengeance, this occurrence sits at the community-justice pole -- willingness to see the wrong punished within the church body.

10621.text: This occurrence expresses a produced disposition -- readiness for corrective justice generated as a fruit of the grief, not an act already carried out.

10622.text: No structural opposite term (e.g. mercy/pardon) for ekdikesis is present among related terms in this verse.

10623.text: No person-type term (e.g. avenger) for ekdikesis is present among related terms in this verse.

10624.text: No supplication/seeking-term for punishment is present among related terms in this verse.

10625.text: As NT Greek, ekdikesis here follows the sense already visible in the LSJ's cited NT usages (Luke, Acts) of legal/corrective satisfaction; the Testament context doesn't shift the sense further in this verse.

10626.text: Ekdikesis is attested pre-NT in Polybius (2nd c. BC) for 'giving satisfaction'; not a NT coinage.

10627.text: As accusative plural adjective (A-APM), 'innocent' describes the Corinthians themselves as proved pure/blameless in the matter, the outcome of the whole process described.

10628.text: Here hagnos denotes moral purity/blamelessness -- the state the Corinthians have proven themselves to be in regarding the offense, following their godly-grief-driven response.

10629.text: As the concluding predicate adjective applied to the Corinthians, it constitutes the verse's final verdict -- the whole chain of reactions is shown to have vindicated them as pure in the matter.

10630.text: Root sense of ritual/moral purity shows the term operating here as declared moral blamelessness, established through the community's corrective response.

10631.text: This occurrence's sense (morally pure/blameless/innocent) matches the term's usual NT ethical usage; no divergence.

10632.text: As an accusative plural adjective modifying 'yourselves', it functions predicatively, ascribing the quality of innocence to the Corinthians as the proven result of the proceeding events.

10633.text: Within a range from cultic/ritual purity to general moral uprightness, this occurrence sits at the ethical-innocence end, describing exoneration from complicity in the wrongdoing.

10634.text: This occurrence expresses a proven quality/condition (innocence established), not an act or a received quality bestowed from elsewhere.

10635.text: No structural opposite term (e.g. guilt/defilement) for hagnos is present among related terms in this verse.

10636.text: No person-type term for one who habitually possesses hagnos-purity is present among related terms in this verse.

10637.text: No supplication/seeking-term for purity/innocence is present among related terms in this verse.

10638.text: As NT Greek, hagnos here carries forward the classical sense of purity/chastity but is applied ethically to communal innocence in a dispute, a specifically Pauline moral extension rather than the cultic/ritual purity common in classical usage.

10639.text: Hagnos is attested from Homer onward (Odyssey, Pindar, Sophocles); not a NT coinage.

11470.text: As an adverb ('full'/exactly) modifying 'done', its form shows it names the manner of compliance rather than an independent quality of its own.

11472.text: Its adverbial force ties the king's decree directly to the standard God's house requires, implying total, unqualified obedience to avert wrath.

11473.text: Its root sense of exactness/diligence shows the command demands precise, careful execution, not a loose approximation.

11474.text: As an adverb, its grammatical form shows it modifies the verb 'done', specifying the manner of the decree's execution rather than naming an entity.

11475.text: This occurrence sits at the core diligence/exactness sense of the term's range, applied to compliance with a royal-divine decree.

11476.text: This occurrence expresses an act (how the decree is to be carried out) rather than a disposition or condition.

11477.text: No related term functioning as a structural opposite to this adverb of exactness is present in this verse.

11478.text: No person-type related term (one who habitually exercises exactness) is relevant to this occurrence.

11479.text: No supplication/seeking term related to this adverb is relevant here; the verse concerns compliance, not petition.

11480.text: As Aramaic administrative diction in a Persian royal decree, the OT context frames this exactness as compliance owed to both the king's authority and the God of heaven.

11484.text: The term implies a directional threat: divine anger directed against the realm and royal house as consequence of disobedience.

11485.text: Its root meaning of God's anger shows it operates here as a feared, avertable consequence contingent on obedience to the decree.

11486.text: Used in its standard sense of divine wrath, with no divergence from its usual meaning elsewhere.

Once the will is invited with if: "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land" (Isa 1:19).

12497.text: God's will, and the reason each verse gives: after intercession, "the Lord listened to me that time also. The Lord was unwilling to destroy you" (Deu 10:10); for a promise, "the Lord was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant" (2Ki 8:19), "because of the covenant that he had made with David" (2Ch 21:7); in grace, "the Lord was gracious to them and had compassion on them" "and would not destroy them" (2Ki 13:23); out of love, "the Lord your God would not listen to Balaam" "because the Lord your God loved you" (Deu 23:5; Jos 24:10). And against: "the Lord will not be willing to forgive him" (Deu 29:20), of the one who "blesses himself in his heart" (29:19); "he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the Lord would not pardon" (2Ki 24:4).

12521.text: The will word also carries wanting to know and stated wishes: "desiring to know the real reason" (Act 22:30; 23:28); "We wish to know therefore what these things mean" (Act 17:20); "I would like to hear the man myself" (Act 25:22); "I refuse to be a judge of these things" (Act 18:15). Paul's wishes in teaching each come with their reason: "I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1Ti 2:8); "So I would have younger widows marry" (1Ti 5:14); "I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works" (Tit 3:8); "I want you to know" (Phi 1:12); "so that our joy may be complete" (2Jo 12); "I want to remind you" (Jude 5).

12743.text: Face I. Not fearing (7 / 7 hits and verses; surfaces afraid · fear · feared · tremble): By faith not afraid; no fear of God; not trembling while blaspheming.

12746.text: Face P. Fear for another (4 / 4 hits and verses; surfaces afraid · fear): An apostle for a church; a tribune for a prisoner.

12748.text: Face T. Called for (10 / 8 hits and verses; surfaces Fear · fear · afraid): "Fear God"; "fear him"; "be afraid"; "fear lest"; "so that the rest may stand in fear".

12762.text: One's own conduct: a ruler is "a terror" to bad conduct; "respect" is owed; the same root.

12771.text: Fear and faith, set against each other by question.

12799.text: The root ḥûl, "to twist, whirl", is rendered as dance, whirl, storm: the daughters of Shiloh "dance in the dances" (Judg 21:21); "a whirling tempest" (Jer 23:19).

12814.text: Fear and M33 Rest & Peace: in 38 verses (20 within three words) the commonest near pairs are tremble + rest; fear + peace (Isa 7:4, Hab 3:16, Jer 30:10).

12815.text: Fear and M02 Anger & Wrath: in 35 verses (12 within three words) the commonest near pairs are Deu 9:19, Psa 90:11, Psa 88:16, Heb 11:27.

12840.text: H7264 rāgaz "to tremble" is rendered raging / raged / enraged (5): 2Ki 19:27–28, Isa 37:28–29, Eze 16:43.

12845.text: H7264 rāgaz "to tremble" is rendered quaked: 1Sa 14:15, Isa 5:25.

12862.text: H4867 is tagged M01 but the English renders another face: waves / breakers (2Sa 22:5, Psa 42:7, 88:7, 93:4).

12866.text: H6125 is tagged M01 but the English renders another face: oppression (Psa 55:3).

12867.text: H0367 is tagged M01 but the English renders another face: idols (Jer 50:38).

12872.text: Fear and anger meet in Psa 90:11: "the power of your anger ... your wrath according to the fear of you".

12874.text: "Long of nostrils": slow to anger is understanding, glory, better than the mighty; ruling one's spirit is better than taking a city.

12876.text: The inner word is often named in the other party, or in the contrast figure: the opponents' hardened heart (Mar 3:5); the builders' "mind to work" (Neh 4:6); "his heart is steady" (Psa 112:8); Daniel "resolved" (Dan 1:8); Stephen "full of the Holy Spirit" (Act 7:55).

12883.text: God's intent carried by his anger, understood afterwards.

12884.text: Nations rage and peoples plot, in one line.

12885.text: The sufferer feels God's reckoning as enmity ("counts me as his adversary").

12886.text: The mind's desires and "children of wrath".

12887.text: Saul's anger at the song becomes a plan to make David fall.

12889.text: The nations at ease furthered the disaster.

12893.text: Face of aph (H0639), "Long of nostrils": patience: Said of God first, then of the wise; and of the one who is not angry but bears another's anger (Pro 25:15) (Exo 34:6; Pro 14:29; 16:32; 19:11; 25:15). A long nose takes time to heat. The virtue and the divine name share one idiom (S, lexical).

12897.text: Face of aph (H0639), A nose given a hook: "Because you have raged against me … I will put my hook in your nose" (2Ki 19:28 = Isa 37:29). The raging nose is led back the way it came (S).

12900.text: chemah (H2534): heat/wrath · venom, poison · a drink poured for others · God's wrath "abated", "calm" (Est 7:10; Deu 32:33; Psa 58:4; 140:3; Hab 2:15; Eze 16:42). Anger as heat, as poison carried in speech, and as a drink that comes back to the one who poured it (S).

12901.text: charah (H2734): anger kindled · "fret" = heat yourself (Gen 4:5; Jon 4:1, 4, 9; Psa 37:1, 7, 8; Pro 24:19). Turned on another, it burns outward. Turned inward at the wicked's success, it "tends only to evil" (S).

12902.text: ka'as (H3707/3708): provocation done (to God) · vexation borne (Hannah, Job) · sorrow that does good ("by sadness of face the heart is made glad") · the fool's vexation that kills him · God-induced vexation of the nations (Deu 32:16, 21; 1Sa 1:6–16; Job 6:2; 17:7; Ecc 7:3; Job 5:2; Eze 32:9). Done to another, it is provocation. Borne, it is suffering. Taken to heart, it can make the heart good (Ecc 7:3). The word follows the direction of the act (S/R).

12903.text: 'ebrah (H5678): wrath · overflow · insolence and pride · "overflowings of your anger" offered ironically to Job (Pro 21:24; Isa 16:6; Jer 48:30; Job 40:11). The root image is overflow. It overflows as anger or as arrogance (S, lexical).

12904.text: za'am (H2194/2195): indignation · to denounce or curse (Num 23:7–8; Pro 24:24; Isa 10:5). Void when it goes beyond God's verdict (Balaam); valid when it follows justice (Pro 24:24) (S).

12905.text: qatsaph (H7107/7110): wrath (human and divine) · a twig on the water (homonym, H7110B) (Est 1:12; Hos 10:7). Data note only.

12907.text: qinah (H7015): lament, dirge (tagged in M02; 16 verses, e.g. David over Saul and Jonathan, 2Sa 1:17) (Jer 7:29; Eze 19:1, 14; 2Sa 1:17). The lament is the human answer to wrath that has come (S). Tagging note.

12908.text: orgē / orgizō: human anger to be put away · "be angry and do not sin" · Jesus's anger · God's wrath revealed, stored, remaining · the authority as God's servant of wrath · "leave it to the wrath of God" (Col 3:8; Eph 4:26; Mar 3:5; Rom 1:18; 2:5; Joh 3:36; Rom 13:4; 12:19). Who bears it, and what it serves. Jesus's anger heals; the same chapter's opponents plot (S).

12909.text: thumos: rage · "the wine of the passion" (Luk 4:28; Rev 14:8). Never seated (pilot §1.1); its picture is drink (S).

12911.text: aganakteō / -ēsis: the disciples indignant at waste, at rivals · Jesus indignant for the children · indignation as the fruit of godly grief (Mat 26:8; 20:24; Mar 10:14; 2Co 7:11). On behalf of a norm, a rival, a child, or one's own wrong (S).

12912.text: eris, machē, Meribah: strife, fights, a place named for a quarrel (Gal 5:20; Jam 4:1; Exo 17:7; Psa 95:8). The quarrel stored in a place name, and read again as a hardened heart (S).

12914.text: Factor Toward / against whom, and for what: Confirmed; decisive. For the wronged (Neh 5:6; Mar 10:14) or for one's own will (Est 1:12). Jesus's anger is aimed at healing (Mar 3:5).

12915.text: Factor Joined with: Confirmed. grief (Mar 3:5); jealousy, which makes it unappeasable (Pro 6:34; 27:4); envy (Gal 5:26; Jam 4:2); the Spirit (1Sa 11:6).

12916.text: Factor Heart state: Confirmed. the lifted heart before anger (2Ch 26:16); the heart already set (Dan 11:28); the godless heart that cherishes it (Job 36:13).

12917.text: Factor Alone / together, counsel: Confirmed. "I took counsel with myself" before acting (Neh 5:7); counsel restrains (Act 5:39); company teaches it (Pro 22:24–25).

12918.text: Factor Where / when: Confirmed, new: duration. the bed (Psa 4:4); time is a governing circumstance for anger: before sunset (Eph 4:26), "for a moment" (Psa 30:5), "forever" (Amo 1:11), "he forgets what you have done to him" (Gen 27:45).

12919.text: Factor What comes back: Confirmed. the cup comes round (Hab 2:16); provocation shames the provoker (Jer 7:19); "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (Jam 1:20).

12921.text: Factor Ease / distress: Confirmed, and double-edged. "the nations that are at ease … furthered the disaster" (Zec 1:15); distress produces the cry or more faithlessness (§H AN-59).

12922.text: Factor Haste / pause: Confirmed strongly. quick in spirit / slow to anger (Ecc 7:9; Pro 14:29; Jam 1:19).

12923.text: Factor Brought before God: Confirmed strongly. be still and wait (Psa 37:7); leave it to God's wrath (Rom 12:19); Jonah's anger brought to God and met by a question (Jon 4:2–4).

12924.text: Factor New: the answer it meets: New factor. a question or a reframing turns it (Gen 4:6; Gen 45:8; Luk 15:32); a soft answer or a harsh word (Pro 15:1).

12925.text: Factor New: whether it is seen truly: New factor. kindled by a lie (Gen 39:19); misreading (1Sa 17:28); the heavy hand misread from fear (Mat 25:24–25).

12926.text: Factor New: the person's position: New factor. the same "strong hand" is deliverance or terror depending on where one stands (Deu 6:21; Jer 21:5).

12927.text: B5 verses are still open (2Ki 3:27): the bearer of the anger is not given; recorded, not interpreted.

12928.text: Remembering and forgetting: remembering and forgetting run through anger: "he forgets what you have done to him" (Gen 27:45); "when the anger … had abated, he remembered Vashti" (Est 2:1); "remember and do not forget how you provoked" (Deu 9:7); "they forgot God" (Psa 106:21); "have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isa 51:13), which feeds the fear of anger.

12929.text: remembering God's deeds answers the fear of being cast off (Psa 77:9–11), and "this I call to mind … therefore I have hope" (Lam 3:21).

12930.text: God remembers too: "in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2); "he remembered that they were but flesh" (Psa 78:39); "remember me" (Job 14:13).

12932.text: It is kindled, burns and is poured: "So the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel"; "my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place"; "At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him"; "Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury".

12933.text: It is set off by something heard or seen, for God and for people: "when the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled"; "As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him … his anger was kindled"; "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath"; "when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate … he was filled with wrath".

12934.text: It moves and has a span: "wrath has gone out against you from the Lord"; "For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime"; "with them the wrath of God is finished"; "the wrath of God remains on him"; Edom "kept his wrath forever".

12935.text: It is felt in the body and the person: "Your wrath lies heavy upon me"; "There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation"; "So Cain was very angry, and his face fell"; "I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit"; "my spirit drinks their poison".

12936.text: It is drunk: "you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath"; "he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger".

12937.text: What human anger is said to do and not do: "for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God"; "anger lodges in the heart of fools"; "Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel!"; "Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?".

12938.text: Governed, and put away: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger"; "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty"; "Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you". The first and last stand five verses apart, with different Greek words (AG-223).

12939.text: God's anger named with who God is: "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger"; "I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man"; "until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart"; "I have no wrath".

12940.text: Named by its absence: "lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling"; love "is not irritable or resentful"; the overseer "must not be arrogant or quick-tempered".

12941.text: orgē (G3709): God's wrath in 29 of 35; the same noun is the anger people must put away (Col 3:6, 8).

12942.text: The verses speak of anger in the same words for God and for people, and keep some words almost wholly for God (ḥārôn, zaʿam, qeṣep̄, and orgē in the Greek); the same pictures (kindled, burning, poured, drunk) are used on both sides, and where the verses mark a difference they mark it in restraint: "for I am God and not a man" (Hos 11:9).
