13887.text: Zep 2:3, "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord": the call comes before "the burning anger of the Lord" (2:2); the people called are already humble and already doing his commands, and are told to seek humility; the verse promises nothing, "perhaps"; being hidden is God's act.

13888.text: Deu 31:29, "after my death you will surely act corruptly and turn aside from the way that I have commanded you ... provoking him to anger through the work of your hands": Moses grounds what he knows in what he has seen, "For I know how rebellious and stubborn you are ... How much more after my death!" (31:27); the provocation is named as "the work of your hands".

13889.text: Eze 20:33, "As I live, declares the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you", answers a thought, "What is in your mind shall never happen ... 'Let us be like the nations ... and worship wood and stone'" (20:32); the wrath poured out goes with bringing out and gathering (20:34), with judgment "face to face" (20:35), and with bringing them "into the bond of the covenant" (20:37): God answers a thought in the mind with an oath by his own life and with his rule.

13890.text: Isa 51:17-22: the call "Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up"; the one who drank, with "none to guide her ... none to take her by the hand" among her sons (51:18); "who will comfort you?" (51:19); her sons "full of the wrath of the Lord" (51:20), "drunk, but not with wine" (51:21); the figure is drunkenness: wrath that has been drunk leaves a person staggering and without a guide.

13891.text: The call to wake in Isa 51:17 goes to one who cannot rise without a hand, and the hand that takes the cup is God's, "who pleads the cause of his people" (51:22).

13892.text: Pro 11:4, "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death": the day of wrath tests what a person has relied on; the next verses go on, "The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight" (11:5), and "the treacherous are taken captive by their lust" (11:6).

13893.text: Pro 29:8, "Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath": the scoffer's words set a whole city alight, and the wise turn the anger away; around it the fool is set beside the wise: "the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet" (29:9); "A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back" (29:11).

13894.text: The wise man who turns another's wrath away (Pro 29:8) is the same man who holds his own back (29:11).

13896.text: Anger lodges and is cherished, and the lodging is the fool's.

13897.text: Fear and anger follow one another: anger at God, then fear of God (2Sa 6:8–9); fear first, then anger at a weaker target (Dan 11:30).

13899.text: Put off what the wrath comes on, including one's own anger (Col 3:6 then 3:8).

13900.text: Seat (v2): none in-verse or ±2. The next verse after Song 1:6 has "you whom my soul loves" (Song 1:7). Genuine. The bearer's own. The one who bears her brothers' anger turns at once to the one her soul loves.

13901.text: In the verse: Job 36:13 "heart" (lev). The bearer's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.1 read it as human anger in the inner seat. G v3 §16.5 read it with 36:14 as death as accountability. Both stand. The phenomenon adds only that the heart here is where anger is kept, not where it flares.

13902.text: Outside the verse: Ecc 7:8 "patient in spirit … proud in spirit". Genuine. Pro 6:32 "he who does it destroys himself" (nephesh). Genuine. The adulterer's own self, two verses before the husband's fury. The fury of Pro 6:34 is the other party's answer to one who has already destroyed his own soul.

13911.text: Exo 11:10 "the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart". Genuine. The offender's heart, hardened. New here (no batch cites it). Moses's hot anger (11:8) is set between God's announcement and the heart that will not yield.

13918.text: Ecc 1:16–17 "I said in my heart … I applied my heart to know". Genuine. The bearer's own (E v2 §1.3; B v3 §1.2, §1.11; C v3 §10). New here is only the link: the heart that seeks knowledge comes before the vexation that knowledge brings.

13922.text: Outside the verse: no seat in Gen 45:2–9 or Job 18:1–7.

13925.text: Outside the verse: Num 11:12 "Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child". The bearer's own, relational and bodily. Moses's displeasure (11:10) comes out as a protest about the bosom he is asked to carry the people in (E v2 data note). Num 11:13 "meat" is spurious.

13947.text: Outside the verse: none in Deu 1:34–40; 3:23–29; 4:18–25.

13952.text: Seat. None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is God's, given (divine; C v3 §1.6). Pointer: U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed against God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint. Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.

13955.text: In the verse: Num 11:33 "meat" (basar). Spurious. Pilot §0 lists it among the links that do not count.

13966.text: Outside: Job 6:7 "My appetite refuses to touch them" (nephesh). Appetite-sense, the bearer's own (C v3 §1.1, §9.4). Job 9:4 "wise in heart" is God's (#1890 findings §4.1). Job 14:13 is the verse G v3 §16 left for M20 or unit 2 (U1 §R-V). It is read here: its movement is hiding until the wrath passes, followed by being remembered. It is not a death-wish.

13986.text: 1. Part A: seven of the nine are genuine. Num 11:33 is spurious and Job 4:9 is divine. Six of the seven are a particular person's seat: three are Hezekiah's own heart in his two episodes (2Ch 29:10; 32:25–26), one is the provoker's heart (Solomon), one is the receiving spirit (Job), and one is another person's glad heart (Aaron). The seventh, Num 16:22, is God's relation to every human spirit.

13995.text: Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13).

13996.text: Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32).

13997.text: In Joseph's story the anger that imprisons also positions. "The Lord was with Joseph" in the prison (Gen 39:21), and the officers imprisoned by Pharaoh's anger bring about Joseph's release (41:9–13).

13998.text: Elihu burns with anger three times (Job 32:2, 3, 5). Then comes a long speech (32:6 onward).

14006.text: New here: in Qoheleth the heart is where vexation stays at night (2:23) and where it must be removed from (11:10). In 7:3, though, the heart is what gains from sorrow.

14009.text: What it leads to. Destruction of the object (Exo 32:20), purge and execution (Num 31:17), a lesser victory (2Ki 13:19), or approval once the explanation is heard (Lev 10:20).

14011.text: A burden shared: Moses (H v1 §3.3, "Moses' burden, then the Spirit shared", Num 11:10–17).

14014.text: What it leads to. Blessing instead of curse (Num 23:11). The judgment turned back on the pursuers (Job 19:29).

14019.text: Directions of flow: Batch A §2.4 read 1Sa 11:5–7 as "hearing → Spirit → anger → act → dread spreading to the people", in contrast with 1Sa 18:8–10: "jealous anger → a harmful spirit → a spear". Both stand. New here: Judg 14:19 runs Spirit → killing → hot anger afterwards. The anger is the aftermath of a Spirit-driven act, not its cause, and it comes out as going home, not as more violence.

14037.text: What it leads to. Release: "He who is bowed down shall speedily be released" (Isa 51:14). Endurance (Heb 11:27), and a test passed (Dan 1:12).

14039.text: Where it comes from. A will to see another's nakedness (Hab 2:15). For Babylon, luxury and trade ("the merchants of the earth have grown rich", 18:3).

14042.text: What it leads to. "At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter" (2Cor 7:11). The comfort of the other: "his spirit has been refreshed by you all" (7:13). Meeting together and encouraging (Heb 10:25).

14046.text: Every request is granted, and no anger comes. "I will not do it, if I find thirty there" (Gen 18:30); "God did so that night" (Judg 6:40). The anger feared never appears in either passage.

14049.text: What it leads to. Moses speaks of his exclusion to the people as a warning to them. Deu 4:21–22 is followed at once by "Take care, lest you forget the covenant" (4:23) and "the Lord your God is a consuming fire" (4:24). His own bearing of the anger becomes his teaching.

14054.text: The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5).

14056.text: Intercession sits alongside the intercessor's own anger. The same chapter has Moses' own anger breaking the tablets (Exo 32:19; U1 §11 LD; Deu 9:17). Moses is angry at the people and pleads for them against God's anger, within one episode.

14059.text: The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17.

14063.text: Intermarriage. "they would turn away your sons from following me" (Deu 7:4).

14075.text: From youth, turning the back: "done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth" (Jer 32:30); "They have turned to me their back and not their face … they have not listened to receive instruction" (32:33).

14076.text: Discouraging the heart: the spies "discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land" (Num 32:9), and "the Lord's anger was kindled on that day" (32:10).

14079.text: Spoken against: "Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them (Num 12:8–9). The charge is a lack of fear.

14081.text: Killed: after Jehoiada died, "the king listened to them [the princes]"; prophets "testified against them, but they would not pay attention"; Zechariah, whom "the Spirit of God clothed", was stoned "in the court of the house of the Lord" (2Ch 24:17–21).

14086.text: Where it comes from. From seeing. "as you see with your own eyes" (2Ch 29:8); "when they see the afflictions of that land" (Deu 29:22).

14107.text: The formula: "the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and which he made Israel to sin" (1Ki 14:16; 15:30; 16:13, 26).

14113.text: "it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence" (2Ki 24:20).

14120.text: From awareness of accumulated guilt ("our guilt is already great", 2Ch 28:13; "we have greatly transgressed", Ezr 10:13).

14126.text: Psa 79:6 is followed by "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8).

14127.text: Lam 3:66 comes with "You will give them dullness of heart" (3:65).

14131.text: Past mercy as the ground: "You forgave the iniquity of your people … You withdrew all your wrath … Restore us again" (Psa 85:2–4); "Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?" (85:6).

14148.text: Every man against his brother: "Every man's sword will be against his brother" (Eze 38:21), as in Isa 9:19–21.

14152.text: "The Lord was very angry with your fathers … Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will return to you … Do not be like your fathers" (Zec 1:2–4).

14153.text: Flight commanded (§39, Jer 51:45) set against flight forbidden here (42:19). Fear of the sword drives them into the wrath.

14155.text: Data note. Lam 3:2 has no verse row in `iba.db`. This is by design (`governance.verse_gap_by_design`), and the reading went on to 3:3.

14162.text: Where it comes from. From people coming to be baptized: "confessing their sins" (Mat 3:6); in Matthew, "many of the Pharisees and Sadducees" (3:7).

14170.text: the heart that rejoices when protected (§3; Isa 30:29; 66:14).

14173.text: What it does: "Cain was very angry, and his face fell" (Gen 4:5); Ahab went home "vexed and sullen … lay down on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food" (1Ki 21:4); In 1Ki 20:43 the same pair, "vexed and sullen", takes him home to Samaria; The movement is inward and downward: face, bed, refusing food.

14174.text: Where it comes from. From a denial the person cannot reverse: no regard from God for Cain's offering while Abel's is regarded (Gen 4:4–5); the prophet's verdict, "your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people" (1Ki 20:42); Naboth's refusal, "I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers" (1Ki 21:3–4).

14175.text: How it co-exists: Someone else reads it off the body and names it. God asks Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?" (Gen 4:6). Jezebel asks Ahab, "Why is your spirit so vexed that you eat no food?" (1Ki 21:5). The angry person names nothing. The inner state is put into words by the questioner; The questioner then offers a way forward, and the two ways are opposites; God: "If you do well, will you not be accepted? … sin is crouching at the door … you must rule over it" (Gen 4:7). This is mastery of the anger from within; Jezebel: "Arise and eat bread and let your heart be cheerful; I will give you the vineyard" (1Ki 21:7). This is removing the denial by a crime.

14177.text: Seat: In the verse: none of the four; Whose seat: in context, named by the other party. 1Ki 21:5 "spirit" is Ahab's own, but Jezebel names it, not the narrator. Genuine; Outside the verse:; Before: 1Ki 20:42 nephesh "your life shall be for his life". Life-sense only. It is the verdict on Ahab's life that sends him home sullen; After: 1Ki 21:7 "let your heart be cheerful". Genuine. The heart is offered as the place where the anger will be undone, and the price is Naboth; Gen 4: no seat word in Gen 4:2–9. God's question and the image of sin "crouching at the door" do the seat's work: the inner struggle is given as a scene at a door, not as an organ. This agrees with pilot §1.4 and does not change it.

14178.text: What it does: Abram refuses it: "Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kinsmen" (Gen 13:8); God forbids it: "Do not harass Moab … because I have given Ar to the people of Lot" (Deu 2:9). Likewise Ammon, "the sons of Lot" (Deu 2:19); The men of Judah and Israel fight over the king with kinship as the weapon: "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter?" (2Sa 19:42).

14181.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: Kin offence hardens. "A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city, and quarreling is like the bars of a castle" (Pro 18:19). The closer the tie, the harder the wall. This is the reverse of Gen 13's reason for yielding ("for we are kinsmen"); Brothers' anger takes the form of imposed labour: "My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!" (Song 1:6). The anger is felt by the one it lands on as the loss of her own vineyard. The next verse turns straight to "you whom my soul loves" (1:7); Edom against his brother: anger that never turns away. Edom "pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath forever" (Amo 1:11). God will deal with Edom "according to the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them" (Eze 35:11), with its speech: "They are given us to devour" (35:12); This is exactly the opposite of Gen 27:44–45. There Rebekah waits for Esau's anger to "turn away" and for him to "forget", and it does (Gen 33:4). Esau the man let his anger pass. Edom, his nation, "kept his wrath forever". The same bloodline shows anger's two courses; Amo 1:9 names the same failure for Tyre: "did not remember the covenant of brotherhood"; Anger at a brother judged like murder, and the remedy is reconciliation before worship: "everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment" (Mat 5:22); "leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother" (5:24). The worship waits on the relationship; Brothers in the work part without the yielding: "there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark … but Paul chose Silas" (Act 15:39–40). It began over Mark, "who had withdrawn from them" (15:38). Separation, as in Gen 13:11, but here neither party gives the other the choice. Both are "commended … to the grace of the Lord" (15:40) and the work goes on in two directions; Seat : none in-verse or ±2. The next verse after Song 1:6 has "you whom my soul loves" (Song 1:7). Genuine. The bearer's own. The one who bears her brothers' anger turns at once to the one her soul loves.

14182.text: What it does: It runs a course and passes, with time and forgetting: "until your brother's fury turns away … until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him" (Gen 27:44–45); It is held and fed: "The godless in heart cherish anger" (Job 36:13); It draws the bearer on: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (Job 36:18); It kills its bearer: "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2).

14183.text: Where it comes from: For Esau, from the stolen blessing: "Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing" (Gen 27:41); Job 36:13 gives its source in the heart: "the godless in heart".

14184.text: How it co-exists: With a murder plan spoken inwardly: "Esau said to himself, '… then I will kill my brother Jacob'" (Gen 27:41). And Rebekah's reading of it: "your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you" (27:42). The anger is kept going by a plan that soothes it; With the refusal to cry out: "they do not cry for help when he binds them" (Job 36:13). Cherished anger shuts off the cry; Rebekah's movement is the counter-weight: removing the object (flight) and waiting for the anger's course to end. Her own inner state follows at once: "Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?" (27:45), and "I loathe my life" (27:46).

14185.text: What it leads to: For Esau: the anger turns away over years, and there is no killing. When they meet, "Esau ran to meet him and embraced him … and they wept" (Gen 33:4). Rebekah's "until he forgets" comes true, beyond embrace; For the godless: "They die in youth" (Job 36:14); For the fool: death by his own vexation (Job 5:2); Eliphaz sets this beside "man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward" (Job 5:7). Trouble is universal, but dying of vexation is the fool's.

14186.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 36:13 "heart" (lev). The bearer's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.1 read it as human anger in the inner seat. G v3 §16.5 read it with 36:14 as death as accountability. Both stand. The phenomenon adds only that the heart here is where anger is kept, not where it flares; Outside the verse: Gen 27:41 "said to himself" (Hebrew in his heart). Genuine, the bearer's own. The seat arrives three verses before the anger word, as the place where the plan is spoken; Job 36:18: no seat. Whose wrath it is was settled in §36.

14187.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: Anger lodges, and where it lodges is named. "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools" (Ecc 7:9). This joins Job 36:13 ("cherish anger"). Anger that stays has a lodging, and the lodging is the fool's. The verse before sets up the pair: "the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" (7:8); Its duration is limited to a day: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil" (Eph 4:26–27). Where Gen 27 waited years for anger to turn away, the NT sets a limit of one day. The reason given is what anger left overnight opens: "opportunity to the devil"; It repeats: "A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again" (Pro 19:19). Great wrath is a pattern, not an event. Rescue does not end it; It is weighed:; "A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both" (Pro 27:3). This echoes Job's "heavier than the sand of the sea"; "Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?" (Pro 27:4). Anger is measured, and jealousy is found to be worse; Jealousy makes it unappeasable: "jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation" (Pro 6:34–35). This is the one anger in Proverbs that a gift will not avert. Compare §23: "A gift in secret averts anger" (Pro 21:14); It shows at once: "The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult" (Pro 12:16). The fool's anger cannot be hidden, while the prudent one lets the insult pass unanswered; It is where the wicked end up: "the expectation of the wicked [ends] in wrath".

14188.text: Seat : In the verse: Ecc 7:9 "spirit" (ruach) and "heart" (literally bosom). The bearer's own. Genuine. Nothing new is needed; Outside the verse: Ecc 7:8 "patient in spirit … proud in spirit". Genuine. Pro 6:32 "he who does it destroys himself" (nephesh). Genuine. The adulterer's own self, two verses before the husband's fury. The fury of Pro 6:34 is the other party's answer to one who has already destroyed his own soul.

14189.text: (a) A demand the angry one cannot meet. Gen 30:2: "Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, 'Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?'": It comes from Rachel's "Give me children, or I shall die!" (30:1), which itself came from envy: "she envied her sister" (30:1); The anger answers an impossible demand by naming who alone could meet it. Rachel then turns to a workaround: "Here is my servant Bilhah" (30:3).

14190.text: (b) Thwarted and made a fool of: Balaam: "Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff" (Num 22:27). When the donkey speaks, he gives his reason: "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you" (22:29). The anger is about being shamed, and it wishes to kill; Balak: "Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together … 'I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times'" (Num 24:10). It ends in dismissal and the withholding of honour: "the Lord has held you back from honor" (24:11); Naaman: "Naaman was angry and went away, saying, 'Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me …'" (2Ki 5:11), and "he turned and went away in a rage" (5:12). What the anger releases is a disappointed expectation of honour, quoted as his own thought. Pilot §1.4 read the whole movement: rage → persuasion → obedience → restoration; The Ephraimite army, discharged, "became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger" (2Ch 25:10), and later "raided the cities of Judah" (25:13). Anger at being sent away returns as violence against those who sent it.

14191.text: (c) Rebuked by a holy person: Asa, told by the seer that he "relied on the king of Syria", "was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks … for he was in a rage with him" (2Ch 16:10). The rage spreads: "Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time" (16:10); Uzziah, withstood by the priests at the altar: "Uzziah was angry … and when he became angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead" (2Ch 26:19); In both, the anger is against the messenger of a boundary, and the story ends with the angry king's own body struck: Asa "diseased in his feet … Yet even in his disease he did not seek the Lord" (16:12); Uzziah "a leper to the day of his death" (26:21).

14192.text: (d) Refused by a subordinate, or exposed: Vashti's refusal: "the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him" (Est 1:12). The counsellor at once generalises the fear to every household: "there will be contempt and wrath in plenty" (1:18). One refusal is read as a threat to the whole order of husbands, and answered by decree (1:19–20); The king of Syria, whose plans Elisha keeps disclosing: "the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled because of this thing" (2Ki 6:11). He suspects a traitor: "Will you not show me who of us is for the king of Israel?" (6:11). The servant's answer shows how completely he is exposed: Elisha "tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom" (6:12).

14193.text: How it co-exists: With a prior high state: Uzziah "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2Ch 26:16), and the king's "heart … merry with wine" (Est 1:10). Anger comes where a lifted state is checked. F v4 §7 already read Est 1:10 as "the merry heart as the threshold"; this adds Uzziah; With striking (Num 22:27; 24:10, hands; 2Ch 16:10), and with going away (2Ki 5:12; 2Ch 25:10).

14196.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The four strands hold, and each gains an instance: Strand (a), a demand no one can meet, with the angry one now the demander. "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand … no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:10–11). Then "Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (2:12). This is the mirror of Gen 30:2. Jacob, faced with an impossible demand, named God as the only one who could meet it. Nebuchadnezzar hears the same answer ("except the gods") and orders a massacre; The anger is answered by "prudence and discretion" (Dan 2:14): Daniel's; Strand (b), thwarted and made a fool of. "Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children" (Mat 2:16). "Tricked" is Balaam's "you have made a fool of me" (Num 22:29). This time the killing is carried out, and it ends in "Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted" (Mat 2:18); Strand (d), refused by subordinates; Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13); After their answer, "But if not … we will not serve your gods" (3:18), "Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more" (3:19); The face changes outward, against them. This is the reverse of §1's fallen face, which turns inward; The outcome reverses the anger: "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego … who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command" (3:28). The king blesses the very refusal that enraged him; A new instance, thwarted from outside and turned against the weaker: "ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant" (Dan 11:30). "News from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy" (11:44). Fear comes first, then anger. The anger is turned on a weaker target than the one that thwarted him.

14198.text: What it does to the one who holds it. It turns at once into custody or death: Potiphar, hearing his wife's story, "his anger was kindled", and "Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison" (Gen 39:19–20); "Pharaoh was angry with his two officers … and he put them in custody" (Gen 40:2–3; recalled at 41:10); the king "arose in his wrath" and says "Hang him on that" (Est 7:7, 10).

14199.text: What it does to those beneath it: Pleading against it before it rises:; Judah: "let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself" (Gen 44:18). The plea is a long retelling of the father's love (44:19–21 onward); Rachel: "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me" (Gen 31:35). The plea for no anger covers a concealment: she is sitting on the stolen gods (31:34); Reading it as a sign: "If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him" (1Sa 20:7). Saul's anger is to be read as the evidence of Saul's intent. Jonathan's knowledge follows the same path: after the spear, "Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death" (20:33); Anticipating it and scripting a reply: Joab to the messenger: "if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city?' … then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also'" (2Sa 11:20–21). The anger is foreseen, and so is the one sentence that will turn it. That sentence works because the king had wanted Uriah dead. The line manages the king's anger by exposing the king's own secret; Plotting against it from below: "Bigthan and Teresh … became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus" (Est 2:21). This is anger rising from the servants, discovered through Mordecai (2:22); Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32); A group overrules its king: "the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him … 'Send the man back … how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord?'" (1Sa 29:4). The king Achish yields: "Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you" (29:6). The anger comes from suspicion: they fear a loyalty they cannot see.

14200.text: Where it comes from. A report heard (Gen 39:19; Judg 9:30), an offence by servants (Gen 40:1–2), or suspicion (1Sa 29:4). In Gen 39 the anger is kindled by a lie, and the text lets the reader see that the anger is misdirected.

14201.text: How it co-exists. With abating and remembering: "when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her" (Est 2:1), and "Then the wrath of the king abated" (7:10): Anger's time-course shows in the powerful as abating after the act, not before; Memory returns once the anger is gone, and the decree cannot be undone.

14202.text: What it leads to. Imprisonment (Joseph, the officers), hanging (the baker, Haman, the eunuchs), a friend sent away (David from the Philistines): In Joseph's story the anger that imprisons also positions. "The Lord was with Joseph" in the prison (Gen 39:21), and the officers imprisoned by Pharaoh's anger bring about Joseph's release (41:9–13).

14203.text: Seat: In the verse: Est 7:7 "life" (nephesh): "Haman stayed to beg for his life". The other party's. Life-sense only. C v3 §7.5 read it under "the soul-life hunted". In this phenomenon the seat word names what the powerful one's anger puts at stake in the one beneath, as M20 §2's Seat found for the hunted; Outside the verse:; Est 7:5 "dared" (literally "whose heart has filled him to do this"). The offender's heart, as the king asks about it. Genuine. New here (no batch cites it). The king's wrath two verses later is aimed at the heart that dared; 1Sa 20:4 "Whatever you say [your soul says], I will do for you". Genuine. The other party's (David's), pledged to by Jonathan. New here. It stands three verses before 1Sa 20:7: Jonathan binds himself to David's soul just before they plan how to read Saul's anger. This adds to F v4 §1.1 (Jonathan and David) without changing it; Gen 41:8 "his spirit was troubled". Genuine. The bearer's own (Pharaoh's), though in a different scene from his anger. The same king appears once with an angry act and once with a troubled spirit. The seat word comes with the trouble, not with the anger.

14204.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: The narratives become sayings. Proverbs states as general truths what Genesis and Esther showed:; "A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass" (Pro 19:12); "The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life" (20:2); "A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully" (14:35).

14205.text: Seat : In the verse: Pro 20:2 "forfeits his life" (nephesh). The other party's (the provoker's). Life-sense only. This matches Est 7:7 exactly: the king's wrath puts the subject's nephesh at stake; Outside the verse: Dan 8:8 "four winds". Spurious.

14206.text: What it does. It speaks at length, and the speech counts years or services: Jacob: "Jacob became angry and berated Laban … 'What is my offense? … These twenty years I have been with you … I bore the loss of it myself'" (Gen 31:36–39); Abner: "Am I a dog's head of Judah? To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul … And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman" (2Sa 3:8); Elihu burns with anger three times (Job 32:2, 3, 5). Then comes a long speech (32:6 onward).

14207.text: Where it comes from: A final provocation on top of the store: Laban's search (31:33–35), Ish-bosheth's accusation (3:7); For Elihu, an argument that has failed: at Job "because he justified himself rather than God", at the friends "because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong" (32:2–3).

14210.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 32:2 "himself" (nephesh): Job "justified himself rather than God". Genuine, as the reflexive self. But it is the other party's (Job's), not Elihu's. The anger is at a self that has made itself right; Outside the verse:; After, Job 32:8: "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand". Genuine. Elihu justifies speaking despite his youth; Further on, Job 32:18: "the spirit within me constrains me". Genuine, the bearer's own. New here (outside the ±3 window; read in this session). The seat of Elihu's released anger arrives as a spirit under pressure, with the belly as its bodily image.

14211.text: Luk 15:28: the elder brother. "But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, but he answered his father, 'Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat …'" (15:28–29): The phenomenon's shape holds exactly. A final provocation (the feast for the returned brother, 15:27) is laid on a store that is counted in years ("these many years"), just like Jacob's "these twenty years" and Abner's "to this day". Three texts, three speakers, one form: the anger releases a ledger; What the parable adds is the answer. Jacob asked for judgment, and Abner switched sides. The father goes out and entreats, then reframes the ledger: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate … for this your brother was dead, and is alive" (15:31–32). The son had said "this son of yours" (15:30). The father gives the brother back to him. This is the reframing of §9 (Joseph's "not you … but God"), used on held anger. The parable does not say whether the son goes in; The body refuses ("refused to go in"). This links to §1's fallen face; Seat: none in-verse or ±2. As the pilot noted, the inner state was held behind service and comes out through anger.

14212.text: What it does: "The men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel … for such a thing must not be done" (Gen 34:7). The anger states a norm; "Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food … for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him" (1Sa 20:34); "David's anger was greatly kindled against the man … 'the man who has done this deserves to die'" (2Sa 12:5); "I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words" (Neh 5:6); "He went out from Pharaoh in hot anger" (Exo 11:8).

14213.text: Where it comes from. Hearing or seeing the wrong: "as soon as they heard of it" (Gen 34:7); "when I heard their outcry" (Neh 5:6); "When King David heard of all these things" (2Sa 13:21); Jonathan seeing the spear thrown at himself (1Sa 20:33); David hearing a parable (2Sa 12:1–4).

14214.text: How it co-exists: With grief: Jonathan's anger is joined to being "grieved for David" (1Sa 20:34). Pilot §1.4 noted "anger, grief and fasting together"; With deliberation: Neh 5:6 → 5:7, "I took counsel with myself"; With a hidden self-accusation: David's verdict on the rich man is turned on himself: "You are the man!" (2Sa 12:7). Indignation at another's outrage becomes the instrument of the angry man's own conviction; With inaction: 2Sa 13:21 says only "he was very angry". Nothing follows from David, and Absalom acts instead. "Absalom hated Amnon" (13:22). "After two full years" (13:23) he orders, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine … then kill him" (13:28). The verse sets the king's anger that does nothing beside the brother's hatred that waits. Read further on (2Sa 13:39): "the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead." The king's anger passes into longing for the killer.

14216.text: Seat: In the verse: none of the six; Outside the verse:; Neh 5:7 "I took counsel with myself [my heart]". Genuine. The bearer's own. It arrives in the next verse, with the deliberation; Gen 34:8 "The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter". Genuine, but the offender's. The indignation of the brothers and the desire of the offender's soul stand side by side in consecutive verses; Exo 11:10 "the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart". Genuine. The offender's heart, hardened. New here (no batch cites it). Moses's hot anger (11:8) is set between God's announcement and the heart that will not yield; 2Sa 13:20 "do not take this to heart" (Absalom to Tamar). Genuine. The victim's, told to suppress. 2Sa 13:39 "spirit of the king". Genuine. The bearer's own, the angry king's spirit after the killing, turned to longing. New here is only the link back to the anger at 13:21; 2Sa 12:3, 8 "arms" (chêq, bosom): the lamb "lie in his arms", and "your master's wives into your arms". Relational and bodily, not inner (D v2 R6; E v2 R8). The parable's bosom and David's bosom are the same word: that is how the parable catches him. This is noted as a link, not as a seat; Neh 5:5 "our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers" is kinship-sense. Spurious as a seat.

14217.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The one wronged is now God, or God's law, rather than a sister, a friend or the poor: The indignation seizes its bearer: "Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law" (Psa 119:53). The bearer is its object as well as its subject. It is framed between comfort in God's rules (119:52) and "Your statutes have been my songs" (119:54). The indignation sits inside a life held by the law it defends; The spirit provoked by what it sees: "while Paul was waiting … his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue … and in the marketplace every day" (Act 17:16–17). This is the same movement as Neh 5:6–7: indignation, then an inner act, then public speech. Here the seat is named in the indignation verse itself; Annoyance that finally acts: the slave girl "kept doing this for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you … come out of her'" (Act 16:18); What annoys him is a true proclamation ("These men are servants of the Most High God", 16:17) from a wrong source; The anger builds over "many days" before the act; The act sets off anger in others: "when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas" (16:19).

14219.text: What it does: It wears down over time: "her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her … So it went on year by year" (1Sa 1:6–7); It stops eating and brings weeping: "Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat" (1:7); It dims the eye and wastes the body: "My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow" (Job 17:7); It cannot be weighed: "Oh that my vexation were weighed … it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash" (Job 6:2–3); It shows in the face: Joseph "saw that they were troubled", and asks "Why are your faces downcast today?" (Gen 40:6–7).

14220.text: Where it comes from: A rival's provocation, "because the Lord had closed her womb" (1Sa 1:6); calamity and God's "arrows" (Job 6:2, 4); being made "a byword of the peoples" (Job 17:6); dreams with "no one to interpret them" (Gen 40:8).

14221.text: How it co-exists: With the sufferer's own speech that explains it. Hannah: "I am a woman troubled in spirit … I have been pouring out my soul before the Lord … I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation" (1Sa 1:15–16). Job: "therefore my words have been rash" (Job 6:3). The vexation is given as the reason the sufferer's speech looks the way it does: drunk to Eli, rash to the friends; With misreading by the onlooker: Eli takes Hannah "to be a drunken woman" (1:13–14).

14224.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

14225.text: Seat . Four in-verse, all genuine and all the bearer's own: Psa 31:9 "soul"; Ecc 2:23 "heart"; Ecc 7:3 "heart"; Ecc 11:10 "heart" + "body".

14226.text: What it does: Joseph to his brothers: "do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here" (Gen 45:5). The brothers' self-directed anger is expected, and Joseph forbids it; Bildad to Job: "You who tear yourself in your anger" (Job 18:4). Anger that wounds its bearer.

14227.text: Where it comes from: Joseph's brothers: guilt, now uncovered. "They were dismayed at his presence" (45:3), and "I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold" (45:4); Job: his protest, as Bildad hears it.

14228.text: How it co-exists. With a reframing that removes its ground. "For God sent me before you to preserve life … So it was not you who sent me here, but God" (45:5, 8): Joseph does not deny the act ("you sold me"). He re-assigns its meaning, and the anger at oneself is released by the new meaning; Bildad offers the opposite of a reframing: the world will not change for Job, "shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed?" (18:4).

14230.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 18:4 "yourself" (nephesh). The bearer's own. Genuine, as the self that anger harms; Gen 45:5 "with yourselves" is literally "in your eyes" [lexical, not in DB]. It is not tagged as a seat in the DB. [verify] if the researcher wants the Hebrew checked; Outside the verse: no seat in Gen 45:2–9 or Job 18:1–7.

14231.text: What it does: It separates the speaker's self from the angry: "Let my soul come not into their council; O my glory, be not joined to their company" (49:6); It curses the anger, not the men: "Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel!" (49:7).

14232.text: Where it comes from. The deed: "in their anger they killed men, and in their willfulness they hamstrung oxen" (49:6). The reader carries Gen 34 here. That link is the reader's, not the verse's.

14234.text: What it leads to. Scattering: "I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel" (49:7).

14235.text: Seat: In the verse: Gen 49:6 "soul" (nephesh), and "glory" (kāvôd) in parallel. Genuine. The speaker's own, not the angry ones'. The seat is the self that withdraws from the anger; Outside the verse: none in 49:3–10.

14236.text: Pro 22:24–25: the same refusal as teaching. "Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.": Jacob's refusal of the angry brothers' company (Gen 49:6) becomes a rule; The reason is stated: anger is learned from company, and what it catches is the self; Seat. Pro 22:25 "yourself" (nephesh). Genuine. The learner's own self, as what the snare catches. It is not in any batch: new; Gen 49:6 and Pro 22:25 put the same seat word, nephesh, at the same point: the self that must not go into the angry one's company. In Genesis the soul refuses. In Proverbs the soul is the one at risk.

14237.text: What it does: It flares at the sight: "as soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger burned hot" (Exo 32:19); It breaks what was given: "he threw the tablets … and broke them" (32:19); It destroys the object: the calf "burned … ground it to powder … made the people of Israel drink it" (32:20); It rebukes by question: "Why have you not eaten the sin offering …?" (Lev 10:17); "Have you let all the women live?" (Num 31:15); It states the limit that was missed: "You should have struck five or six times … now you will strike down Syria only three times" (2Ki 13:19).

14238.text: Where it comes from. Disobedience to a given word: "they did not listen to Moses" (Exo 16:20); the calf (32:19); the sin offering burned instead of eaten (Lev 10:16); the women of Midian spared "on Balaam's advice" (Num 31:14–16); the king striking only three times (2Ki 13:18); rebels refusing to come: "We will not come up" (Num 16:12–14).

14239.text: How it co-exists: With appeal to God against those who resist: "Moses was very angry and said to the Lord, 'Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them'" (Num 16:15). The anger is carried straight into a plea of innocence before God; With the one beneath deflecting it: Aaron, "Let not the anger of my lord burn hot. You know the people, that they are set on evil … I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf" (Exo 32:22–24). Deflection by blaming the people and making the act passive; With being answered: Aaron's reply to the Lev 10 rebuke ("such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the Lord have approved?", 10:19) meets "And when Moses heard that, he approved" (10:20). The leader's anger yields to a reason.

14246.text: What it does: "David was angry because the Lord had broken out against Uzzah" (2Sa 6:8 = 1Ch 13:11); "the anger of the Lord blazed hotly, and Moses was displeased" (Num 11:10); "'I regret that I have made Saul king' … And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night" (1Sa 15:11).

14247.text: How it co-exists. With fear, straight after: "David was afraid of the Lord that day, and he said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'" (2Sa 6:9; 1Ch 13:12). Anger at God and fear of God follow one another in consecutive verses. A new pairing, not read in the batches: With complaint to God: Moses, "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? … Did I conceive all this people? … 'Carry them in your bosom'" (Num 11:11–12); With all-night crying: Samuel (1Sa 15:11). Later, Samuel "grieved over Saul" (15:35). Anger turns to crying out, and then to grief.

14248.text: What it leads to: Withdrawal from what God struck: David will not take the ark home (2Sa 6:10). The anger ends in avoidance, and the ark's blessing goes to Obed-edom instead (6:11); A burden shared: Moses; Obedience with grief: Samuel goes to meet Saul the next morning (15:12).

14249.text: Seat: In the verse: none; Outside the verse: Num 11:12 "Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child". The bearer's own, relational and bodily. Moses's displeasure (11:10) comes out as a protest about the bosom he is asked to carry the people in (E v2 data note). Num 11:13 "meat" is spurious; The unit-2 side of these four verses is God's own anger (Num 11:10; 2Sa 6:7; 1Ch 13:10), for unit 2.

14250.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The occasion widens from God striking to God's mercy, and to the consequences of one's own folly: Jonah: anger at God's mercy; The occasion: "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster" (Jon 3:10). "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry" (4:1); He quotes God's own character against him: "I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster" (4:2). Pilot §2.1 read this. The anger is at the very attribute that is the opposite of anger; It asks to die: "please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (4:3). After the plant withers, "It is better for me to die than to live" (4:8), and "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" (4:9); God asks a question, as he did with Cain: "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4, 9). Compare "Why are you angry?" (Gen 4:6). Twice in Scripture God meets a man's anger by asking about it. Both times, the question comes before a decisive act or teaching, and both times the answer is left open; God reframes by comparison: "You pity the plant … And should not I pity Nineveh …?" (4:10–11). The anger is set beside the pity the angry man feels for a plant. The book ends on God's question. Jonah's answer is not given; The heart rages at God for one's own ruin: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the Lord" (Pro 19:3). The anger is misdirected: the cause is his own folly, and the target is God; Deprivation turns to cursing God, then darkness: "when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness" (Isa 8:21–22). The face turns up in anger and finds nothing, then down and finds darkness. It is set after "should not a people inquire of their God?" (8:19).

14251.text: Seat : In the verse: Pro 19:3 "heart" (lev). The bearer's own. Genuine. New here: the only in-verse seat in §13 locates anger at God in the heart, and the verse says it is misdirected; Outside the verse: Jon 4:3 "my life" and Jon 4:8 "that he might die" (nephesh). The bearer's own. Life-sense, as the thing asked to be ended. Jonah's anger takes his own nephesh as its object. This links to §9: anger turned on oneself.

14252.text: What it does: Balaam cannot pronounce it: "How can I curse whom God has not cursed? How can I denounce whom the Lord has not denounced?" (Num 23:8). Human denunciation is shown to be derivative: it cannot go beyond God's; God offers it ironically to Job: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). This comes inside the challenge, "Have you an arm like God …?" (40:9), and "Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you" (40:14). Anger that abases the proud belongs to the one who can save by his own right hand; Job warns his friends that their own wrath is answerable: "be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment" (Job 19:29). This comes after "If you say, 'How we will pursue him!'" (19:28).

14257.text: What it does: Given by the Spirit: "the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1Sa 11:6); "the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him … In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (Judg 14:19); Shared as God's jealousy: Phinehas "has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them" (Num 25:11). A human's zeal is counted as God's own, and it stops God's wrath; Exceeding God's commission: "because the Lord … was angry with Judah, he gave them into your hand, but you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven" (2Ch 28:9). Human rage goes beyond the divine anger it served, and becomes its own guilt: "Have you not sins of your own …?" (28:10); "the fierce wrath of the Lord is upon you" (28:11).

14259.text: How it co-exists: Directions of flow: Batch A §2.4 read 1Sa 11:5–7 as "hearing → Spirit → anger → act → dread spreading to the people", in contrast with 1Sa 18:8–10: "jealous anger → a harmful spirit → a spear". Both stand. New here: Judg 14:19 runs Spirit → killing → hot anger afterwards. The anger is the aftermath of a Spirit-driven act, not its cause, and it comes out as going home, not as more violence; Saul's anger ends in mercy that same day: "Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the Lord has worked salvation" (1Sa 11:13).

14261.text: Seat: In the verse:; Judg 14:19 and 1Sa 11:6 "Spirit" (ruach). Divine, the other party's, received by the human. The human anger follows in the same verse; Num 25:11 and 2Ch 28:9 have no seat; The seat-sense question these verses raise: where the Spirit is the seat word, the seat is God's, and the anger is the human's. This matches M20 v3 §20's Eze 39:29 row: "God's, received by Israel: the human side is the receiving".

14262.text: Part 2 verses: the prophet as the vessel of God's anger, plus human wrath taken up into God's praise: Filled, and worn out by holding it: "I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (Jer 6:11). The cause is the hearers' closed ears: "their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen … the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn" (6:10). The wrath fills the prophet because the word it belongs to has nowhere to go; Filled after being fed: "Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart" (Jer 15:16). Then "I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (15:17), and "Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable?" (15:18); The same words that delighted the heart fill the prophet with indignation and isolate him. The next movement is God's call to return (15:19) and a promise: "I will make you … a fortified wall of bronze … I am with you" (15:20); Carried by the Spirit, in the heat of his own spirit: "The Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the Lord being strong upon me. And I came to the exiles … and I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days" (Eze 3:14–15); Two spirits in one verse: the Spirit that carries, and the prophet's own spirit, heated; The heat ends in seven days of silence among the people before the word comes again (3:16); Across the three prophets, God's anger in the human does not come out as violence. It comes out as weariness (Jer 6:11), isolation and pain (Jer 15:17–18), bitterness and being overwhelmed (Eze 3:14–15). The human bearing of divine anger is suffering, not action. Compare Samson and Saul (Judg 14:19; 1Sa 11:6), whose Spirit-linked anger acted. Those were deliverers; these are prophets; Human wrath taken up into God's praise: "Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt" (Psa 76:10, B2). Human wrath is neither aligned with God's nor exceeding it. It is used by God. This is a fourth relation, beside §15's aligned (Phinehas), exceeding (2Ch 28:9) and following (Samson). The context is God "who cuts off the spirit of princes".

14264.text: What it does: Measure for measure: "They have made me jealous with what is no god; they have provoked me to anger with their idols. So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation" (Deu 32:21). Human anger is induced by God as the mirror of the anger they induced in him; The enemy's taunt: "had I not feared provocation by the enemy, lest their adversaries should misunderstand, lest they should say, 'Our hand is triumphant, it was not the Lord who did all this'" (32:27). The enemy's ka'as is a misreading of events, claiming God's work as their own; The enemy's nature: "their wine is the poison of serpents and the cruel venom of asps" (32:33).

14265.text: Where it comes from. Idolatry (32:16–21), and the enemy's lack of understanding: "a nation void of counsel, and there is no understanding in them" (32:28).

14268.text: Seat. None in the verses or ±3. The human inner operations here (being made jealous and angry, misunderstanding) are carried by the verbs and by "understanding" (32:28–29): Pointer: Rom 10:19 quotes Deu 32:21 and belongs to part 2.

14269.text: Part 2 verses: what they add (both were B8: human vexation induced by God): Paul reads Deu 32:21 as a statement about understanding: "But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, 'I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry'" (Rom 10:19). Then "I have been found by those who did not seek me" (10:20), and "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people" (10:21); The induced anger is set inside God's outstretched hands. It is a provocation meant to bring them back, not only a punishment; Compare Deu 32:29, "If they were wise, they would understand this"; God troubles the nations' hearts at another's fall: "I will trouble [ka'as] the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations" (Eze 32:9), and "They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life" (32:10). The vexation God induces comes from seeing a great power fall. It is a trouble of the onlooker, and it turns to fear for one's own life.

14271.text: What it does: It reads the rival's heart as evil: Eliab, "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle" (1Sa 17:28); It reckons the rival's future: Saul, "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?" (18:8); It attacks one's own son as the rival's ally: "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman … as long as the son of Jesse lives … neither you nor your kingdom shall be established" (20:30–31); It jeers: Sanballat "was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews … 'What are these feeble Jews doing?'" (Neh 4:1–2); It enlarges its target: Haman "disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone … sought to destroy all the Jews" (Est 3:6).

14272.text: Where it comes from. Seeing or hearing the rival's rise or refusal: the women's song (1Sa 18:7); David's question in the camp (17:26–28); "when Sanballat heard that we were building" (Neh 4:1), and "that the breaches were beginning to be closed" (4:7); "when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down" (Est 3:5), and "that he neither rose nor trembled before him" (5:9).

14273.text: How it co-exists: With surveillance: "Saul eyed David from that day on" (1Sa 18:9); With joy that flips. Haman "went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai … he was filled with wrath" (Est 5:9). Then he goes home and recounts "the splendor of his riches" (5:11). A v3 §4.4 read this ("Haman's swing"), and H v1 §2.1 read it as "wealth does not satisfy a heart set on a grievance". Both stand; With restraint that is only postponement: "Haman restrained himself and went home" (5:10); With plotting: "they all plotted together to come and fight" (Neh 4:8).

14275.text: Seat: In the verse:; 1Sa 17:28 "heart" (levav). Genuine, but the rival's heart as the angry man reads it, and misread. The angry man's own seat is not named; Est 5:9 "heart" (lev). Genuine. The bearer's own, in the state just before the anger; Outside the verse:; 1Sa 18:10 "a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul". The other party's (God's) sending, received by Saul, the day after the anger; Neh 4:6 "the people had a mind [heart] to work". Genuine. The heart of the rival party, the builders. New here. Between the enemy's two outbursts (4:1, 4:7) stands the builders' heart set on the work. The angry party has no seat named, and the ones they are angry at do. This fits M20 v3 §20 point 4, "the seat named in the contrast figure".

14276.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: The body's end of rivalrous anger: "The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!" (Psa 112:10). What he sees is the righteous man, whose "horn is exalted in honor" (112:9). Seeing the rival's rise ends in the angry one dissolving, not in the spear of 1Sa 18; Contrast seat: "His heart is steady; he will not be afraid" (112:8), said of the righteous one, two verses before. The seat is again named in the one the anger is aimed at (see Neh 4:6 above). Genuine; Rivalry among the disciples: "when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers" (Mat 20:24 = Mar 10:41). What they heard was Jesus's answer about the two brothers' place: "to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant" (Mat 20:23; Mar 10:40); Jesus answers by redefining greatness: "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them … It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant" (Mat 20:25–26; Mar 10:42–43); The anger at a rival's rise is not rebuked directly. The standing it is about is re-defined, so the rise it resented no longer counts. This is a reframing, the §9 and §6 move used on rivalry; Seat : none in-verse.

14277.text: Context (3:24–27) was read and gives no bearer. The wrath could be divine, Moabite, or a terror in Israel. The verse does not say, and this reading does not supply one.

14278.text: What it does: It divides by allegiance: "there is quarreling among you … each one of you says, 'I follow Paul,' or 'I follow Apollos'" (1Cor 1:11–12); it creates obstacles: "those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine" (Rom 16:17); it breeds: "they breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23); it spoils prayer: "lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1Ti 2:8).

14287.text: What it does, in the sayings' own images: Fuel: "As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife" (26:21), and the verse before: "For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases" (26:20); Pressure: "pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife" (30:33). The "nose" is aph itself: squeeze the anger-nose and blood comes; Weather: "The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks" (25:23); Danger to the meddler: "Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears" (26:17).

14288.text: Where it comes from: The angry person: "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife" (15:18); "A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression" (29:22); The evil heart: "with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord" (6:14); The tongue: a backbiting tongue (25:23), and the whisperer (26:20, 22); Wine: "Who has strife? Who has complaining? … Those who tarry long over wine" (23:29–30).

14291.text: Seat: In the verse: Pro 6:14 "heart". The sower's own. Genuine. The heart is where discord is devised before it is sown. Pro 25:23 "wind". Spurious; Outside the verse: Pro 26:23 "fervent lips with an evil heart". Genuine. The whisperer's.

14292.text: What it is. The governed form of anger: "long of nostrils", the human side of the idiom God uses of himself (Exo 34:6).

14293.text: What it does: It rules the self: "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Pro 16:32). Governing one's spirit is set above taking a city; It overlooks: "Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense" (19:11); It orders speech: "let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger" (Jam 1:19).

14294.text: Where it comes from. Understanding and good sense: "Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly" (Pro 14:29); "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (19:11); in 1Cor 13:5, love: "it is not irritable or resentful".

14296.text: What it leads to: Understanding (14:29), glory (19:11), and the righteousness that human anger cannot produce: "for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. Therefore put away all filthiness … and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:20–21). Slowness to anger opens the way to receiving the word; A "cool spirit" belongs to the "man of understanding" (Pro 17:27).

14297.text: Seat: In the verse:; Pro 16:32 "spirit" (ruach). The bearer's own, as what is ruled. Genuine; Pro 14:29 "temper" (ruach, "short of spirit"). The bearer's own. Genuine; Outside the verse:; Pro 14:30 "a tranquil heart gives life to the flesh". Genuine; Pro 17:27 "a cool spirit". Genuine; Jam 1:21 "save your souls". Genuine; Across §22 the seat is the ruach, as the thing ruled or kept cool. The anger word and the spirit word stand side by side, and "slow/long" and "short" describe both.

14298.text: What it does. It turns the other's anger: "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (15:1); "a wise man will appease" a king's wrath (16:14); "A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath" (21:14); "With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone" (25:15); "the wise turn away wrath" while "scoffers set a city aflame" (29:8).

14299.text: How it co-exists. Softness is set against its opposite each time: a soft answer against a harsh word (15:1), wise men against scoffers (29:8): The gift is the ambiguous instrument. "A gift in secret averts anger" (21:14) sits in a chapter that also knows "A wicked man accepts a bribe in secret to pervert … justice". The saying reports that it works. It does not approve it; The narrative parallels in part 1:; Judah's plea (Gen 44:18) and Joab's scripted line (2Sa 11:20) are §5's pleading and scripting strands; Naaman's servants turn his rage by a soft question (2Ki 5:13).

14302.text: What it does. It heats the self, and "it tends only to evil" (Psa 37:8). The anger turns inward on its bearer, and outward into wrongdoing.

14305.text: What it leads to. A reason is given in the next verse, each time: the wicked "will soon fade like the grass" (37:2); "the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land" (37:9); "the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out" (Pro 24:20). The fretting is answered by a longer view of time, which links to §3's anger that has a course: Pro 24:17–18, just before: "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the Lord see it and be displeased". Neither heating oneself at the wicked's success nor rejoicing at their fall is allowed.

14307.text: What it does. It stands among its companions: "envy, murder, strife, deceit" (Rom 1:29); "quarreling and jealousy" (Rom 13:13); "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Cor 12:20); "enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy" (Gal 5:20–21); "bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander … malice" (Eph 4:31); "anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Col 3:8).

14309.text: How it co-exists. Each list faces an opposite: "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience …" (Gal 5:22); "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (Eph 4:32); "put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge" (Col 3:10); "put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14); In Eph 4:30–31 the list comes straight after "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God". Anger is set as something that grieves the Spirit.

14312.text: Where it comes from. Seeing the good done: "when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out … 'Hosanna'" (Mat 21:15); "when the disciples saw it" (Mat 26:8); "because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath" (Luk 13:14); "because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well" (Joh 7:23); "because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection" (Act 4:2).

14313.text: How it co-exists. It is answered in each case by a reframing of the norm: "She has done a beautiful thing to me" (Mat 26:10; Mar 14:6); "Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox …? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham … be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?" (Luk 13:15–16); "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision … are you angry with me because … I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances" (Joh 7:23–24); "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise" (Mat 21:16).

14316.text: What it does. It fills, cuts, grinds and cries out: "all in the synagogue were filled with wrath" (Luk 4:28); "they were enraged [literally sawn through] and wanted to kill them" (Act 5:33); "they were enraged [cut to the heart], and they ground their teeth at him" (Act 7:54); "they were enraged and were crying out, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'" (Act 19:28); "Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain?" (Act 4:25, quoting Psa 2).

14317.text: Where it comes from. Hearing: "When they heard these things" (Luk 4:28; Act 5:33; 7:54; 19:28); the grace to the widow of Zarephath and to Naaman rather than to Israel (Luk 4:26–27); "the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him" (Act 5:32); "you who received the law … and did not keep it" (Act 7:53); a threat to trade and to a goddess's standing (Act 19:26–27).

14319.text: What it leads to: Trying to throw him off a cliff (Luk 4:29), stoning (Act 7:58), a riot (Act 19:29); The end God sets: "all who were incensed against him … shall come and be ashamed" (Isa 45:24); "The nations raged, but your wrath came" (Rev 11:18, B2). The collective rage meets the divine wrath at the end. This is Psa 2 as the apostles read it: "against the Lord and against his Anointed … for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus" (Act 4:26–27).

14320.text: Seat: In the verse:; Act 7:54: the M47 tag's surface is "enraged". The Greek reads dieprionto tais kardiais autōn, "they were sawn through in their hearts" [lexical, not in DB]. The ESV folds "hearts" into "enraged". Genuine. The enraged ones' own heart, as where the word cut. Not in any batch: new; Compare pilot §1.3 (cholaō built on bile) and §1.1 (thumos). Here the seat is a separate word, hidden by the translation, not by the Greek; Act 5:33 uses the same verb without "hearts" [lexical]; Act 4:25 "Holy Spirit". Divine, speaking (the Spirit speaking through David's psalm). Spurious for the ragers; Outside the verse: Act 7:55 "full of the Holy Spirit"; Act 5:32 "the Holy Spirit … given to those who obey". Divine, as received by the other party.

14321.text: What it does to the one attacked: It swallows: "they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us; then the flood would have swept us away" (Psa 124:3–4); It bears a grudge and drops trouble: "they drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me" (Psa 55:3); It poisons through speech: "They make their tongue sharp as a serpent's, and under their lips is the venom of asps" (140:3); "They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear" (58:4). Venom is the image of the enemy's anger in speech. Compare §16's Deu 32:33; In Paul's case it is summed up without detail: "our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn — fighting without and fear within" (2Cor 7:5). Outer conflict and inner fear are named as a pair.

14323.text: How it co-exists: With the attacked one's inner state named next: "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me" (Psa 55:4–5). The enemy's anger (55:3) is felt as anguish of heart (55:4); With an appeal to God's anger against it: "Arise, O Lord, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies" (Psa 7:6, B2). The human's answer to another's anger is to call on God's. Compare §24, where the answer to the wicked's success is waiting, not heating oneself.

14324.text: What it leads to. Deliverance, looked back on or asked for: "If it had not been the Lord who was on our side" (Psa 124:1–2); "you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me" (138:7); "all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame" (Isa 41:11), after "fear not, for I am with you" (41:10); "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2Cor 7:6).

14326.text: What it does: It shakes the heart: "the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind" (Isa 7:2); it goes on all day: "you fear continually all the day because of the wrath of the oppressor" (Isa 51:13); it makes a subordinate refuse: "I fear my lord the king … So you would endanger my head with the king" (Dan 1:10).

14327.text: Where it comes from. From the other's anger, and from forgetting God: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isa 51:12–13).

14328.text: How it co-exists. The freedom is given in the same verses as the fear: "Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin" (Isa 7:4). The anger is shrunk to smoking stubs. "If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all" (7:9); "And where is the wrath of the oppressor?" (Isa 51:13). The anger is questioned out of existence; "By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible" (Heb 11:27). Seeing the invisible makes the king's anger nothing to fear; Daniel's answer to the eunuch's fear is a test: "Test your servants for ten days" (Dan 1:12). This follows "Daniel resolved [set on his heart] that he would not defile himself" (1:8).

14329.text: Seat: In the verse: Isa 7:4 "heart" (levav). The bearer's own, as what must not faint. Genuine; Outside the verse:; Isa 7:2 "the heart of Ahaz … shook". Genuine; Dan 1:8 "resolved" [set on his heart]. Genuine. The contrast figure's own. The one afraid of the king (the eunuch) has no seat named. The one who is not afraid (Daniel) has a heart that resolved.

14330.text: What it is. 'Ebrah in its sense of overflowing: arrogance that spills out, rendered "insolence" or "pride".

14335.text: What it does. It acts at once, with no interval: "in anger his master delivered him to the jailers" (Mat 18:34); "The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city" (22:7); "the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, 'Go out quickly … and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame'" (Luk 14:21).

14337.text: How it co-exists. In Luk 14:21 anger turns into a wider invitation, not punishment. The anger that invitations were refused fills the house with the poor: "compel people to come in, that my house may be filled" (14:23). Of the three parable angers, one ends in grace to outsiders. Mat 22:8–9 does the same after the destruction: "invite to the wedding feast as many as you find".

14340.text: What it does: "he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, 'Stretch out your hand'" (Mar 3:5). The anger looks, then acts to heal; "when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, 'Let the children come to me; do not hinder them'" (Mar 10:14). The indignation is on behalf of the children, like §7's indignation for another.

14342.text: How it co-exists. With grief, in the same clause: "with anger, grieved". This is the one M02 verse where anger and grief are held together, at the same object, by the same person. Part 1 had Jonathan's anger with grief (1Sa 20:34), but that grief was for David, not at the one he was angry with. Jesus grieves over those he is angry with. With blessing: "he took them in his arms and blessed them" (Mar 10:16).

14344.text: Seat: In the verse: Mar 3:5 "heart" (kardia). The other party's hardened heart, as the object of both the anger and the grief. Genuine. Jesus's own seat is not named; his opponents' hardened heart is. This is the §1 and §38 point 3 pattern again; Outside the verse: Mar 3:4 "to save life" (psychē). Life-sense, the life at stake.

14348.text: What it does: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink — you pour out your wrath and make them drunk, in order to gaze at their nakedness!" (Hab 2:15). The anger (or venom, chemah) is poured out to shame another; Babylon "made all nations drink the wine of the passion [thumos] of her sexual immorality" (Rev 14:8). "All nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality" (18:3).

14349.text: How it co-exists. The drink comes back to the one who gave it, as God's cup: "You will have your fill of shame instead of glory. Drink, yourself … The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (Hab 2:16); "he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger" (Rev 14:10, divine, read as context).

14350.text: What it does: "let us consider how to stir up [paroxusmos, the word of Act 15:39's 'sharp disagreement'] one another to love and good works" (Heb 10:24); "your zeal has stirred up most of them" (2Cor 9:2); "what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you … what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment!" (2Cor 7:11).

14353.text: The anger is very often kindled by something perceived: Part 1: thirteen verses name "heard" or "saw" in the verse itself (Gen 34:7; 39:19; Exo 32:19; Judg 9:30; 1Sa 11:6; 17:28; 2Sa 13:21; Neh 4:1, 7; 5:6; Est 3:5; 5:9; Job 32:5); Part 2 adds Psa 112:10; Mat 2:16; 20:24; 21:15; 26:8; Mar 10:14; 10:41; Luk 4:28; Act 5:33; 7:54; 17:16; 19:28; These are counted from the texts cited. No wider count was made.
