14354.text: The answer the texts give to human anger is most often a question or a reframing, not a rebuke. This is observed across the passages above, not counted over M02: God's question to Cain (Gen 4:6) and to Jonah (Jon 4:4, 9); Joseph's "not you … but God" (Gen 45:8); the father's "this your brother" (Luk 15:32); Jesus's reframing of the norm for the indignant and of greatness for the rival disciples; Nathan's parable turned round (2Sa 12:7).

14357.text: In-verse seats new to M47: Psa 95:8; Eze 32:9; Act 4:25; 7:54; 16:18; 2Cor 7:5.

14358.text: The lion's growl is the image. The subject's life is what is at stake, as it was for Haman (Est 7:7).

14359.text: All genuine. All the bearer's own. The sequence runs: named by another (1:8) → the narrator (1:10) → the heart as the place of voiceless prayer (1:13) → named by herself (1:15). The M02 word comes last (1:16), in her own summary.

14360.text: Anger's constant neighbours are envy and jealousy (4 of the 6 lists: all but Eph 4:31 and Col 3:8) and speech-sins (slander, clamor, obscene talk).

14361.text: The frame's words are the seat's substitutes, and nothing here changes that. New: Eph 4:30–31 puts the Spirit's grief directly before the anger list. So the other party affected by human anger is named as the Holy Spirit.

14492.text: What it does: Abraham: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there" (Gen 18:30), and at the last: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten" (18:32); Gideon, after the fleece was wet: "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece" (Judg 6:39); The same form appears in two different kinds of asking. Abraham asks for a city he does not belong to. Gideon asks for assurance for himself.

14493.text: How it co-exists: Boldness and restraint in one sentence. The plea not to anger does not stop the asking. It is what allows the asking; Every request is granted, and no anger comes. "I will not do it, if I find thirty there" (Gen 18:30); "God did so that night" (Judg 6:40). The anger feared never appears in either passage.

14494.text: What it does. Two different occasions: At the call: "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else." "Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against Moses" (Exo 4:13–14). The anger is answered at once by provision: Aaron "is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart" (4:14); "I will be with your mouth and with his mouth" (4:15); At the end: "Even with me the Lord was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there'" (Deu 1:37); "the Lord was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me … 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again'" (3:26); "I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan" (4:21–22).

14495.text: Where it comes from: Exo 4: the servant's refusal of the call; Deuteronomy: "on your account" / "because of you", three times (Deu 1:37; 3:26; 4:21). Moses traces the anger at himself to the people. The leader bears God's anger as the people's leader, and says so.

14497.text: Seat: In the verse: Exo 4:14 "glad in his heart". The other party's (Aaron's). Genuine. Already read in G v3 §13.2 ("the heart goes out to meet"). Read from the M02 side, it shows that the anger at Moses is met with a glad heart coming towards him; Outside the verse: none in Deu 1:34–40; 3:23–29; 4:18–25.

14498.text: Part B: Psa 106:32. "They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psa 106:32–33): The psalm gives an inner route for the "because of you" that Moses spoke of in Deuteronomy. The people's provocation reaches a spirit, and Moses' rash speech follows; Whose spirit is not determinable. The M47 spirit classification v2 marks Psa 106:33 as [U] (#1880 item C-R4; C v3 R4). It could be Moses' spirit embittered, or God's Spirit rebelled against (compare Isa 63:10). Either way, the verse ties Meribah to Moses' loss "on their account".

14499.text: What it does: Sung by the rescued: "you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble" (Exo 15:7); Promised to the obedient: "if you carefully obey his voice … then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries" (Exo 23:22); Released by the cry of the weak: "If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn" (Exo 22:23–24); Released by the psalmist's call: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … my cry came to his ears. Then the earth reeled … because he was angry" (2Sa 22:7–8).

14501.text: How it co-exists: The enemy's own appetite. In the song, the enemy boasts, "my desire [nephesh] shall have its fill of them" (Exo 15:9), and is answered by the wind of God (15:10). The enemy's appetite and God's fury meet over the same people. Already read in F v4 §8.4 ("the enemy's soul and the pursued soul"); The same anger threatens the one it protects, if roles reverse. Exo 22:24 is said to Israel about their own widows: "I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows". God's anger is for the weak, whoever the oppressor is.

14502.text: Part B: Psa 7:11; 18:7; 21:9; 78:49; 78:50; 110:5; Isa 30:27; 30:30; 66:14; 66:15: Psa 18:7 is the psalm text of 2Sa 22:8: "In my distress I called upon the Lord … because he was angry" (Psa 18:6–7); The upright in heart, and the call to repent. "God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psa 7:11). This follows "you who test the minds and hearts … who saves the upright in heart" (7:9–10), and is followed by "If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword" (7:12). The protection is for the upright in heart, and the indignation waits on repentance; The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5); The Exodus retold: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psa 78:50). "Then he led out his people like sheep" (78:52); The protected rejoice in the heart; "You shall have a song … and gladness of heart" (Isa 30:29), while "the Assyrians will be terror-stricken" (30:31); "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you … You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass" (66:13–14); The protected are the people the anger struck earlier: "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26); Seat ; In the verse: Isa 66:14 "your heart shall rejoice". The comforted people's own. Genuine. Psa 78:50 "them" (nephesh) is the Egyptians' life. Life-sense; Outside: Psa 7:9–10 "hearts" / "upright in heart". Isa 30:29 "gladness of heart"; What part B adds. Part A had only praise (Exo 15). Part B places the joy of the protected in the heart.

14503.text: Part C: Eze 36:6; Nah 1:2; Hab 3:8; 3:12; Zec 8:2: Anger for the reproached: "Behold, I have spoken in my jealous wrath, because you have suffered the reproach of the nations" (Eze 36:6). Edom took the land "with wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (36:5). "you will soon come home" (36:8); "I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath. … I have returned to Zion" (Zec 8:2–3). "The Lord … keeps wrath for his enemies" (Nah 1:2); Habakkuk's prayer, from inside the fear:; "O Lord, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O Lord, do I fear … in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2); "Was your wrath against the rivers …? … You went out for the salvation of your people" (3:8, 13); the enemy came "rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret" (3:14); then: "I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver … rottenness enters into my bones … Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us" (3:16); and: "Though the fig tree should not blossom … yet I will rejoice in the Lord" (3:17–18).

14504.text: What it does: God himself leaves the door open: "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them" (Exo 32:10). The anger waits on whether Moses will let God alone; Moses argues. He argues from ownership: "why does your wrath burn hot against your people, whom you have brought out" (32:11). He argues from God's reputation: "Why should the Egyptians say, 'With evil intent did he bring them out'?" (32:12). He argues from promise: "Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel" (32:13); He argues from justice between the one and the many: "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" (Num 16:22); With the body: "I lay prostrate before the Lord … forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water" (Deu 9:18); For the particular man: "the Lord was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also" (Deu 9:20).

14505.text: Where it comes from. From fear. "For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the Lord bore against you" (Deu 9:19). The intercessor's own fear of God's anger drives the plea for others. It does not stop it.

14506.text: How it co-exists: Intercession sits alongside the intercessor's own anger. The same chapter has Moses' own anger breaking the tablets. Moses is angry at the people and pleads for them against God's anger, within one episode; It is answered: "the Lord relented" (Exo 32:14); "the Lord listened to me that time also" (Deu 9:19).

14508.text: Seat: In the verse: Num 16:22 "spirits of all flesh". God's relation to every human spirit, given as the ground of the plea. Genuine. Nothing new; Outside: none in Exo 32:7–15; Deu 9:15–22; Pointer: the fasting body (Deu 9:18) does the seat's work here, as the face and bed do in U1 §1.

14509.text: Part B: Psa 106:23. "Therefore he said he would destroy them — had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.": The psalm names Moses' intercession (Exo 32; Deu 9) "standing in the breach". Its context is "They forgot God, their Savior" (106:21); Part B also shows intercession forbidden and absent:; forbidden: "As for you, do not pray for this people … do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you"; absent: "there was no one to intercede"; repaid with evil: Jer 18:20.

14510.text: Part C: Eze 9:8; Dan 9:16; Zec 1:12: The prophet refused. "while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, 'Ah, Lord God! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel …?'" (Eze 9:8). The answer is no: "The guilt … is exceedingly great … For they say, 'The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare" (9:9–10). Some are spared: the mark is put "on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations" (9:4, context read). Those who grieve over the sin are marked. The one who pleads for the rest is not answered; Daniel's confession-intercession:; "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem … because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem … [has] become a byword" (Dan 9:16); "the Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (9:14); "for your own sake" (9:17); "we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy" (9:18); An angel intercedes: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem …, against which you have been angry these seventy years?" This is answered with "gracious and comforting words" (Zec 1:12–13).

14511.text: What it does. Three moments: Proclaimed and received: "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger" (Exo 34:6). Moses "quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped" (34:8); Pleaded back: Moses quotes it to God word for word as his argument: "'The Lord is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love …' Please pardon the iniquity of this people" (Num 14:18–19). It is answered: "I have pardoned, according to your word" (14:20); Recited in confession, as history: "they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (Neh 9:17). The name is now told as what God has shown himself to be through Israel's whole story.

14512.text: Where it comes from. From God's own mouth first (Exo 34:6). Every human use goes back to that proclamation.

14513.text: How it co-exists: The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17; The name includes its limit: "but who will by no means clear the guilty" (Exo 34:7; Num 14:18). Moses quotes the limit too, and still pleads.

14514.text: Seat. None in-verse. Neh 9:20 "your good Spirit to instruct them" is God's, given. Pointer: U1 §13 has Jonah using the same creed against God (Jon 4:2). With Moses and the Levites of Neh 9, one creed is used three ways: worship, plea, and complaint. Pilot §2.2 already notes the idiom shared between God and the wise (Pro 14:29 and others), and U1 §22 reads the human side of it.

14515.text: Part B: Psa 86:15; 103:8; 145:8. Three more uses of the name. Pilot §2.2 already lists all three as uses of the idiom: An individual's plea against "insolent men": "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger … Turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psa 86:14–16); A recital with its reasoning: "He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins" (103:9–10). This comes straight after "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7). The psalm names Moses as the one to whom the name was made known; Praise: "The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made" (145:9); The one creed is now used five ways: worship (Exo 34:8), plea (Num 14; Psa 86), confession (Neh 9), complaint and praise (Psa 145); Seat . Outside: Psa 86:13 "you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol". The pleader's own. Genuine.

14516.text: Part C: Mic 7:18; Nah 1:3: "Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression …? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love" (Mic 7:18); "you will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea" (7:19). (#1892 pointer: read.) This is the creed turned into a question of wonder; Used against an enemy: "The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and the Lord will by no means clear the guilty" (Nah 1:3), against Nineveh. The same words that Jonah complained were used to spare Nineveh are here used to announce its end; The creed is now used eight ways: worship, plea, confession, complaint, praise, wonder (Micah), the announcement of judgment (Nahum), and the ground for returning.

14517.text: What it does: The guard: "the Levites shall camp around the tabernacle of the testimony, so that there may be no wrath on the congregation" (Num 1:53); "keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath" (Num 18:5). The guard is a people placed in a ring, and "any outsider who comes near shall be put to death" (Num 1:51; 18:7); Grief held back: after Nadab and Abihu die, Aaron and his sons may not mourn: "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation" (Lev 10:6). "And Aaron held his peace" (10:3). The priest's own grief is withheld because of the holy. The rest of Israel "may bewail the burning" (10:6); The breaking out: "Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah" (2Sa 6:6–7; 1Ch 13:9–10). The act was a reflex to steady the ark.

14518.text: How it co-exists: The breaking out stops a celebration. "David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord" (2Sa 6:5; 1Ch 13:8); It produces anger at God, then fear of God. "David was angry … David was afraid of the Lord that day … 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'" (2Sa 6:8–9; 1Ch 13:11–12). This is U1 §13 and §37; (New here, from context.) The fear is resolved by seeing blessing on someone else. "The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household … So David went and brought up the ark … with rejoicing" (2Sa 6:11–12). David does not reason his way past the fear. He watches another household live with the ark.

14520.text: Part C: Eze 43:8. "setting their threshold by my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them. They have defiled my holy name … so I have consumed them in my anger." Then: "Now let them put away their whoring … and I will dwell in their midst forever" (43:9), and the temple is to be described "that they may be ashamed of their iniquities" (43:10): Part A's nearness was a danger of approach (Uzzah). Here the nearness is profaned by building one's own house against God's. The remedy is a new dwelling and shame.

14521.text: What it does. It is warned of in advance (Lev 26; Deu 4–32; Jos 23) and narrated afterwards (Judg 2; 1Ki 11; 2Ki 17; 2Ch 28). The same act appears as prediction and as history.

14522.text: Where it comes from. This is where the texts give most. The roots named in the context of these verses: Forgetting. "take care lest you forget the Lord" (Deu 6:12); "You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth" (Deu 32:18); Fullness. "Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him" (Deu 32:15); "when … they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods" (Deu 31:20). Plenty comes before the turn; A deceived or turning heart. "Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside" (Deu 11:16); "a man or woman … whose heart is turning away today" (Deu 29:18); Solomon's "heart had turned away" (1Ki 11:9), because "his wives turned away his heart" (1Ki 11:4); False security in the heart. The man who "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'" (Deu 29:19). Here the anger is said to refuse forgiveness to one man, singled out: "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him … the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will smoke against that man" (29:20); Intermarriage. "they would turn away your sons from following me" (Deu 7:4); Distress. "In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the Lord — this same King Ahaz. For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him" (2Ch 28:22–23). Distress drives Ahaz further from God, not back. Contrast §16, where distress leads to crying out; Stubbornness, and not believing. "they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the Lord their God" (2Ki 17:14); "I know how rebellious and stubborn you are" (Deu 31:27).

14523.text: How it co-exists: You become what you follow. "They went after false idols and became false" (2Ki 17:15). In exile "you will serve gods of wood and stone … that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell" (Deu 4:28); Walking contrary meets walking contrary. "if … you will not listen to me, but walk contrary to me, then I will walk contrary to you in fury" (Lev 26:27–28). The anger answers in the form of the provocation. The next verses are the famine ("eat the flesh of your sons", 26:29) and "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). F v4 §4 reads this as mutual abhorrence; What is known in the heart. Joshua ties the threat to what the people already know: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things … so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (Jos 23:14–15). The heart's own knowledge of God's faithfulness is made the ground for believing the warning; The generation that did not know. "there arose another generation after them who did not know the Lord or the work that he had done" (Judg 2:10), and they "provoked the Lord to anger" (2:12).

14524.text: What it leads to. Scattering, drought ("he will shut up the heavens", Deu 11:17), being given to plunderers, removal "out of his sight" (2Ki 17:18). Also the hidden face.

14525.text: Seat: In the verse: 1Ki 11:9 "his heart had turned away". Solomon's own. Genuine, the cause. Already read in A v3 §2.2 and pilot §2 ("the heart that provokes the anger"); Outside the verse (all genuine unless noted):; Deu 11:16 "lest your heart be deceived" (before) and 11:18 "lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul" (after). The deceived heart is the cause; the heart filled with the words is the guard. B v3 §4.1; C v3 §8.2; E v2 §4.1; G v3 §10; H v1 §5.1; Deu 29:18–19 "whose heart is turning away" / "blesses himself in his heart … stubbornness of my heart". E v2 §4.1, §12; C v3 §9.1; F v4 §9.6. Pilot §1.6 reads 29:20 with it; 1Ki 11:4 "his wives turned away his heart … his heart was not wholly true"; Jos 23:14 "you know in your hearts and souls". B v3 §1.1 ("the heart as the knower"); Lev 26:29–30 "flesh" (bodily) and "my soul will abhor you"; Nothing new in the seat itself. What part A adds is how regularly the heart is named in the verses around the anger verse, and not in the anger verse itself. Pilot §2 had said that the "anger was kindled" series carries "the human inner cause by narrative". Part A confirms this, and finds that the seat is named nearby, in warnings and explanations.

14526.text: Part B: Psa 78:58, 78:59, 78:62; Isa 65:3; Jer 7:18, 7:19, 7:20; 11:17; 15:14; 17:4; 25:6, 25:7; 32:29, 32:30, 32:31, 32:32 (16 verses): More roots; Treachery like the fathers': "turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow" (Psa 78:57); Self-holiness: "who say, 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you'" (Isa 65:5). This is said to a God who says "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2); Trust in man: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5); From youth, turning the back: "done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth" (Jer 32:30); "They have turned to me their back and not their face … they have not listened to receive instruction" (32:33); Whole households, all ranks: "The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough … to provoke me to anger" (Jer 7:18); "their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets" (32:32); The provocation turns on the provoker. "Is it I whom they provoke? declares the Lord. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?" (Jer 7:19); "that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm" (25:7); Pilot §2 lists Jer 7 in the ka'as series; What part B adds is the text's own statement that the provoking harms the provoker. Part A had "they … became false" (2Ki 17:15). Jeremiah adds "to their own shame" and "to your own harm"; Seat . Outside: Jer 17:5 "whose heart turns away". Genuine. Nothing new.

14527.text: Part C: Eze 8:17; 8:18; 20:28; Hos 8:5; 12:14: "Is it too light a thing …? … they put the branch to their nose" (Eze 8:17), with "their backs to the temple of the Lord, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun" (8:16); Prayer refused: "And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them" (8:18); God's own "how long?": "How long will they be incapable of innocence?" (Hos 8:5). The question the laments ask of God is asked by God of the people; "Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers …?" (Eze 20:30); "Ephraim has given bitter provocation" (Hos 12:14).

14528.text: What it does: Complaint: "the people complained in the hearing of the Lord about their misfortunes, and when the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled" (Num 11:1); Craving: "While the meat was yet between their teeth … the anger of the Lord was kindled" (Num 11:33). The place is named after it: "there they buried the people who had the craving" (11:34). Already read in A v3 §2.2 ("craving and anger"); Unbelief: "Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the Lord your God … And the Lord heard your words and was angered" (Deu 1:32–34); Discouraging the heart: the spies "discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land" (Num 32:9), and "the Lord's anger was kindled on that day" (32:10).

14530.text: How it co-exists: The provocation is inherited. "you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the Lord" (Num 32:14). The sons are warned that they are repeating the fathers. They answer by offering to go armed before their brothers (32:16–17); Remembering is commanded against self-righteousness. "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (Deu 9:4); "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (9:7). Memory of provoking God is the cure for the heart's claim to righteousness; Moses caught between. In Num 11:10–15 Moses hears the weeping, is "displeased", and says: "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? … kill me at once … that I may not see my wretchedness" (11:11, 15). The leader between God's anger and the people's complaint asks to die.

14531.text: What it leads to. Fire, plague, forty years of wandering "until all the generation that had done evil … was gone" (Num 32:13), and a list of place names that keeps the memory: "At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the Lord to wrath" (Deu 9:22).

14532.text: Seat: In the verse: Num 11:33 "meat" (basar). Spurious. Pilot §0 lists it among the links that do not count; Outside: Num 32:7, 9 "discourage the heart of the people". The people's own heart, as what the spies weakened. Genuine. Deu 9:4–5 "Do not say in your heart … the uprightness of your heart". Genuine. Num 32:7, 9 is not cited in any batch. New as an M02 context seat: discouraging the heart of others is what provokes the anger.

14533.text: Part B: Psa 78:21, 78:31; 95:11: Psalm 78 retells the wilderness:; "Can God spread a table in the wilderness?" (78:19), answered by anger "because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power" (78:22); "before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose" (78:30–31); "In spite of all this, they still sinned … So he made their days vanish like a breath, and their years in terror" (78:32–33); Psa 95:11: "I swore in my wrath, 'They shall not enter my rest'", after "They are a people who go astray in their heart" (95:10). Part B's form of "remember" is a psalm that is sung, so that the hearers "do not harden your hearts"; Seat . Psa 95:10 "heart". Nothing new. Psa 78:37 "heart" is read under §33.

14534.text: Part C: Heb 3:10; 3:11; 3:17; 4:3: Hebrews reads Psalm 95 to a new audience:; "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today,' that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin" (Heb 3:12–13); "So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief" (3:19); "let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it" (4:1); "we who have believed enter that rest" (4:3); The wilderness provocation is made a daily warning, kept by exhorting one another — part A's "remember and do not forget" (Deu 9:7) in a new form; Seat ; In the verse: Heb 3:10 "go astray in their heart". The fathers'. Genuine; Outside: Heb 3:8, 15 "do not harden your hearts"; 3:12 "evil, unbelieving heart".

14535.text: What it does: Spoken against: "Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them (Num 12:8–9). The charge is a lack of fear; Silenced: Amaziah to the prophet: "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" (2Ch 25:16). The prophet stops, but says: "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."; Killed: after Jehoiada died, "the king listened to them [the princes]"; prophets "testified against them, but they would not pay attention"; Zechariah, whom "the Spirit of God clothed", was stoned "in the court of the house of the Lord" (2Ch 24:17–21).

14536.text: Where it comes from: From rivalry (Miriam and Aaron, Num 12:1–2, not read here); From loss of the restraining figure: "after the death of Jehoiada the princes … paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them" (2Ch 24:17); From pride after victory: Amaziah worships "the gods of a people who did not deliver their own people from your hand" (2Ch 25:15).

14537.text: Part C: 1Th 2:16. "who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out … by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved — so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!" (1Th 2:15–16): The messenger spurned now includes hindering the message from reaching others; The same passage has Paul "torn away from you … in person not in heart".

14538.text: What it does: Atonement carried into the plague: "Take your censer … carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the Lord" (Num 16:46). Aaron "ran into the midst … And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped" (16:47–48). The priest's body stands on the line; Execution of the leaders: "hang them in the sun before the Lord, that the fierce anger of the Lord may turn away from Israel" (Num 25:4). Then Phinehas's spear (25:7), read in U1 §15 (SP, 25:11); Nothing of the devoted thing kept: "None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the Lord may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you" (Deu 13:17).

14539.text: Where it comes from. From the command (Num 25:4; Deu 13) or the leader's urgency (Num 16:46: "carry it quickly").

14540.text: What it leads to. The plague stops; the anger turns; mercy and compassion are promised in the same verse as the purging (Deu 13:17).

14542.text: What it does. "God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the Lord took his stand in the way as his adversary" (Num 22:22). "The donkey saw the angel … And Balaam struck the donkey" (22:23, 25).

14544.text: How it co-exists. Balaam's own anger at the donkey falls on the creature that saved him. Balaam is angry at the donkey while God is angry at Balaam, and only the donkey sees it.

14546.text: What it does: Outsiders ask: "the next generation … and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will say … 'Why has the Lord done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?'" (Deu 29:22, 24); An answer is given: "It is because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord" (29:25), "Therefore the anger of the Lord was kindled against this land" (29:27), "and the Lord uprooted them from their land in anger and fury and great wrath … as they are this day" (29:28); The sufferers ask: "they will say in that day, 'Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?'" (Deu 31:17). The people read their trouble as God's absence; A king reads it to his people: "the wrath of the Lord came on Judah and Jerusalem … as you see with your own eyes" (2Ch 29:8); Exiles explain it to foreign officials: "because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar" (Ezr 5:12).

14549.text: Part B: Jer 8:19. "Behold, the cry of the daughter of my people …: 'Is the Lord not in Zion? Is her King not in her?' 'Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images …?'" Then: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved" (8:20): The people read the ruin as God's absence, as in Deu 31:17. God answers with a counter-question about their provocation; Between them stands the prophet: "My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me" (8:18); "For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn" (8:21). See §45; Seat . Jer 8:18 "my heart is sick". The prophet's own. Genuine. Jer 8:21 "my heart" is the ESV's; there is no M47 tag in the DB for that verse. It is not counted as a seat.

14550.text: Part C: Eze 36:18. "I poured out my wrath upon them … I scattered them among the nations." Then: "wherever they came, they profaned my holy name, in that people said of them, 'These are the people of the Lord, and yet they had to go out of his land'" (36:18–20): The nations read the exile as a failure of God. This is the reverse of Deu 29:24–25, where the nations read it rightly; The exiles, simply by being exiles, give the wrong reading.

14556.text: What it does: "the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan … took some … And the anger of the Lord burned against the people of Israel" (Jos 7:1). One man took, and the text says the people broke faith; The fear drives a confrontation. The tribes fear the eastern altar: "if you too rebel against the Lord today then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel" (Jos 22:18). "Did not Achan … break faith … and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And he did not perish alone for his iniquity" (22:20).

14557.text: How it co-exists: Accusation and generosity together. The same speech that threatens also offers land: "pass over into the Lord's land … and take for yourselves a possession among us" (Jos 22:19); The accused answer by appealing to God's knowledge: "The Mighty One, God, the Lord! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion … do not spare us today" (Jos 22:22); The reverse plea. Moses argues against collective anger. David, after the census, asks to bear it alone: "I have sinned … But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house". The one who sinned asks that the anger fall on himself only.

14558.text: What it leads to. The offender removed ("Why did you bring trouble on us? The Lord brings trouble on you today", Jos 7:25), a heap of stones, "Then the Lord turned from his burning anger" (7:26). The misunderstanding over the altar is resolved (22:21–23 onward).

14559.text: What it does: An oath kept, though obtained by deceit: "We have sworn to them by the Lord … now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath" (Jos 9:19–20). "Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders" (9:18); A brother warned: judges are to "warn them, that they may not incur guilt before the Lord and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers" (2Ch 19:10). Warning another guards both of them; A foreign king's decree: "Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full … lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons" (Ezr 7:23). Fear of God's wrath appears in a Persian king.

14561.text: How it co-exists. Against the crowd: in Jos 9 the leaders keep the oath while "all the congregation murmured".

14563.text: What it does: Given over: "he gave them over to plunderers … so that they could no longer withstand their enemies … And they were in terrible distress" (Judg 2:14–15); Crying out: "when the people of Israel cried out to the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer" (Judg 3:9); "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God" (10:10); "do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day" (10:15); Seeking favour: "Jehoahaz sought the favor of the Lord, and the Lord listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel" (2Ki 13:4); Relapsing: "whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers … They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways" (Judg 2:19); "Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam" (2Ki 13:6).

14565.text: Part B: Psa 106:40: "they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters … Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against his people, and he abhorred his heritage; he gave them into the hand of the nations" (106:38–41); The psalm sums the whole cycle: "Many times he delivered them, but they were rebellious in their purposes and were brought low through their iniquity. Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented" (106:43–45); This confirms the part-A reading that God answers the cry and the distress, not a completed repentance.

14566.text: What it does. "Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the Lord has done this thing to you this day" (1Sa 28:18).

14567.text: Where it comes from. From disobedience in the commission (1Sa 15, not read here).

14570.text: What it does. "Again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, 'Go, number Israel and Judah'" (2Sa 24:1). Joab objects: "why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" (24:3). The king's word prevailed (24:4). Chronicles records that "Joab … began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this" (1Ch 27:24).

14571.text: Where it comes from. 2Sa 24:1 names God's anger as the source of the incitement. The verse gives no inner cause in David. Joab's question names a delight in the king.

14574.text: What it does: Foreseen in Solomon's prayer: "If they sin against you — for there is no one who does not sin — and you are angry with them … yet if they turn their heart … and repent … with all their heart and with all their soul … then hear" (1Ki 8:46–49; 2Ch 6:36–39); Josiah hears the book: "he tore his clothes … 'great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not obeyed'" (2Ki 22:11, 13; 2Ch 34:19, 21). The answer names the heart: "because your heart was penitent [tender], and you humbled yourself … and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you" (2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 34:27); Rehoboam and the princes: "humbled themselves and said, 'The Lord is righteous.' When the Lord saw that they humbled themselves … I will not destroy them" (2Ch 12:6–7); "when he humbled himself the wrath of the Lord turned from him" (12:12); Hezekiah's pride and humbling: "Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came … But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah" (2Ch 32:25–26); Ezra confesses: "you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved … shall we break your commandments again …? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us …? … you are just … none can stand before you" (Ezr 9:13–15); Manasseh: "when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly … Then Manasseh knew that the Lord was God" (2Ch 33:12–13).

14578.text: Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 32:25 "his heart was proud" and 32:26 "the pride of his heart". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; D v2 §9.1, §10.1, §11; pilot §2; Outside (all genuine, the bearer's own):; 1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul"; 2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27 "your heart was penitent / tender"; 2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord"; Nothing new in any single seat. What part A adds is a third kind of seat for pilot §2. The pilot has the heart that provokes (the cause) and the spirit that receives (the effect). Part A adds the heart that turns, and so turns the anger away. In these verses, and in §22, it is the human seat most often named in the context of God's anger. For the researcher: whether pilot §2 takes this as a third row.

14579.text: What it does: The formula: "the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and which he made Israel to sin" (1Ki 14:16; 15:30; 16:13, 26); Each king is measured by the one before: Baasha "walked in the way of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:2); Omri "did more evil than all who were before him" (16:25); Ahab "did more to provoke the Lord … than all the kings of Israel who were before him" (16:33); Ahaziah walked "in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam" (22:52–53); Manasseh "led them astray to do more evil than the nations" (2Ki 21:9; 2Ch 33:9).

14580.text: Where it comes from: Contempt: "you … have cast me behind your back" (1Ki 14:9); Ingratitude for elevation: "Because I exalted you from among the people" (1Ki 14:7); "Since I exalted you out of the dust" (16:2); Self-sale: "you have sold yourself to do what is evil" (1Ki 21:20). "There was none who sold himself … like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited" (21:25); Lightness: "as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:31); The measure given is David's heart: "you have not been like my servant David, who … followed me with all his heart" (1Ki 14:8).

14581.text: How it co-exists: The executor is also judged. Baasha is condemned "both because of all the evil that he did … in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it" (1Ki 16:7). Carrying out the prophesied judgment did not make the executor righteous; One found pleasing in a condemned house. Jeroboam's child "shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the Lord" (1Ki 14:13); Recognition without turning. "Have you found me, O my enemy?" (1Ki 21:20). Ahab recognises the prophet as his enemy.

14583.text: Part C: Zec 10:3. "My anger is hot against the shepherds, and I will punish the leaders." This follows "the household gods utter nonsense … they tell false dreams and give empty consolation. Therefore the people wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd" (10:2): The leaders' failure leaves the people without a shepherd. Compare §20's kings who "made Israel to sin", and Isa 9:16 in §36.

14584.text: What it does: "my wrath will be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched" (2Ki 22:17; 2Ch 34:25); Even after the fullest turning: "Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the Lord with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might … Still the Lord did not turn from the burning of his great wrath … because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him" (2Ki 23:25–26); "it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence" (2Ki 24:20); "they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord rose against his people, until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16).

14585.text: Where it comes from: From accumulated provocation: "since the day their fathers came out of Egypt, even to this day" (2Ki 21:15); From the king's heart hardened against turning: Zedekiah "stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the Lord" (2Ch 36:13).

14588.text: Part B: Jer 21:5; 52:3: Jer 52:3 is 2Ki 24:20; "Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands … I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath" (Jer 21:4–5); "He shall not pity them or spare them" (21:7). God's anger turns the people's own weapons back on them.

14589.text: What it does: Removal: Josiah "removed all the shrines … which kings of Israel had made, provoking the Lord to anger" (2Ki 23:19); Covenant formed in the heart: "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord … in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us. My sons, do not now be negligent" (2Ch 29:10–11); A call to return: "Do not now be stiff-necked as your fathers were, but yield yourselves to the Lord … that his fierce anger may turn away from you. For if you return … your brothers and your children will find compassion" (2Ch 30:8–9); Separation: "Let our officials stand for the whole assembly … until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us" (Ezr 10:14); Sabbath restored: "Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath" (Neh 13:18), then the gates are shut (13:19); Captives released:; Oded: "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven … Have you not sins of your own against the Lord your God? … send back the captives … for the fierce wrath of the Lord is upon you" (2Ch 28:9–11); The chiefs: "you propose to bring upon us guilt against the Lord in addition to our present sins … there is fierce wrath against Israel" (28:13); Then: "with the spoil they clothed all who were naked among them … provided them with food and drink, and anointed them, and carrying all the feeble among them on donkeys, they brought them to their kinsfolk" (28:15). Fear of adding to the wrath turns into care for enemies who are also kin; Rebuke acted on: "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you … Nevertheless, some good is found in you … you … have set your heart to seek God" (2Ch 19:2–3). Jehoshaphat "went out again among the people … and brought them back to the Lord" (19:4).

14590.text: Where it comes from: From reading the ruin; From a prophet's word (2Ch 19:2; 28:9); From awareness of accumulated guilt ("our guilt is already great", 2Ch 28:13; "we have greatly transgressed", Ezr 10:13); From the fathers' example as a warning ("Did not your fathers act in this way …?", Neh 13:18; "Do not be like your fathers", 2Ch 30:7).

14593.text: Seat: In the verse: 2Ch 29:10 "it is in my heart to make a covenant". Hezekiah's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.2; E v2 §7.1; Outside: 2Ch 19:3 "set your heart to seek God"; The seat of reform is where the intent to turn is formed. This joins §19 (see there).

14594.text: What it does. "For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers … since we had told the king, 'The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him'" (Ezr 8:22).

14597.text: What it does. "Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads … Do not cover their guilt … for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders" (Neh 4:4–5).

14602.text: Part B: Psa 56:7; 59:13; 69:24; 79:6; Jer 10:25; 18:23; Lam 3:66 (seven verses). The imprecation is a recurring form in part B, as part A's pointer expected: The grounds given:; enemies who "injure my cause … have waited for my life" (Psa 56:5–6); "the sin of their mouths … the cursing and lies" (59:12); "they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded" (69:26): they add to God's striking; "the nations that do not know you … have devoured Jacob" (79:6–7; Jer 10:25 in the same words); Restraint inside the imprecation: "Kill them not, lest my people forget … consume them in wrath … that they may know that God rules over Jacob" (Psa 59:11, 13). The purpose given is knowledge; Tears and trust beside it: "put my tears in your bottle … This I know, that God is for me" (56:8–9); Paired with the speaker's own plea against anger:; Psa 79:6 is followed by "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Jer 10:25 is preceded by "Correct me, O Lord … not in your anger"; The one who asks for wrath on the nations asks to be corrected without it; The intercessor turned imprecator; "Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (Jer 18:20); Three verses later: "Forgive not their iniquity … deal with them in the time of your anger" (18:23); The one who turned the anger away now asks for it, because good was repaid with evil: "they have dug a pit for my life" (18:20). See §45; Lam 3:66 comes with "You will give them dullness of heart" (3:65); Seat ; In the verse: none; Outside: Lam 3:65 "dullness of heart". The enemies'. Genuine. Psa 56:6 "my life" (nephesh). Life-sense.

14603.text: What it does: Eliphaz: "who that was innocent ever perished? … those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed" (Job 4:7–9); Zophar: "To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body" (20:23); "dragged off in the day of God's wrath. This is the wicked man's portion" (20:28–29); Job contests it from what he has seen: "How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? … That God distributes pains in his anger?" (21:17); "Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath" (21:20). He also cites travellers' testimony "that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath" (21:29–30); Elihu: "because his anger does not punish … Job opens his mouth in empty talk" (35:15–16); God: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (42:7).

14607.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 4:9 "blast" (ruach). God's breath. Divine; not a human seat. A v3 §2.3 ("anger, breath and nose"); Outside: Job 21:18 "wind" (not inner-being).

14608.text: What it does: Within: "the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me" (Job 6:4); As an enemy: "He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me" (16:9); "He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary" (19:11); As a trial with fresh witnesses: "You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me" (10:17); As irresistible and unanswerable: "God will not turn back his anger … How then can I answer him …? Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser" (9:13–15). He "removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger" (9:5).

14610.text: How it co-exists: Isolation. "He has put my brothers far from me … My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me" (19:13–14). "Men have gaped at me with their mouth" (16:10); Not being able to see God. "Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not" (9:11). "If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice" (9:16); A wish not to have been born. "Why did you bring me out from the womb?" (10:18). "leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer" (10:20); Hope beyond the anger, in the same breath. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me! … You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). Job asks for a hiding place from God's anger in God's own keeping, and expects God to long for him afterwards.

14612.text: Seat: In the verse: Job 6:4 "my spirit drinks their poison". Job's own, as receiver. Genuine. A v3 §1; pilot §2 ("the spirit that receives the anger"); U1 §8 and §39; Outside: Job 6:7 "My appetite refuses to touch them" (nephesh). Appetite-sense, the bearer's own. Job 9:4 "wise in heart" is God's. Job 14:13 is the verse G v3 §16 left for M20 or unit 2. It is read here: its movement is hiding until the wrath passes, followed by being remembered. It is not a death-wish; Nothing new in the seat. Part A has Job 6:4 as its single verse where God's anger is located inside the human seat by the bearer himself. Parts B and C are expected to add the laments.

14613.text: Part B: Psa 88:7; 88:16; 102:10: Psalm 88, like Job, gives no cause. "Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves" (88:7); "Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me" (88:16); "Afflicted and close to death from my youth up" (88:15); Isolation: "You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them" (88:8); "my companions have become darkness" (88:18); Not seeing God: "O Lord, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?" (88:14); Calling continues: "Every day I call upon you, O Lord; I spread out my hands to you" (88:9); Unlike Job, Psalm 88 has no turn. Its last verse (88:18) ends in darkness; Psa 102:10: "For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink, because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down" (102:9–10). His enemies "use my name for a curse" (102:8). Then "But you, O Lord, are enthroned forever" (102:12); Seat . Outside: Psa 88:14 "cast my soul away". The bearer's own. Genuine. Pilot §2 (second row) cites Psa 88:7, 16.

14614.text: What it does. "Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury" (Psa 2:5). "Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him" (2:10–12).

14616.text: How it co-exists: Fear and joy together: "rejoice with trembling"; The refuge is in the one whose wrath is quick. One verse holds the threat and the blessing (2:12).

14617.text: What it does: "O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath" (Psa 6:1; 38:1 in the same words); "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing" (Jer 10:24); The asker does not refuse the correction. He asks for its measure.

14619.text: How it co-exists: The body and the soul. "heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O Lord — how long?" (Psa 6:2–3). "your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me. There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation" (38:2–3); Two causes for one bodily state. Psa 38:3 names both: "because of your indignation … because of my sin".

14621.text: Seat: In the verse: Psa 38:3 "flesh" (basar). The bearer's own body, as where the indignation lands. Genuine, bodily; Outside: Psa 6:3 "My soul also is greatly troubled". The bearer's own. Genuine. Not found in the batches, the pilot or unit 1: new as a context seat.

14622.text: What it does. "Hide not your face from me. Turn not your servant away in anger, O you who have been my help. Cast me not off; forsake me not" (Psa 27:9). "Will the Lord spurn forever …? Has his steadfast love forever ceased? … Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" (77:7–9).

14627.text: What it does: "his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning" (Psa 30:5); "In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you" (Isa 54:8). "I have sworn that I will not be angry with you" (54:9, "like the days of Noah"); "in my wrath I struck you, but in my favor I have had mercy on you" (60:10); "in a very little while my fury will come to an end" (10:25); "I have no wrath" (27:4); Thanksgiving: "though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me" (12:1); Gathering after the driving out: "I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger … I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever" (Jer 32:37, 39). "I have hidden my face from this city … Behold, I will bring to it health and healing" (33:5–6).

14628.text: Where it comes from. Mostly from God's own word. Two human voices testify from inside it: the psalmist (Psa 30) and "you will say in that day" (Isa 12).

14633.text: What it does: Why? "O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?" (Psa 74:1); How long? "How long, O Lord? Will you be angry forever?" (79:5); "how long will you be angry with your people's prayers?" (80:4); "How long, O Lord? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?" (89:46); Restore. "you have been angry; oh, restore us" (60:1); "Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!" (85:4).

14635.text: How it co-exists: Past mercy as the ground: "You forgave the iniquity of your people … You withdrew all your wrath … Restore us again" (Psa 85:2–4); "Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?" (85:6); Relationship as the ground:; "the sheep of your pasture" (74:1); "Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old" (74:2); "you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand … please look, we are all your people" (Isa 64:8–9); Confession, or none; Isa 64 confesses: "you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? … all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment" (64:5–6); Psa 79 asks: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (79:8); Psa 89 does not confess. It holds God to his covenant (89:38–39); The anger reaches even prayer:; "angry with your people's prayers" (Psa 80:4); "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7).

14637.text: What it does. "But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?" (Psa 76:7). "At his wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure his indignation" (Jer 10:10).

14642.text: Part C: Nah 1:6; Rev 6:17: "Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the heat of his anger?" (Nah 1:6). The next verse: "The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him" (1:7); "for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?" (Rev 6:17), said by those hiding in the caves; In unit 2 the question comes four times (Psa 76:7; Jer 10:10; Nah 1:6; Rev 6:17), each time by or about those facing the anger; Nahum and Psalm 2 both follow the anger with refuge in the same God.

14643.text: What it does: "Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath" (Psa 78:38); "For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off" (Isa 48:9); "For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (57:16).

14644.text: Where it comes from: the reasons: Human frailty: "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psa 78:39); The human spirit's limit: "the spirit would grow faint before me" (Isa 57:16); God's name: Isa 48:9, 11; Two of the three reasons are about what the human is.

14645.text: How it co-exists. The human heart has not changed: "Their heart was not steadfast toward him" (Psa 78:37); "they flattered him with their mouths" (78:36); "he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17); "from before birth you were called a rebel" (48:8).

14647.text: Seat: In the verse:; Isa 57:16 "spirit". The human spirit, as what would faint. Genuine; Isa 57:17 "his own heart". The backslider's. Genuine; Outside: Psa 78:37 "heart"; 78:39 "flesh … wind"; Isa 57:15. Nothing new.

14648.text: Part C: Eze 20:8; 20:13; 20:21; Hos 11:9: Three times in one chapter: "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them … But I acted for the sake of my name" (Eze 20:8–9, 13–14, 21–22: "I withheld my hand"). The chapter ends: "you shall remember your ways … and you shall loathe yourselves … when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways" (20:43–44); Hosea gives another reason: "How can I give you up, O Ephraim? … My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hos 11:8–9). The people were "bent on turning away from me" (11:7). They will return "trembling like birds from Egypt" (11:11); The reasons given for restraint now include God's own nature ("God and not a man"), beside human frailty and the name; What the restrained do:; they remember and loathe themselves (Eze 20:43; also 16:63: "that you may remember and be confounded … when I atone for you"); they come trembling (Hos 11:10–11); Seat . Outside: Hos 11:8 "My heart recoils". God's. Divine.

14649.text: What it does. "For we are brought to an end by your anger; by your wrath we are dismayed" (Psa 90:7). "all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh" (90:9). "Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?" (90:11).

14653.text: What it adds. Psa 90:11–12 makes considering the anger the way to a wise heart.

14654.text: What it does: "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death" (Pro 11:4); "The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it" (22:14); "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him" (24:17–18); "Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?" (Ecc 5:6).

14655.text: How it co-exists: The anger works through the person's own folly: the one under anger falls into the pit (Pro 22:14); Gloating redirects the anger, away from the enemy (24:18); Fear: "God is the one you must fear" (Ecc 5:7).

14656.text: Seat: In the verse: Ecc 5:6 "lead" (basar): literally "let not your mouth cause your flesh to sin". The speaker's flesh, as the self that sins. Genuine; Outside:; Pro 24:17 "let not your heart be glad". Genuine; Pro 22:15 "Folly is bound up in the heart of a child".

14657.text: What it does: The refrain, five times: "For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still" (Isa 5:25; 9:12, 17, 21; 10:4); "The people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the Lord of hosts" (9:13); "it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (42:25); "The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart" (Jer 12:11).

14659.text: How it co-exists: The people consume themselves: "no one spares another. They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry … each devours the flesh of his own arm, Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh" (Isa 9:19–21); Futility: "They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing" (Jer 12:13); Wealth is no refuge: "What will you do on the day of punishment …? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth?".

14661.text: Seat: In the verse: Isa 42:25 "he did not take it to heart". The people's own heart, as where the meaning of the blow should be received, and is not. Genuine; Outside: Jer 12:11 "no man lays it to heart". Isa 9:20 "flesh of his own arm" (bodily, figurative).

14662.text: Part C: Zep 3:8; Zec 7:12; Mal 1:4: Correction refused: "I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction' … But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt" (Zep 3:7). The next verse (3:8) is wrath on the nations, followed by "a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the Lord" (3:9); The heart made hard against hearing: "they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears … They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came" (Zec 7:11–12); Refusal returned in kind: "As I called, and they would not hear, so they called, and I would not hear" (7:13); Rebuilding against the blow, again: "If Edom says, 'We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins,' the Lord of hosts says, 'They may build, but I will tear down … the people with whom the Lord is angry forever'" (Mal 1:4). This is Isa 9:10's "we will build with dressed stones" said by another nation; Seat . In the verse: Zec 7:12 "hearts diamond-hard". The people's own. Genuine. The same verse has "his Spirit" (God's; divine). Outside: Zec 7:10 "devise evil against another in your heart"; What part C adds. Part B's "heart that does not take it in" was a failure to understand. Zec 7:12 names an act: the heart made hard so as not to hear.

14663.text: What it does: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him" (Isa 10:5–6); "I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones" (13:3); "the weapons of his indignation" (13:5; Jer 50:25).

14664.text: Where it comes from: the agent's own heart: Assyria: "But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few; for he says: 'Are not my commanders all kings?'" (Isa 10:7–8); Babylon: "I was angry with my people … I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. You said, 'I shall be mistress forever,' so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end" (47:6–7). And "who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me'" (47:8).

14665.text: How it co-exists: Pride: "proudly exulting" (13:3); "the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria" (10:12); Excess beyond the commission: "you showed them no mercy" (47:6).

14668.text: Revisit of part A §17 and §20: Saul failed to carry out the wrath. Here the agents carry it out beyond what was meant. Both are judged; Part A §20 found Baasha condemned "also because he destroyed" Jeroboam's house (1Ki 16:7). §37 shows the same pattern with nations as the agents.

14669.text: Part C: Zec 1:15. "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease; for while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster." The agents went beyond the measure, as in Isa 47:6. Part C also has aligned agents; they are read separately in §53.

14670.text: What it does: "Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger" (Isa 13:9); "the Lord is enraged against all the nations" (34:2); "the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the Lord" (Jer 25:37); The human side:; "Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them … They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame" (Isa 13:7–8); "like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land" (13:14); "No refuge will remain for the shepherds … the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock!" (Jer 25:35–36); "I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life" (49:37); Onlookers: "everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds" (50:13).

14673.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 49:37 "life". Elam's. Life-sense; Outside: Isa 13:7 "every human heart will melt". Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

14674.text: Part C: Eze 7:12; 7:14; 7:19; 21:17; 21:31; 30:15; 38:18; 38:19; Mic 5:15; Zep 1:15; 1:18; Luk 21:23: Ordinary life suspended: "Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all their multitude" (Eze 7:12); Paralysis: "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but none goes to battle" (7:14); The body: "All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water. They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces" (7:17–18); Survivors "moaning, each one over his iniquity" (7:16); Wealth useless: "Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord. They cannot satisfy their hunger … For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity" (7:19); "Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the Lord" (Zep 1:18). The wisdom saying of Pro 11:4 appears in prophecy twice; Blindness: "I will bring distress on mankind, so that they shall walk like the blind" (Zep 1:17); "the mighty man cries aloud there" (1:14); Hearts melting: "that their hearts may melt" (Eze 21:15); Every man against his brother: "Every man's sword will be against his brother" (Eze 38:21), as in Isa 9:19–21; In the Gospel: "Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people" (Luk 21:23), with "let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains" (21:21); Seat ; In the verse: Eze 7:19 "hunger" (nephesh). The people's appetite. Appetite-sense; Outside: Eze 21:15 "that their hearts may melt". Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

14675.text: What it does. "Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isa 26:20). "Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the Lord!" (Jer 51:45).

14678.text: Job asked for this. "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past". In Isa 26:20, God offers his people what Job asked for. Revisit note for §26.

14679.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 51:45 "life". The people's own. Life-sense; Outside: Jer 51:46 "Let not your heart faint". Genuine.

14680.text: Part C: Zep 2:2; 2:3; Rev 6:16: Hiding offered, with "perhaps": "Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation, before the decree takes effect … Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land … seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:1–3). The way to be hidden is seeking, humility and righteousness, and even then only "perhaps"; Hiding from God, not in him: "the kings of the earth and the great ones … and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb'" (Rev 6:15–16); This is the reverse of Isa 26:20. There God calls his people into their chambers. Here people ask the mountains to hide them from God.

14681.text: What it does: "you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath, who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering" (Isa 51:17); "Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street like an antelope in a net; they are full of the wrath of the Lord" (51:20); The prophet as cup-bearer (B3): "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They shall drink and stagger and be crazed" (Jer 25:15–16). "So I took the cup from the Lord's hand" (25:17); "You must drink!" (25:28).

14683.text: What it leads to. The cup is taken away and given to the tormentors: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more; and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors" (Isa 51:22–23). It is done by "your God who pleads the cause of his people" (51:22).

14685.text: Revisit of U1 §34 and its pointer. U1 §34 is "anger and passion as a drink given to others" (Hab 2:15; Rev 14:8; 18:3). Its pointer was "the cup that comes round" (Hab 2:16; Rev 14:10): Isa 51:22–23 is the cup coming round: taken from the one who drank and given to the tormentors; Part C (Hab 2:16; Rev 14:10) will be read against it.

14686.text: Part C: Rev 14:10; 16:19: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality". Then: "he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger" (14:10). And: "God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath" (16:19); Context read for the U1 §34 pointer: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink — you pour out your wrath and make them drunk … Drink, yourself … The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (Hab 2:15–16); "The cup that comes round" now has three texts:; Isa 51:22–23: taken from Zion, given to the tormentors; Hab 2:16: the one who made others drink must drink; Rev 14:8–10 and 16:19: Babylon made the nations drink, and drains God's cup; The human side is the maker of drink who becomes the drinker. "Here is a call for the endurance of the saints" (Rev 14:12); Under the cup, cursing, not repenting: "they cursed God for the plague of the hail" (16:21); "They did not repent and give him glory" (16:9; also 16:11). Compare §36.

14687.text: What it does: "He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation" (Isa 59:16); "wrath to his adversaries" (59:18); "I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me" (63:3); "I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled, but there was no one to uphold; so my own arm brought me salvation, and my wrath upheld me" (63:5).

14688.text: Where it comes from. The human side here is an absence: Part A §4 had Moses standing before the anger, and Psa 106:23 says "had not Moses … stood in the breach"; Isa 64:7 gives the people's side of the same absence: "There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you".

14692.text: Part C: Eze 14:19; 22:24; 22:31: "I found none": "And I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none. Therefore I have poured out my indignation upon them" (Eze 22:30–31, context read); Ezekiel uses the image of Psa 106:23, to say that no one did; Before it, every group is named as having failed: prophets (22:25, 28), priests (22:26), princes (22:27), the people of the land (22:29); Even the righteous could not stand for others: "even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it … they would deliver neither son nor daughter. They would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness" (14:20); Part A §4 had intercession that succeeded. Part C has intercession sought and not found (22:30), refused (9:8–10), and declared insufficient (14:20); Seat . Outside: Eze 14:20 "their own lives" (nephesh). Life-sense. Eze 22:25 "devoured human lives".

14693.text: What it does: "you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned'" (Jer 2:35). This is said to a people with "the lifeblood of the guiltless poor" on their skirts (2:34); The prophets "say continually to those who despise the word of the Lord, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you'" (23:17). The answer: "Behold, the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth" (23:19).

14698.text: Part C: Eze 13:13; 13:15: The whitewashed wall: "When the wall falls, will it not be said to you, 'Where is the coating …?'" (13:12). "the prophets of Israel who … saw visions of peace for her, when there was no peace" (13:16), and the daughters "who prophesy out of their own hearts" (13:17); False peace is a wall coated over, and the wrath is what shows what the coating hid; Seat ; In the verse: Eze 13:13 "wind". Spurious; Outside: Eze 13:17 "out of their own hearts". The false prophetesses'. Genuine.

14699.text: What it does: "Return, faithless Israel, declares the Lord. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful … I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt" (Jer 3:12–13); "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord; remove the foreskin of your hearts … lest my wrath go forth like fire" (4:4); "Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire" (21:12); "It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the Lord, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the Lord has pronounced against this people" (36:7).

14701.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 4:4 "foreskin of your hearts". The hearers' own heart, as what must be opened. Genuine; Outside: Jer 3:10 "whole heart … pretense".

14702.text: What it adds. Part A §22 had reformers acting to turn the anger away. Here God calls to the heart itself: the heart is named as the place of the change required (4:4), and pretense in the heart as what fails (3:10).

14703.text: Part C: Hos 14:4; Zec 1:2: Hosea gives the words to say: "Take with you words and return to the Lord; say to him, 'Take away all iniquity … Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses; and we will say no more, "Our God," to the work of our hands. In you the orphan finds mercy.'" (Hos 14:2–3). The answer: "I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them" (14:4); "The Lord was very angry with your fathers … Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will return to you … Do not be like your fathers" (Zec 1:2–4); What part C adds. In Hos 14:2–3 God gives the returning people the words to say, and the answer is that his anger has turned. The words renounce three false refuges: Assyria, horses, and idols. Jer 3:13 ("Only acknowledge your guilt") gave what to acknowledge. Hosea gives the whole speech.

14704.text: What it does: "For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the Lord has not turned back from us" (Jer 4:8); "Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the Lord has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath" (7:29); The land itself: "I looked, and behold, there was no man … the fruitful land was a desert … before his fierce anger" (4:25–26); "For this the earth shall mourn" (4:28).

14707.text: Pointer. In part A §6, Aaron's sons were forbidden to mourn, "lest … wrath come" (Lev 10:6). Here mourning is commanded because the wrath has come.

14708.text: Part C: Eze 19:12. "And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel" (19:1, context read). "But the vine was plucked up in fury … This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation" (19:12, 14). Also Eze 6:11: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas". The lament is commanded of the prophet himself: Seat . Eze 19:12 "east wind". Spurious.

14709.text: What it does: "In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach" (Jer 15:15); "Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart … I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (15:16–17); "Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (18:20). The same verse: "they have dug a pit for my life".

14711.text: How it co-exists: Grief for the people under the anger: "My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me"; Isolation: "I sat alone" (15:17); Imprecation after rejection: 18:23.

14713.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 18:20 "life". The prophet's. Life-sense; Outside:; Jer 15:16 "delight of my heart"; Jer 8:18 "my heart is sick".

14714.text: Revisit of U1 §15 and pilot §2.3.
