The pilot calls Jer 6:11 and 15:17 "the one place in M02 where divine anger becomes a human inner operation", and U1 §15 adds Eze 3:14: Part B adds what the vessel costs the prophet from the people: reproach (15:15) and a pit dug for him (18:20); The pilot's statement about the anger inside the prophet stands.

14715.text: What it does. "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jer 23:20). "Behold the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth" (30:23), and "The fierce anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. In the latter days you will understand this" (30:24).

14717.text: Seat: In the verse: Jer 23:20 "heart" and 30:24 "mind". God's. Divine; Outside: Jer 30:21 "of himself" (lev, "who would pledge his heart"). The prince's own. Genuine. Not found in the batches: new as a context seat.

14718.text: What it does: "As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt" (Jer 42:18); In Egypt: "Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live …?" (44:8).

14721.text: What it leads to. "You shall become an execration … You shall see this place no more" (42:18); "cut off … a curse and a taunt among all the nations" (44:8).

14723.text: What it adds: Flight commanded set against flight forbidden here (42:19). Fear of the sword drives them into the wrath; Part A §12 said that reading the ruin rightly was the first step back (2Ch 29; Ezr 5). Jer 44 is the counter-case: they saw the ruin (44:2) and did not turn.

14724.text: What it does: "Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which was brought upon me, which the Lord inflicted on the day of his fierce anger" (Lam 1:12); "The Lord has become like an enemy" (2:5). "He has bent his bow like an enemy … and he has killed all who were delightful in our eyes" (2:4). "The Lord has made Zion forget festival and Sabbath" (2:6); "you have killed them in the day of your anger, slaughtering without pity" (2:21); "on the day of the anger of the Lord no one escaped or survived" (2:22); "I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath" (3:1); "You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us, killing without pity; you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through" (3:43–44); "The Lord gave full vent to his wrath" (4:11).

14726.text: How it co-exists: The body of the one speaking: "From on high he sent fire; into my bones he made it descend … he has left me stunned, faint all the day long" (1:13); "He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones" (3:4); "He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy; though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer" (3:7–8); Hunger at its worst: "The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children" (4:10); "Should women eat the fruit of their womb …?" (2:20); Pouring out the heart: "Arise, cry out in the night … Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! Lift your hands to him for the lives of your children" (2:19); "Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven" (3:41); Hope inside the lament (context of Lam 3:1, read this session):; "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me. But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases" (3:20–22); "For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion … for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men" (3:31–33); "Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the Lord!" (3:40); Outsiders' disbelief: "The kings of the earth did not believe … that foe or enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem" (4:12).

14727.text: What it leads to. "Restore us to yourself, O Lord, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old — unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us" (5:21–22). The book ends on the question.

14729.text: #1892 pointer: Lam 3:7 against 3:33. Both were read here in context: The same speaker holds both: the experience of being walled in and chained (3:7), and the confession that God "does not afflict from his heart" (3:33); The #1892 first pass already set the two side by side. What part B adds is that Lam 3:1, an M02 verse, puts the whole chapter under "the rod of his wrath". No change to #1892.

14730.text: Compared with §31. The community laments in Psalms ask "how long?". Lamentations speaks after the day itself, and adds confession, the body, and the unfinished question (5:22).

14731.text: What it does: "Thus shall my anger spend itself, and I will vent my fury upon them and satisfy myself. And they shall know that I am the Lord — that I have spoken in my jealousy" (Eze 5:13); "Then you will know that I am the Lord, who strikes" (7:9); For the nations too: "Then they will know that I am the Lord, when I lay my vengeance upon them" (25:17), the Philistines having "acted revengefully and took vengeance with malice of soul" (25:15); As a sign to others: "You shall be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror, to the nations all around you" (5:15).

14732.text: Where it comes from. From the anger carried through to its end: "the end is upon you … I will judge you according to your ways" (7:3); "My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity" (5:11; 7:4, 9).

14733.text: How it co-exists: The prophet's gesture: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas" (6:11); No refuge by distance or survival: "He who is far off shall die of pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and is preserved shall die of famine" (6:12); Pride named: "the rod has blossomed; pride has budded" (7:10).

14736.text: Linked to earlier sections: Part B §24: "that they may know that God rules" (Psa 59:13); Part B §46: "In the latter days you will understand" (Jer 23:20); Across the unit, God's anger is said to be for knowledge: of his rule (Psalms), of his purpose later (Jeremiah), of his name now (Ezekiel).

14737.text: What it does: "You also played the whore with the Egyptians, your lustful neighbors, multiplying your whoring, to provoke me to anger" (Eze 16:26); "I will judge you as women who commit adultery and shed blood are judged, and bring upon you the blood of wrath and jealousy" (16:38); Carried out by others (B3): "I will direct my jealousy against you, that they may deal with you in fury" (23:25).

14738.text: Where it comes from: Never satisfied: "you played the whore also with the Assyrians, because you were not satisfied; yes, you played the whore with them, and still you were not satisfied" (16:28); Forgetting: "you have not remembered the days of your youth" (16:43); The blood of children: "because of the blood of your children that you gave to them" (16:36).

14740.text: What it leads to: The anger ends in calm: "So will I satisfy my wrath on you, and my jealousy shall depart from you. I will be calm and will no more be angry" (16:42); "I will put an end to your lewdness … so that you shall not lift up your eyes to them or remember Egypt anymore" (23:27); The chapter's end (context read): "that you may remember and be confounded, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I atone for you" (16:63).

14742.text: What it does: "What is in your mind shall never happen — the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.' As I live … surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you" (Eze 20:32–33); "I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you … with wrath poured out. And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face" (20:34–35); "Where now is your king, to save you …? Where are all your rulers — those of whom you said, 'Give me a king and princes'? I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath" (Hos 13:10–11).

14744.text: How it co-exists. Wrath and gathering in one act. "with wrath poured out" is said of the gathering itself (20:34), not only of the scattering.

14747.text: What it adds. What the people asked for (a king; to be like the nations) is answered in anger: by being given it (Hosea) and by being refused it (Ezekiel). Compare Psa 78's craving granted with anger.

14748.text: What it does: "the house of Israel has become dross to me … As one gathers silver and bronze and iron and lead and tin into a furnace, to blow the fire on it in order to melt it, so I will gather you in my anger and in my wrath, and I will put you in and melt you" (Eze 22:18, 20); "you shall know that I am the Lord; I have poured out my wrath upon you" (22:22); The pot: "Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it, and whose corrosion has not gone out of it!" (24:6). "To rouse my wrath, to take vengeance, I have set on the bare rock the blood she has shed, that it may not be covered" (24:8).

14749.text: Where it comes from: Refused cleansing: "because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you" (24:13); Effort without change: "She has wearied herself with toil; its abundant corrosion does not go out of it" (24:12); Blood left uncovered (24:7).

14751.text: What it leads to. Melting (22:22), and cleansing by fire only after the offer of cleansing was refused.

14753.text: What it does: "I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Edom according to my anger and according to my wrath" (Eze 25:14). Edom had "acted revengefully against the house of Judah" (25:12); "he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Rom 13:4).

14754.text: How it co-exists: Fear, and the approval of good conduct: "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good" (13:3); Conscience beside the fear: "Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience" (13:5).

14756.text: Seat. In the verse: Rom 13:5 "conscience". The subject's own. Genuine. Not read for seat sense in the batches; only the unit-1 side-split lists the verse.

14757.text: Compared with §37. §37's agents had their own hearts (Assyria, Babylon) and exceeded the commission (also Zec 1:15). §53's agents are appointed. For the person under the authority, the motive to obey is fear of wrath, and beyond it conscience (Rom 13:5).

14758.text: What it does. "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end" (Dan 8:19). "He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done" (11:36).

14759.text: How it co-exists: The seer's fear and collapse: "I was frightened and fell on my face … I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up" (8:17–18); The proud king prospers within the time: "the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god" (11:36); The wise are refined within it: "some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end" (11:35).

14760.text: What it does. "The princes of Judah have become like those who move the landmark; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water" (Hos 5:10). "Can I forget any longer the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is accursed? Shall I acquit the man with wicked scales …?" (Mic 6:10–11).

14763.text: What it leads to. Wrath "like water" (Hos 5:10).

14764.text: Linked to earlier sections. Part A §3 had God's anger on behalf of the widow and orphan (Exo 22:24). Part B §43 had "Execute justice in the morning … lest my wrath go forth" (Jer 21:12). §55 is the same line: injustice among people draws God's anger as surely as idols do.

14765.text: What it does: "'Yet even now,' declares the Lord, 'return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments.' Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger … Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him …?" (Joe 2:12–14); The king of Nineveh: "Let neither man nor beast … taste anything … let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jon 3:7–9).

14766.text: How it co-exists: Fasting and the body, and the heart: "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joe 2:13). Outward signs are not refused; the heart is named as what must be torn; Awe: "the day of the Lord is great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joe 2:11).

14768.text: Seat: In the verse: Joe 2:13 "rend your hearts". The hearers' own. Genuine; Outside: Joe 2:12 "with all your heart".

14769.text: Linked to earlier sections: Part B §43 had "It may be" (Jer 36:7). Part C §39 has "perhaps you may be hidden" (Zep 2:3); Returning that knows no guarantee is a recurring form; Revisit of U1 §13. Jonah's anger at God's mercy (Jon 4) follows this relenting. The mercy he resented was given to a people who turned without knowing it would come.

14770.text: What it does. "I will bear the indignation of the Lord because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication" (Mic 7:9).

14773.text: What it leads to. Vindication (7:10), then the confession of §5: "Who is a God like you …? He does not retain his anger forever" (7:18).

14774.text: Compared with earlier sections: Part B §28 asked "correct me, but not in anger". Job and Psalm 88 bore the anger without a cause; Mic 7:9 bears it willingly, with a cause named ("because I have sinned"); Lam 3:39 said the same from another side: "Why should a living man complain … about the punishment of his sins?" (read as context in part B).

14775.text: What it does. "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. And do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father,' for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham" (Mat 3:7–9; Luk 3:7–8).

14778.text: Linked to earlier sections. Presuming on descent is a form of false peace. "We have Abraham as our father" plays the part of "surely his anger has turned from me" (Jer 2:35).

14779.text: What it does: "the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (Rom 1:18); "because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (2:5); "for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury" (2:8); "whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (Joh 3:36); "the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression" (Rom 4:15).

14781.text: How it co-exists: Wrath is paired each time with its opposite:; "eternal life" for "patience in well-doing" (Rom 2:7); "glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good" (2:10); "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life" (Joh 3:36); "the righteousness of God … from faith for faith" (Rom 1:17); "it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace" (4:16); Wrath accumulates: "storing up … for yourself" (2:5).

14782.text: Seat: In the verse: Rom 2:5 "hard and impenitent heart". The one who presumes, his own. Genuine; Outside:; Rom 2:9 "every human being who does evil" (psyche). Person-sense. Not found in the batches; Joh 3:34 "the Spirit without measure": God's, divine. Not found in the batches.

14783.text: Linked to earlier sections: Rom 2:5 is part A §21's heart "hardened against turning" and part C's heart "diamond-hard" (Zec 7:12); Rom 2:4 gives the purpose of the delay that §33 described: "God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance.".

14784.text: What it does: "we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. But God, being rich in mercy …" (Eph 2:3–4); "Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God" (Rom 5:9); "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come" (1Th 1:10); "God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation" (5:9).

14786.text: How it co-exists: A past remembered: "In these you too once walked" (compare Col 3:7); Turning and waiting: "you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven" (1Th 1:9–10); Soberness and hope: "let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation" (5:8); Joy: "we also rejoice in God" (Rom 5:11).

14788.text: Seat: In the verse: Eph 2:3 "flesh" ×2. The speaker's and the readers' own former way of life. Genuine; Outside: Eph 2:2 "the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience". A hostile spirit.

14789.text: What it adds: Unit 2 has many who plead against the anger, and some who come through it; Isa 12:1 spoke of the anger as turned away for one person. §60 is the first group that speaks of a wrath still to come as one they are delivered from, while it remains certain for others; The human response is not fear but waiting, soberness and encouragement.

14790.text: What it does. "What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy" (Rom 9:22–23).

14792.text: How it co-exists: Patience toward the vessels of wrath (9:22); A call that crosses peoples: "even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles" (9:24).

14794.text: What it does. "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.' To the contrary, 'if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink'" (Rom 12:19–20).

14797.text: Linked to earlier sections: Part A §24 and part B §24 (the imprecation) asked God to pour out wrath on enemies. Jer 18 showed the intercessor turning to imprecation; Rom 12:19 keeps the same confidence that wrath belongs to God. What changes is the prayer: the wronged person leaves room for the wrath, and feeds the enemy; U1 §31 (the parable master's anger and "forgive your brother from your heart", Mat 18:35) sits beside this. Pointer only.

14798.text: What it does: "Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Therefore do not become partners with them" (Eph 5:6–7); "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry. On account of these the wrath of God is coming. In these you too once walked … But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk" (Col 3:5–8).

14799.text: How it co-exists: Deception about the wrath: "Let no one deceive you with empty words" (Eph 5:6), a New Testament echo of §42; Thanksgiving in place of crude talk: "instead let there be thanksgiving" (5:4).

14801.text: Revisit of U1 §25 (VL, "anger in the lists: put off with the old self"). Col 3:8 is in U1 §25. Part C shows that two verses earlier, God's wrath is named as coming on these things (3:6). The human anger to be put off (3:8) stands two verses after the divine wrath that comes (3:6). Revisit note for U1 §25 at consolidation.

14802.text: What it does: "the great winepress of the wrath of God" (Rev 14:19); "seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished" (15:1); "seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God" (15:7); "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God" (16:1); "He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty" (19:15).

14805.text: What it leads to. "It is done!" (16:17); the Word of God on the white horse, "King of kings" (19:13–16).

14806.text: Linked to earlier sections: Isa 63:3: "I have trodden the winepress alone." Rev 14:19 and 19:15 take up the winepress. In Isaiah no one helped; in Revelation "the armies of heaven … were following him" (19:14). Pointer only; "The song of Moses" (Rev 15:3). Part A began with the song of the delivered at the sea. Unit 2 ends with the same kind of song, sung by those who conquered.

14809.text: Part C: Eze 21:15 (hearts melting before the sword). Rom 13:5 is an in-verse seat new as a reading.

14814.text: Exo 32:10–14; Deu 9:7–22: Sequence the text gives: provocation → anger → "let me alone" → intercession from fear, with fasting → relented → the memory made into a warning against self-righteousness; Phenomena: WP · IN · SA.

14815.text: Num 11:1–15, 33: Sequence the text gives: complaint → fire → cry to Moses → prayer → craving → Moses asks to die → plague; Phenomena: WP · IN · U1 AG.

14816.text: Deu 1:32–38; 3:23–28; 4:21–24: Sequence the text gives: unbelief → anger at the people and at Moses "because of you" → plea refused → sight given → successor charged → warning to others; Phenomena: WP · MS.

14817.text: Deu 29:18–29: Sequence the text gives: heart turning / blessing itself → anger smokes, no forgiveness → ruin → onlookers ask why → answer → secret and revealed things; Phenomena: PV · RR.

14818.text: Jos 7; 22:10–34: Sequence the text gives: one man takes → anger on all → defeat → offender removed → anger turns → the memory drives a later confrontation → answer "He knows"; Phenomena: OS · TW.

14819.text: Judg 2:10–23; 10:6–16: Sequence the text gives: a generation not knowing → provocation → given over → distress → cry / confession → pity → deliverer → relapse, worse; Phenomena: PV · CY.

14820.text: 2Sa 24:1–17 (+ 1Ch 27:24): Sequence the text gives: anger → incitement → objection overruled → act → heart strikes → "fall into the hand of the Lord" → "let your hand be against me"; Phenomena: IC · OS.

14822.text: 2Ch 28:9–15: Sequence the text gives: human rage "up to heaven" → prophet names God's wrath → chiefs fear added guilt → captives clothed, fed, carried home; Phenomena: U1 SP · RF.

14823.text: 2Ch 32:24–26: Sequence the text gives: healed → no return for the benefit → proud heart → wrath → humbled for the pride of his heart → deferred; Phenomena: RH.

14826.text: (v2) Psa 106:19–45: Sequence the text gives: forgot God → Moses in the breach → despised the land → Peor → Phinehas, "counted to him as righteousness" → Meribah, Moses' loss → child sacrifice → given to nations → "he heard their cry … relented"; Phenomena: IN · TW · MS · CY.

14828.text: (v2) Isa 9:8–10:7: Sequence the text gives: pride in rebuilding → struck → "did not turn" → leaders mislead → self-devouring → "his hand is stretched out still" (×5) → Assyria as rod, with a heart of its own; Phenomena: ST · UA.

14829.text: (v2) Isa 51:17–23: Sequence the text gives: cup drunk to the dregs → "There is none to guide her" → sons fainted, "full of the wrath" → cup taken, given to the tormentors; Phenomena: CP.

14830.text: (v2) Isa 57:14–18: Sequence the text gives: God dwells with the contrite spirit → "nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me" → struck, hid face → backsliding "in the way of his own heart" → "I will heal him"; Phenomena: RS.

14831.text: (v2) Isa 63:1–64:12: Sequence the text gives: no one to help → God's arm alone → "I will recount the steadfast love" → "you were angry, and we sinned" → no one who calls → "we are the clay … please look"; Phenomena: NI · CL.

14832.text: (v2) Jer 7:16–29: Sequence the text gives: intercession forbidden → whole families provoke → "Is it I whom they provoke? … themselves" → wrath poured → "did not accept discipline" → "cut off your hair … lament"; Phenomena: PV · MN.

14833.text: (v2) Jer 18:18–23: Sequence the text gives: plots against the prophet → "remember how I stood before you … to turn away your wrath" → pit dug for his life → "deal with them in the time of your anger"; Phenomena: VS · IM.

14836.text: (v3) Eze 9:1–10: Sequence the text gives: abominations → mark on those who sigh and groan → slaughter begins at the sanctuary → the prophet alone, face down: "Will you destroy all the remnant?" → "my eye will not spare"; Phenomena: IN.

14839.text: (v3) Eze 22:17–31: Sequence the text gives: dross → melted in the furnace → every rank has failed → "I sought for a man … and stand in the breach … but I found none" → indignation poured out; Phenomena: FU · NI.

14840.text: (v3) Joe 2:11–14; Jon 3:5–10: Sequence the text gives: the day, "who can endure it?" → return with the heart, fasting, sackcloth → the creed (Joel) or the preached word (Nineveh) → "Who knows?" → (Jonah) God relented; Phenomena: WK · SA.

14841.text: (v3) Mic 7:7–20: Sequence the text gives: "I will look to the Lord" → the enemy gloats → "I will bear the indignation … because I have sinned" → vindication → "Who is a God like you …? He does not retain his anger forever"; Phenomena: BE · SA.

14842.text: (v3) Rom 1:16–2:10: Sequence the text gives: gospel, righteousness by faith → wrath revealed against suppression of the truth → without excuse → judging others → presuming on kindness → hard heart storing up wrath → to each by works; Phenomena: WR.

14843.text: (v3) Rom 12:17–21: Sequence the text gives: repay no evil → live peaceably → never avenge yourselves: leave it to the wrath of God → feed the enemy → overcome evil with good; Phenomena: LV.

14965.text: (v3) Hab 3:8 (DL): Context seat: Hab 3:16 "my body trembles … rottenness enters into my bones"; Whose · check: the prophet's · not a seat (no M47 tag); Already read in: —; §: §3.

14966.text: The passage. The Rabshakeh's speech has been heard (2Ki 18). Hezekiah "tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the Lord" (19:1). His message: "This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace" (19:3). Isaiah answers: "Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me" (19:6). A letter comes; Hezekiah "spread it before the Lord" and prays (19:14–19). The Lord answers with an oracle against Sennacherib (19:21–28), and the camp is struck (19:35). 2Ch 32 tells the same campaign with the purpose of the shouting stated (32:18) and the end: "he returned with shame of face to his own land" (32:21).

14975.text: Sennacherib as a passage. Mockery of God sent through servants, letters and shouting; its stated aim is to make the hearers afraid (2Ch 32:18). Hezekiah's response: sackcloth, the house of the Lord, the letter spread before God, prayer (2Ki 19:1, 14–19). God's word to the people: "Do not be afraid" (19:6). God names himself as the one mocked (19:22), knows the mocker's raging (19:27), turns the scorn back (19:21), and the mocker goes home with shame of face (2Ch 32:21). Hezekiah calls the day one "of disgrace" (2Ki 19:3, a contempt word, M06).

14983.text: The passage: Sanballat "was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews" (4:1); "What are these feeble Jews doing?" (4:2; told in 10.15 The mock); Tobiah's fox (4:3). Then this prayer, and: "So we built the wall ... for the people had a mind to work" (4:6). The Hebrew of "had a mind" is "the people had a heart" (lēḇ, M47) to work.

15019.text: Responses to taunt and reproach in these passages (as the verses state them): fear (2Ch 32:18 aim; 1Sa 17:11 in the trial), weeping (1Sa 11:4; Neh 1:4), anger with the Spirit (1Sa 11:6), sackcloth and the house of the Lord (2Ki 19:1), prayer (2Ki 19:16; Neh 4:4), building (Neh 2:17; 4:6), refusing to be afraid (Neh 6:11), blessing God for taking it up (1Sa 25:39).

15057.text: One earlier reading needs correcting: 10.6 states a cause (zeal "draws onto him" the reproach) that Psa 69:9 does not state (§1). Earlier readings were otherwise checked, not assumed: 1Sa 17:11 is in 10.12 and 10.1, Gen 30:1 in 10.6 and Ch 2, Gen 30:2 in 10.13, and Psa 69:9 and 69:20 in five places. What the trial adds to them is named per verse.

15062.text: H0954 also names conduct: the Hiphil participle is "a son who brings shame" (Pro 10:5) and "one who acts shamefully" (Pro 14:35, shared with M02 and M18).

15065.text: The stacked pairs are the paired cries of the psalms and prophets, "let them be put to shame and confounded" (for example Psa 35:4, 26; 40:14; 70:2). H2781 with H7045 is the prophetic list "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (for example Jer 24:9; 42:18; 44:8, 12).

15089.text: Here the word names a thing more than a bearing: what a people stands on: Might; "the pride of your power" (Lev 26:19); Egypt's "proud might" (Eze 30:6, 18) and Israel's "proud might" (Eze 33:28), whose people "rely on the sword" (33:26); "the pride of the strong" (Eze 7:24); Splendour and pomp; Babylon, "the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans" (Isa 13:19); Tyre: "to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth" (Isa 23:9); "the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim ... the fading flower of its glorious beauty" (Isa 28:1, 3); Strongholds. "I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his strongholds" (Amo 6:8). In the passage they lie at ease and are "not grieved over the ruin of Joseph" (6:6); What God gave, used for pride; "His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it" (Eze 7:20); "Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul" (Eze 24:21). God's own sanctuary had become what they gloried in. It sits with delight and yearning: a pride, a delight and a longing all set on one thing; Brought down; "Your pomp is brought down to Sheol" (Isa 14:11). The passage names the heart behind it: "You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven ... I will set my throne on high'" (14:13); The pride of Egypt (Eze 32:12), Assyria (Zec 10:11) and Philistia (Zec 9:6); Carried from M09 (the proud brought low): Isa 25:11, Isa 2:12, Dan 4:37, Job 40:11–12.

15091.text: The same word names a standing that God gives his people: "He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves" (Psa 47:4); "the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel" (Isa 4:2); To a city "forsaken and hated": "I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age" (Isa 60:15); "the Lord is restoring the majesty of Jacob as the majesty of Israel" (Nah 2:2); The Lord is "the sword of your triumph" (Deu 33:29): Israel's "pride" is the Lord himself; "The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: 'Surely I will never forget any of their deeds'" (Amo 8:7). The oath follows the buying of "the poor for silver" (8:6). The verse does not say what "the pride of Jacob" refers to. I read: it may be Jacob's arrogance, sworn by in irony, or the honour God gave Jacob. The verse is held, not settled; God's "proudly exulting ones" are the warriors he summons to carry out his anger (Isa 13:3).

15093.text: Shown in an act: "I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea" (Exo 15:1, 21); "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (15:7); The enemy's own rising is quoted in the same song: "I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them" (15:9).

15098.text: A limit on what rises. The sea: "here shall your proud waves be stayed" (Job 38:11). "You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them" (Psa 89:9).

15099.text: The challenge to Job: "Adorn yourself with majesty and dignity; clothe yourself with glory and splendor. Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him ... Then will I also acknowledge to you that your own right hand can save you" (Job 40:10–14); Majesty is joined to what only God does: abasing every proud one, and saving by his own hand.

15109.text: What the batch 1 verses state: The same words are used of God and of people. gāʾôn, gaʾăwāh, gēʾût and gāʾāh name God's majesty (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10) and human pride (Isa 9:9; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18). So yes: these words describe a characteristic of God. In ESV English the difference shows in the choice of word ("majesty" against "pride"), not in the Hebrew; God's majesty is his own and is not taken on. He is "robed in majesty" while "you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). Nothing in these verses shows it being acquired. It is shown in acts: the sea, the overthrow, the thunder; It is challenged, but it is not overturned. The researcher's word "undisputed" needs one qualification from the verses. God's majesty is disputed: by the enemy at the sea (Exo 15:9), by "all that is proud and lofty" (Isa 2:12), and by the one who says "I will ascend to heaven" (Isa 14:13). Each time the dispute ends with the one who rose brought down. So it is not uncontested; it is never overturned; Majesty goes with what only God can do. Job 40:10–14 makes the test plain: whoever wears majesty must abase every proud one and save by his own hand. Only God does; Human pride in these verses is mostly a standing that is taken, or kept against God; It is said in the heart against the facts: "the bricks have fallen, but we will build" (Isa 9:10); It is worn as a show (Psa 73:6); It is set over the weak (Psa 10:2; Eze 16:49; Pro 15:25); It refuses to hear (Jer 13:15–17); It stands on might and strongholds (Lev 26:19; Amo 6:8; Eze 33:26); This agrees with the researcher's "mostly assumed"; But the same word for people is not always assumed. God gives a "pride" to his people: chosen (Psa 47:4), given (Isa 4:2), made (Isa 60:15), restored (Nah 2:2). The Lord himself is their "triumph" (Deu 33:29). The verses also show a given honour turned into pride (Eze 7:20; 24:21); I read: the line the verses draw is not between God having majesty and people having none. It runs between a standing that is one's own by nature (God), a standing given by God (his people), and a standing taken, or turned against the giver (pride); The Son's majesty is described as received, and it stands beside his being handed over; "he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17); "after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty" (Heb 1:3); At the very moment of "the majesty of God", he speaks of being "delivered into the hands of men" (Luk 9:43–44); This joins 13.1 Lowering himself (M09): the one with majesty did not hold onto it in the way pride holds; I read: where Php 2:6–9 joins the two, it lies outside this batch's words; A majesty that depends on people is the contrast. Artemis's "magnificence" can be "deposed", because it rests on "she whom all Asia and the world worship" (Act 19:27). I read: this is the borrowed standing that pride is, set against God's majesty, which no one confers.

15113.text: The heart rises out of what it has been given. This is the clearest single pattern in the batch, and the verses state it each time: Strength. Uzziah "was marvelously helped, till he was strong. But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2Ch 26:15–16); Healing and honour. Hezekiah was healed, given a sign, and "exalted in the sight of all nations". Then: "But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud" (2Ch 32:23–25). Here pride is a failure to return what was received. It was humbled the next verse (32:26, carried from M09); Greatness and majesty. "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty ... But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down" (Dan 5:18–20). It lasted "until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind" (5:21); Wealth. "by your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth" (Eze 28:5); Beauty. "You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you ... Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor" (Eze 28:15–17); Height. The cedar God made beautiful ("I made it beautiful", Eze 31:9): "its heart was proud of its height" (31:10).

15116.text: It speaks of its own hand: The king of Assyria: "the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes. For he says: 'By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding'" (Isa 10:12–13); In the same passage he is the Lord's rod (10:5, 15). I read: pride credits itself with what it was used for.

15119.text: Against patience. "the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecc 7:8–9). The proud spirit is set beside a quick temper.

15121.text: zîd and zādôn name a pride that acts where it was not sent: Speaking what God did not say. "the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him" (Deu 18:20). Such a word fails, and "You need not be afraid of him" (18:22). Presumption here borrows God's name for its own word; Going up when told not to. "Do not go up ... So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the Lord and presumptuously went up" (Deu 1:42–43). It came straight after "We have sinned ... We ourselves will go up" (1:41). After the defeat, "you returned and wept before the Lord" (1:45). I read: presumption can wear the clothes of repentance. It goes up when the moment to go up has passed; Not obeying; Not obeying the priest or judge (Deu 17:12). The rest "shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13); "they ... acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They ... were not mindful of the wonders that you performed" (Neh 9:16–17); "you warned them in order to turn them back ... Yet they acted presumptuously" (9:29); Joined to these are a stiff neck, a stubborn shoulder, and forgetting the wonders. Each time God's mercy answers: "But you are a God ready to forgive" (9:17); Kept from it. "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me!" (Psa 19:13). It follows "Who can discern his errors?" (19:12). Presumption is asked to be kept from, as something that would rule; Not hearing; "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15); "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Pro 13:10); "When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom" (Pro 11:2, carried); The opposite named for pride is hearing, taking advice, humility; The fool. "a fool is reckless and careless", against the wise who "is cautious and turns away from evil" (Pro 14:16); Scoffing. "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Pro 21:24); Intent. "if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning" (Exo 21:14). It is set against the one who "did not lie in wait for him" (21:13). Here the word names intent carried out against another; Pride named wrongly; Eliab, angry: "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart". David answers: "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?" (1Sa 17:28–29); The passage shows David asking about the one who defies "the armies of the living God" (17:26); I read: the charge of presumption here comes from an older brother's anger. The verses do not show it to be true.

15123.text: Rising up, with God not set before them. "insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them" (Psa 86:14). The answer is "But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (86:15).

15146.text: The verses say outright that pride takes a place that is God's: "you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods' ... yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (Obd 3); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); This is the researcher's "assumed position" in the verses' own words. Pride is a heart made like the heart of a god. It is not so; What was given is turned into pride; "the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar ... kingship and greatness and glory and majesty ... But when his heart was lifted up" (Dan 5:18–20). Majesty is the same word family God wears (batch 1); The pattern recurs: Uzziah's strength (2Ch 26:15–16), Hezekiah's healing (2Ch 32:24–25), the cherub's beauty (Eze 28:17), the cedar's height (Eze 31:9–10); I read: the human standing in these verses is real, and it is given. Pride begins when the heart treats it as its own. Batch 1 showed the same in Eze 7:20 and 24:21; God's height does not keep him from the low. "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar" (Psa 138:6). The high God comes near the lowly. The proud, who make themselves high, are known "from afar"; Lifting up belongs to God. "not from the east or from the west ... comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:6–7). The one who has height by nature is the one who gives height; God is known as greater through his answer to arrogance. "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods, because ... they dealt arrogantly" (Exo 18:11). "you knew that they acted arrogantly ... And you made a name for yourself" (Neh 9:10); God knows and weighs. "Talk no more so very proudly ... for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1Sa 2:3). This is joined to "the Lord weighs the heart" (Pro 21:2) beside "a proud heart" (21:4). I read: pride claims a height that cannot bear being weighed. God's knowing is part of what it runs into; His mercy answers presumption. "they acted presumptuously ... But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful" (Neh 9:16–17). "insolent men have risen up against me ... But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious" (Psa 86:14–15).

15151.text: The Greek picture is swelling, physioō, "to inflate". In Paul it is set again and again against love: Knowledge. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Co 8:1–3). Swelling knowledge is answered not by more knowledge but by being known by God; Love is not. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4). Before this: "if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge ... but have not love, I am nothing" (13:2); Party; "that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:6–7); Here Paul states what the Hebrew verses showed in story: pride holds what was received "as if you did not receive it"; Talk without power. "Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you ... I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1Co 4:18–20). The arrogance rests on Paul being absent; Where grief belongs. "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1Co 5:2). Pride stands where mourning should be; Without reason. "puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Col 2:18–19, carried from M09); The new convert. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6). The verse joins conceit to the devil's condemnation. It does not say what the devil's condemnation was. I read: it is held for 13.3 (other spirits). It is not built on here; Controversy. "he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension" (1Ti 6:4). Conceit is joined to understanding nothing, and to quarrels; With pleasure. "swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2Ti 3:4–5); Among the others; "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Co 12:20); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26), after "let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (5:25); Conceit is named among the things that set people against each other.

15173.text: Conceit among the things that divide people (Gal 5:26; 2Co 12:20; 1Ti 6:4) bears on 10.10, and on 10.6 (envy).

15205.text: Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

15209.text: Builders: Sanballat "was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews. And he said ... 'What are these feeble Jews doing?'" (Neh 4:1–2). Mocking comes with anger, and it belittles; The answer: "The God of heaven will make us prosper" (Neh 2:20).

15219.text: "The Lord ... sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people ... But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord rose against his people, until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:15–16): The mocking answers God's compassion; I read: "until there was no remedy" marks mocking the word as the end of the way back.

15232.text: If they turn to other gods, "Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples" (1Ki 9:7; 2Ch 7:20; Deu 28:37). "a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (Jer 24:9). "a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror" (Eze 5:15).

15237.text: A pride word is used of God here. lāʿag "mock" and lîṣ "scorn" are said of God: "the Lord holds them in derision" (Psa 2:4); "you hold all the nations in derision" (Psa 59:8); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); wisdom: "I will mock when terror strikes you" (Pro 1:26); The verses show how God's derision differs from human mocking; Where it comes from. It comes from the one who "sits in the heavens" (Psa 2:4), from the height that batches 1–3 found is his by nature; What it answers. It always answers a rising against him: kings set "against the Lord and against his Anointed" (Psa 2:2), those of whom it says "'Who,' they think, 'will hear us?'" (Psa 59:7), the scorners (Pro 3:34), those who "refused to listen" (Pro 1:24); Whom it never targets. In these verses it is never aimed at the weak, the poor or the sufferer. Human mocking is aimed at exactly those: the poor (Pro 17:5), a father (Pro 30:17), the sufferer (Psa 22:7), builders called "feeble" (Neh 4:2); I read: God's derision is the laughter of the undisputed height at a dispute that cannot succeed. Human mockery is a self-made height looking down on someone made low; God is not mocked. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7). The mocking of his messengers goes on "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16). This is the batch 1 point again: God's standing is challenged, and is not overturned; The Son is mocked, and does not answer in kind; The one with the undisputed standing is mocked on that very standing: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mat 27:29); "He saved others; he cannot save himself" (Mar 15:31); He "made no answer" (Luk 23:9), and he prays "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34); I read: in the Son, the majesty of batch 1 does not defend itself against mockery. This is the clearest instance of 13.1 Lowering himself in these words. It joins the batch 1 point that his majesty and his being "delivered into the hands of men" stand side by side (Luk 9:43–44); Mocking exposes a false height. Zion scorns Sennacherib (2Ki 19:21). Elijah mocks a god who does not answer (1Ki 18:27). Here the mocking does not come from pride. It names a claim that is empty.

15241.text: Fury at being mocked (Mat 2:16) and anger with jeering (Neh 4:1) bear on OT-103 (M02).

15243.text: Pride sense (42). These include: the heart proud or haughty: 2Ch 32:25–26; 2Ch 26:16; Eze 28:2, 5, 17; Eze 31:10; Pro 16:5; Pro 18:12; Psa 101:5; a haughty spirit: Pro 16:18; Ecc 7:8; haughty eyes and looks: Isa 5:15; 2Ki 19:22 and Isa 37:23 (lifting the eyes against the Holy One); the lofty brought low: Isa 10:33; Isa 26:5; Eze 31:14; "do not become proud, but fear": Rom 11:20; Rom 12:16, 2Co 10:5 ("every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God") and Luk 16:15; Obd 3–4 and Jer 49:16 (the nest set high); Isa 3:16 (the daughters of Zion) and Isa 22:16 (Shebna's tomb on the height). These two have no other M-code.

15257.text: Are any of the pride words indicative of God's characteristics? Yes: The gāʾôn family is used of God's majesty: "majesty", "triumphed gloriously", "robed in majesty" (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10); "Majesty" is used as a name for God (Heb 1:3; 8:1); The mocking words are used of God's derision: "He who sits in the heavens laughs" (Psa 2:4); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); God is never the subject of a boast in these verses. He is its right object: "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jer 9:24).

15258.text: God's height is his own, shown in acts, and not overturned: "robed in majesty ... you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (Exo 15:7); Majesty goes with what only God does: abasing every proud one and saving by his own hand (Job 40:10–14); "God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7); Human pride, in the verses' own words, is a standing taken or assumed; "you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); Mostly, pride holds as its own what was given; "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7); In story: Uzziah's strength, Hezekiah's healing, Nebuchadnezzar's God-given majesty, the cherub's beauty, the cedar's height (2Ch 26:15–16; 32:24–25; Dan 5:18–20; Eze 28:17; 31:9–10); This matches the researcher's "mostly assumed": the standing is real, but it is taken up as if it were not received.

15279.text: This is where the change-of-character reading (#1919) would start. No reading has been done: H1347 gāʾôn: human "pride" (25) versus God's "majesty" (9) versus "the thicket of the Jordan" (3); H1361 gābah: "proud" and "haughty" (Eze 28:2, 5; 2Ch 26:16; 32:25) versus "towered" and "higher" (physical) versus "exalted" of God (Isa 5:16) and of the servant (Isa 52:13); H1364 gābōah and H1363 gōbah: high walls and tall men versus "haughty eyes" and "a haughty spirit" (Pro 16:18); G2744 kauchaomai: "boast" versus "rejoice" (Rom 5:2–3, 11). Boasting in oneself versus "let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17); H1984H hālal: "boast" versus "glory" and "exult" (Jer 9:24, "let him who boasts boast in this"); G1702 empaizō: Jesus "mocked" in the passion accounts versus Herod "tricked" by the magi (Mat 2:16); H7292 rāhab: "insolent" (Isa 3:5) versus "plead urgently" (Pro 6:3) versus "overwhelm" (Song 6:5).

15295.text: The words for God and for people are the same. gāʾôn, gaʾăwāh, gēʾût and gāʾāh are God's majesty (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10) and human pride (Isa 9:9; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18).

15299.text: God's height is his own: "robed in majesty ... you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2); It is shown in acts: "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (Exo 15:7); It is challenged (Exo 15:9; Isa 2:12; Psa 2:2), but never overturned: "God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7).

15301.text: Pride is the given held as one's own: "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7); In story, each time:; "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2Ch 26:16); "did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud" (2Ch 32:25); "when his heart was lifted up" (Dan 5:20); "your heart has become proud in your wealth" (Eze 28:5); "its heart was proud of its height" (Eze 31:10); In the law it is foreseen: "your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God ... Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth'" (Deu 8:14, 17); It credits its own hand. "By the strength of my hand I have done it", said by the one who was the Lord's rod: "Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it" (Isa 10:13, 15). And "which I have built by my mighty power" (Dan 4:30); I read: the line the verses draw is not between having height and having none. It is the source and the direction. Height that is one's own by nature belongs to God alone. Height that is given is held from him. Pride is the given taken as one's own, and turned against the giver or over others. This is the researcher's "assumed position", in the verses' own words.

15306.text: This line runs through every batch: "Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the Lord has spoken" (Jer 13:15); "if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (13:17); "By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom" (Pro 13:10); The scoffer: "does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12); "Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you" (9:8); "do not scoff ... Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23); Presumption acts on its own word:; the prophet "who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him" (Deu 18:20); "you would not listen; but you rebelled ... and presumptuously went up" (Deu 1:43); not obeying the decision given (Deu 17:12); The messengers mocked "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16); God works to keep pride from a person; "he opens the ears of men ... that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17); "to keep me from becoming conceited ... a thorn was given me" (2Co 12:7); The opposite named for pride is hearing, or fear; "So do not become proud, but fear" (Rom 11:20); "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance ... I hate" (Pro 8:13).

15315.text: Pride can be named wrongly: An angry brother says "I know your presumption" (1Sa 17:28), and the chapter shows that David was sent by his father (17:17–18); A friend explains another's fall: "For when they are humbled you say, 'It is because of pride'" (Job 22:29).

15330.text: In every group with an inner bearing, the verses set it against a rising. Humbling oneself answers pride of heart (2Ch 32:26). Failing to humble oneself goes with a lifted-up self, a hardened heart and a stiff neck (Dan 5:22–23; 2Ch 36:12–13). Being humbled by God is set against the heart that is lifted up in plenty (Deu 8:14). The proud are brought low so that "the Lord alone will be exalted" (Isa 2:11, 17).

15331.text: These are the accounts of the kings in Chronicles and Kings, the conditions in Lev 26 and 2Ch 7, Daniel, Ezra, Pharaoh, Belshazzar, and the fast of Isa 58.

The verse before says "his heart was proud" (32:25). Here humbling is the heart's turn back from its own pride: the same heart, in the other direction; "from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God" (Dan 10:12). Here humbling stands beside setting the heart to understand. It is not a response to a rebuke.

15335.text: What it is set against: pride of heart (2Ch 32:25); "you have lifted up yourself against the Lord" (Dan 5:23), as his father's "heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly" (5:20); "He stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning" (2Ch 36:13); "Do not now be stiff-necked … but yield yourselves" (2Ch 30:8), answered by mocking in some and humbling in others (30:10–11; carried); "How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me?" (Exo 10:3), said to Pharaoh, whose heart is hardened (10:1).

15643.text: In the OT accounts, those who humble themselves are mostly kings and the people, in the narrative of 2 Chronicles and Kings: Rehoboam and the princes, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Josiah, and those who did not (Amon, Zedekiah, Belshazzar, Pharaoh): What follows is national and measured: wrath turned "so as not to make a complete destruction" (2Ch 12:12), and disaster delayed to "his son's days" (1Ki 21:29).
