15682.text: Achan's taking of devoted things (Josh 7:1), already analysed in family J as broken faith (ma'al), is the paradigm violation of the herem institution: taking cherem-devoted property for oneself. Two separately grouped families, J's unfaithfulness and A's destruction, converge on the same narrative event from two lexical angles, the betrayal side and the violated-institution side.

15685.text: H2398 (chata, to sin) carries a causative dimension not found elsewhere in the M10 corpus: one person's sin actively causes a group's sin. The repeated Kings formula says Jeroboam sinned and made Israel to sin (1 Kgs 15:30, 16:2, 16:13, 16:26, 21:22): sin is something a leader can transmit to a whole nation through example or policy, not only commit individually. The same corpus also holds the strictly individual model (Ezekiel's righteous man who sins), side by side with the leader-transmits-sin model.

15695.text: H5771 (avon) carries the same forgiveness-formula language as the other families: forgiving iniquity and transgression (Num 14:18, Exod 34:7), pardoning iniquity (Mic 7:18), and blotting out transgressions like mist (already cross-referenced in family G).

15711.text: Transgression is explicitly defined as law-relative, not free-standing. Rom 4:15 states this almost as a formal rule: where there is no law there is no transgression (G3847): the concept requires a prior boundary to cross.

15712.text: Both root words for transgress in this family are spatial-boundary words: G3845 (parabainō, step past) and H5674D (avar, pass over, through or by). H5674D's meaning block runs 25 senses, nearly all literal motion (crossing a river, passing a border, a passer-by), with the moral sense of transgressing a covenant or command appearing as one derived branch among many (Judg 2:20, Dan 9:11, Hos 6:7). The metaphor is the same across both languages: sin as a line stepped over.

15715.text: H6588 (pesha, 58 verses, the single largest strong across all 14 families surveyed so far) shows the same remedy-defined shape: its own meaning block labels sub-senses as recognised by the sinner, as God deals with it, and as God forgives, and the verses bear this out: Ps 32:1 (blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven); Ps 51:1 and 3 (I know my transgressions, my sin is ever before me), the same recognition-language pattern already found in the guilt subgroup's H0816; and Mic 7:18, Isa 43:25 and Isa 44:22, all blotting out or passing over transgression as a divine act.

15717.text: H6588 runs the same three-register split found in family J (unfaithfulness): its meaning block distinguishes transgression against individuals, nation against nation, and against God, the same structure as H4603 and H4604's against man and against God split. Amos's formula for three transgressions and for four (Amos 1:3 to 2:6) applies pesha at the nation-against-nation register, functioning as an indictment formula against foreign powers, not individual ethics.

15720.text: The Hebrew strife nouns (H4066, H4079, H4090, H4683, H4695) are genuine domestic and social discord, the family's only real match to the cluster's apparent theme, overwhelmingly Proverbs material: hot temper, wrath and greed are strife's stated causes (Prov 15:18, 29:22, 28:25).

15727.text: H4603/H4604 (ma'al, 30 verses combined) is the most explicit: its meaning block splits the root directly into against man and against God senses, and the verses bear this out one for one: Achan's sacrilege against devoted objects (Josh 7:1), a wife's suspected unfaithfulness under the jealousy ordeal (Num 5:27), and national apostasy and idolatry (2 Chr 26:16, 28:19, Ezek 14:13, 15:8, 17:20, 39:26) sit in the same lexical family as ordinary interpersonal deception (Lev 6:2, deceiving his neighbor).

15729.text: G0646, G0763 and G0764 (Greek) shift register slightly: less about a specific broken bond, more a general orientation of impiety opposed to godliness as a category (Rom 1:18 pairs ungodliness with unrighteousness; Titus 2:12 opposes it to living self-controlled, upright and godly).

15746.text: Cruelty and ruthlessness are almost never self-attributed; they are the property of the other. Every verse in the set describes an external agent: venom (Deut 32:33), the Day of the Lord as cosmic judge (Isa 13:9), and foreign armies and nations (Jer 6:23, 50:42, Ezek 28:7, 31:12, Isa 25:3-5).

15753.text: Guilt accrues as a load: H0819's guilt is already great and incurred guilt more and more (2 Chr 28:13, 33:23), and H5375J's bear your iniquity, guilt or punishment idiom, treat guilt as cumulative weight, not a binary switch.

15784.text: asebeia (G0763) as a noun in ordinary case variation across most occurrences: Rom 1:18's opening indictment (ungodliness and unrighteousness), the pastoral-epistle warnings (2 Tim 2:16's more and more ungodliness, Titus 2:12's renunciation), and Rom 11:26's eschatological promise (banish ungodliness from Jacob).

15787.text: ma'al (H4603, verb) explicitly against God and the sacred, its own meaning block's against God and against devoted thing sub-senses: Achan's sacrilege against devoted objects (Josh 7:1, the strong's own paradigm case), national apostasy and idolatry (2 Chr 26:16, 2 Chr 12:2, Dan 9:7), and a wife's suspected infidelity handled through a legal-ordeal ritual (Num 5:27).

15789.text: ma'al (H4604, the noun) is in the same broke-faith idiom as its verb counterpart H4603, occurring at several of the same verses (Josh 7:1, Num 5:6 and 5:27, Lev 6:2, 2 Chr 28:19): the noun and verb are used together, not as separately attested alternatives, and H4604's own meaning block's against man and against God split matches H4603's against man, against God, against devoted thing and against husband split almost exactly.

15803.text: H2342J and H2342K (both chul, split by sense) have real, coherent meaning covering dancing, whirling, waiting anxiously and writhing in childbirth. Their combined 10 occurrences are literal in every case: a whirling storm-tempest (Jer 23:19, 30:23), a spindle or dance reference in a curse formula (2 Sam 3:29), the voice of the Lord making a deer give birth (Ps 29:9), a sword raging against cities (Hos 11:6), and anxious waiting (Ps 37:7, Gen 8:10, Judg 3:25, Mic 1:12). None describes moral perversion.

15825.text: Healing comes after the ways are seen: I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners; peace, peace, to the far and to the near (Isa 57:18-19). It comes straight after the man who went on backsliding in the way of his own heart (57:17), and the but joins them: God has seen the heart's way, and he heals anyway.

15829.text: 0. Notes on the data before reading: What distance measures. The positions follow original-language word order, not English (e.g. rûaḥ is at 0 in 1Ch 12:18, where the Hebrew opens with it) [verify]. So distance counts words in the Hebrew or Greek.; d0 = one word carries both tags, e.g. "brokenhearted" (Psa 147:3), "fainthearted" (Heb 12:3), "merry-hearted" (Isa 24:7). These compounds are themselves evidence of fusion.; d1–d2 almost always marks a grammatical tie: "my heart trembled", "bitter in soul".; Larger distances are sometimes still meaningful (e.g. Mar 3:5, d5: "anger, grieved at their hardness of heart"). But they are often incidental: "declares the Lord", or a different subject.; I read every verse, and used distance only as a guide.; Cluster tags that don't mean what the cluster name says. Reported, not silently dropped:

15834.text: H0926 "to dismay" (filed under Faintness): what it actually is in these verses: also "hasty / rash / quick" (Ecc 5:2 "let not your heart be hasty"; Ecc 7:9 "quick in your spirit")

15838.text: A stable heart means no fear [Claude reading: the text makes the heart's state the ground of fearlessness]: "His heart is steady; he will not be afraid" (Psa 112:8); "He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting" (112:7); "my heart shall not fear" (Psa 27:3); "Let not your heart faint … do not fear" (Deu 20:3; Isa 7:4; Jer 51:46); "Say to those who have an anxious heart, 'Be strong; fear not!'" (Isa 35:4); Revisit 2026-09-28: "Faint" here is *rak lēvāv*, the soft / tender heart. Read with context in Batch F §6: the heart yields to what blows on it, and fear spreads from heart to heart (Deu 20:8).; "Be strong" is *ḥāzaq*, the same verb as hardening (Batch G §3.3).; "the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man" (Isa 51:7) — what is *in* the heart sets what the person need not fear.

15845.text: The tremble-word used for anger: "Be angry [*rāgaz*, tremble], and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts" (Psa 4:4) [lexical].

15848.text: Heart: "his heart rages against the Lord" when folly ruins his way (Pro 19:3); "The godless in heart cherish anger" (Job 36:13); "the mind [heart] of the king of Syria was greatly troubled [*sāʿar*, storm]" (2Ki 6:11)

15849.text: Spirit and bosom in sequence: "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart [bosom] of fools" (Ecc 7:9) [H/T].

15850.text: Spirit as temper: "slow to anger" // "rules his spirit" (Pro 16:32) [H]; "hasty temper" (Pro 14:29) [T]; "their anger [rûaḥ] against him subsided" (Judg 8:3) [T]

15852.text: Anger harming the self: "You who tear yourself [nephesh] in your anger" (Job 18:4).

15853.text: Soul withdrawing from others' anger: "Let my soul come not into their council … in their anger they killed men" (Gen 49:6).

15854.text: Vexation in heart, pain in body: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (Ecc 11:10); "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (Ecc 2:23).

15855.text: Heart-state provokes or averts wrath: "because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath" (Rom 2:5); "the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away" (1Ki 11:9); "his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came" / "humbled himself for the pride of his heart … the wrath of the Lord did not come" (2Ch 32:25–26); "remove the foreskin of your hearts … lest my wrath go forth like fire" (Jer 4:4); "it is in my heart to make a covenant … that his fierce anger may turn away" (2Ch 29:10); "they made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear … Therefore great anger came" (Zec 7:12)

15856.text: God's anger carries out his heart's intents: "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart" (Jer 23:20; 30:24 "mind").

15857.text: God's anger and the human spirit: "nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me" (Isa 57:16) [H].; Revisit 2026-09-28: God's restraint before the fragile human spirit, read after "revive the heart of the contrite" (57:15). See Batch F §5 and Batch G §1.2.

15858.text: God's indignation and the flesh: "There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation" (Psa 38:3).

15859.text: Flesh and wrath (Paul): "the passions of our flesh … by nature children of wrath" (Eph 2:3).

15860.text: Craving and anger: "While the meat was yet between their teeth … the anger of the Lord was kindled" (Num 11:33).

15861.text: 2.3 ◆ Anger, breath and nose: "By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast [rûaḥ] of his anger [nose] they are consumed" (Job 4:9).; "a stormy wind break out in my wrath" (Eze 13:13).; [lexical] The Hebrew anger word is "nose / nostrils"; rûaḥ is the breath or blast from it. So anger and breath share a bodily image.

15862.text: 2.4 ◆ Divine Spirit followed by human anger: "the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1Sa 11:6) [D1]; "the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him … In hot anger he went back" (Judg 14:19) [D1]; [Claude reading] Twice, anger follows the Spirit's coming. The text puts them in sequence without comment.

15864.text: 2.5 Anger and grief together: "he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mar 3:5).

15868.text: The bitter-word also means "enraged" and "angry": "enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs" (2Sa 17:8, d0); "lest angry fellows fall upon you" (Judg 18:25, d0). [Claude reading] Bitterness of soul shades into rage.

15873.text: 3.3 Authentic vs performed grief — the heart decides: "return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning … rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joe 2:12–13); "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds" (Hos 7:14); "because your heart was tender … you have wept before me, I also have heard you" (2Ch 34:27; 2Ki 22:19); Revisit 2026-09-28: the same "tender heart" means fear before battle and lack of resolve in youth. What decides is what the heart yields to (Batch F §6).; "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning" (Ecc 7:4); "the living will lay it to heart" (Ecc 7:2)

15893.text: 4.3 Joy's effect on the body: "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "A joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish" (Isa 66:14)

15895.text: 4.4 Joy that is mixed, hidden or morally wrong ◆: "Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief" (Pro 14:13); "no stranger shares its joy" (Pro 14:10) — the privacy of joy; "the heart of fools is in the house of mirth" (Ecc 7:4); "wholehearted joy and utter contempt" (Eze 36:5); "rejoiced with all the malice within your soul" (Eze 25:6); "let not your heart be glad when he stumbles" (Pro 24:17); Haman "joyful and glad of heart" then "filled with wrath" (Est 5:9); Michal saw David "dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart" (1Ch 15:29); Abraham "laughed and said to himself [in his heart]" (Gen 17:17) — laughter with inner speech

15896.text: Revisit 2026-09-28: Eze 25:6; 36:5 and Pro 24:17 are read together in Batch F §8.3. The inner response to an enemy's fall is itself judged. The prophet's heart grieves for Moab (Isa 15:5; Jer 48:36) where Ammon rejoiced "with all the malice within your soul".; Haman's swing from "glad of heart" to "filled with wrath" (Est 5:9) matches the overnight swings of Batch F §7 (Nabal, Ahasuerus).

15937.text: 9. Cross-cutting observations for Batch A [Claude reading]: Each component has its own feeling profile in the text, but they overlap: *Heart:* the widest range, including joy, fear, anger, grief, anxiety, despair.; *Soul:* strongly bitterness, longing, weariness, being troubled.; *Spirit (human):* troubled, broken or crushed, faint, provoked, rejoicing, and temper.; *Flesh:* trembles, faints, rejoices, and is afflicted by divine indignation.; The heart's state governs whether a feeling takes hold. A firm heart has no fear, a blameless heart no shame, a hardened heart no fear of God. A proud heart brings wrath; a humbled heart averts it.; Feelings pass between the inner seat and the body in both directions: glad heart → face; joyful heart → medicine; crushed spirit → dry bones; wine, bread, perfume, eyes' light → heart; meat craved → weeping; The divine Spirit is involved in feeling: it gives joy (1Th 1:6; Act 13:52) and grounds the absence of fear (Hag 2:5; Rom 8:15); it can be grieved (Eph 4:30), and it groans (Rom 8:26); twice, its coming is followed by human anger (1Sa 11:6; Judg 14:19); it is sent to heal the broken heart (Isa 61:1); Breath and wind tie feeling to the body and to God: the blast of God's anger from the "nose"; "fills me with bitterness" instead of breath; the breath that withers grass; despair's speech is "wind".; God is given the same feelings in heart and soul: his heart grieved (Gen 6:6), his joy with all heart and soul (Jer 32:41), anger executing the intents of his heart (Jer 23:20).

15938.text: 0. Data notes: "Set the heart" is a single idiom (H7760K / H7896K "to set: consider", often at d0, i.e. the same token as *lēv*).; It is behind "consider" (Hag 1:5, 7; 2:15, 18; Job 1:8; 2:3; Pro 24:32), "care" (2Sa 18:3), "pay attention" (1Sa 4:20), "mark well" (Eze 44:5) and "take to heart" (2Sa 13:20; Exo 7:23; Isa 42:25; Mal 2:2).; [Claude reading] Attention and consideration are expressed as *placing the heart*.; Speech verbs are elsewhere. *(Corrected in v2.)* "Speak" (H1696G/I) and "speak rashly" (H0981) are filed under M42 Prayer & Petition (→ Ruling R1). "Say" (H0559) is in T3 Operations, so it is not in the pairs file at all (→ Ruling R2). So the "said in his heart" series (depiction v1 §2.1c) is not in this batch, and it will not appear in Batch E either. M65 here holds mainly "word / tell / thing".; Noise, noted and not used: "Ascents" tagged as thought (Psa 131:1); "toss" tagged as wisdom (Job 30:22); G0746 "beginning / authorities / firstfruits" filed under Wisdom; sexual "know" (Num 31:35; Judg 19:22); H1697I "thing / nothing / some" (generic); G5591 "natural" is *psychikos*, the adjective of *psychē* ("soul-ish") [lexical]. It appears here in contrast to "spiritual" (*pneumatikos*). See §8.; The brief's [verify] is resolved. 1 Kgs 3:9 "an understanding mind" carries H3820A (lēv) + H8085J "to hear: understand", at distance 1. The "hearing heart" is tagged in the data exactly as the brief supposed.

15940.text: 1.2 Attention — setting the heart (see §0.1): "Consider your ways" = set your heart on your ways.; "set your heart to understand" (Dan 10:12); "apply my heart to know wisdom" (Ecc 1:17; 7:25; 8:16); "Take to heart all the words" (Deu 32:46); The failure case: "it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isa 42:25).

15952.text: A cool spirit = understanding: "he who has a cool spirit is a man of understanding" (Pro 17:27); "slow to anger has great understanding, but … a hasty temper exalts folly" (Pro 14:29) [T].

15959.text: 1.8 Flesh as a way of knowing: "we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh" (2Co 5:16); "set their minds on the things of the flesh … the Spirit" (Rom 8:5) [D3]; "the desires of the flesh and the mind" (Eph 2:3); "his sensuous mind [mind of flesh]" (Col 2:18); "I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh …" (Rom 7:25)

15965.text: 1.11 ◆ Breath, wind and thought: "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Psa 146:4) — the brief's thought link; "he who … creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought" (Amo 4:13); "windy knowledge" (Job 15:2); "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (Ecc 1:17); "Every man is stupid and without knowledge … there is no breath in them" (Jer 10:14; 51:17)

15968.text: 2.3 Wisdom going wrong through the heart: "your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, 'I am'" (Isa 47:10); "Your heart was proud … you corrupted your wisdom" (Eze 28:17); "by your great wisdom … your heart has become proud" (Eze 28:5); "oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart" (Ecc 7:7)

15969.text: 2.4 Wisdom entering and staying: "wisdom will come into your heart" (Pro 2:10); "Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding" (Pro 14:33); Revisit 2026-09-28: *nûaḥ* "rest" has three residents: wisdom in the heart of the understanding (Pro 14:33), anger in the heart of fools (Ecc 7:9), the Spirit upon the prophet (Num 11:25; Isa 11:2). See Batch F §9.5.; "teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (Psa 90:12); "I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine — my heart still guiding me with wisdom" (Ecc 2:3) — the heart guiding the body's experiment

15972.text: Human spirit, fool vs wise: "A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back" (Pro 29:11) [H].; Revisit 2026-09-28: read in Batch F §9.5 as "holding the spirit back", beside "calmness will lay great offenses to rest" (Ecc 10:4).

15973.text: Foolish prophets: "who follow their own spirit" (Eze 13:3) [H]; "the man of the spirit is mad" (Hos 9:7) [U].

15980.text: 3.2 A hardened heart does not listen: "Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen" (Exo 7:13, 22; 8:15, 19; 9:12); "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … sent by his Spirit" (Zec 7:12) [D1]; "a hard forehead and a stubborn heart … not willing to listen" (Eze 3:7); "every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will [heart], refusing to listen to me" (Jer 16:12, d1); "did not obey or incline their ear, but … walked in the stubbornness of their evil hearts" (Jer 7:24; 11:8; 13:10); "if your heart turns away, and you will not hear" (Deu 30:17)

15987.text: The divine Spirit on hearing: "the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words" (1Sa 11:6) [D1].

15990.text: Inner speech unheard by people: "Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard" (1Sa 1:13); Revisit 2026-09-28 (context 1Sa 1:7–18, Batch G §8.2): Before: she weeps and will not eat; "why is your heart sad?" (7–8). The prayer comes "after they had eaten and drunk" (9).; After: Eli takes her for drunk (14). She answers in exact inner vocabulary: "a woman troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul before the Lord" (15). Then "Go in peace", and "her face was no longer sad" (17–18).; [Claude reading] Unheard heart-speech is misread by a human hearer as drunkenness, the merry-heart state (Batch F §7), and is heard by God. It is the sad-heart counter-case to the merry heart at a feast.

15999.text: Telling the heart: "he told her all his heart" (Judg 16:17–18) — revealing the heart is speech.; Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Judg 16:15–30, Batch G §3.6): Delilah had framed it: "your heart is not with me … you have not told me where your great strength lies" (15).; Telling all the heart = giving away the secret of strength. The sequence runs: soul vexed (16) → heart told (17–18) → strength gone, "the Lord had left him" (19–20) → the Philistines' merry hearts (25) → strength asked for (28) → "let my soul die" (30).

16003.text: For harm: "when she pressed him hard with her words … his soul was vexed to death" (Judg 16:16); Revisit 2026-09-28: the soul gives way before the heart is disclosed. See the Samson sequence (§4.3 above; Batch G §3.6). "Break me in pieces with words" (Job 19:2) is the same harm, read as crushing in Batch F §5.; "troubled you with words, unsettling your minds [psychē]" (Act 15:24); "by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive" (Rom 16:18)

16024.text: One verb, two spirits: "a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved [*prophesied*] within his house" (1Sa 18:10) [O]; Revisit 2026-09-28 (context 1Sa 18:1–12, Batch F §1.1): this follows the day after Saul's anger at the women's song (18:8–9). In the same chapter Jonathan's soul is knit to David's. Compare the opposite order in 1Sa 11:6, where the Spirit comes first and anger follows (Batch A v3 §2.4).; "a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets" (1Ki 22:22–23) [O]

16041.text: Context Job 34:13–15: "Who gave him charge over the earth?" (13); "If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath" (14) [U]; "all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust" (15); [Claude reading] Human life hangs on God's heart: one decision of God's heart would recall every breath. Compare: "the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isa 57:16) — God's restraint (Batch F §5); "as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils" (Job 27:3) [B]; "The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life" (Job 33:4) [D1+B]

16078.text: Revisit (delta): "Vexed to death" and "sorrowful, even to death" are the same idiom of the soul (Judg 16:16; Mat 26:38; Mar 14:34). The soul is pressed to the edge of death in both scenes.; Samson's soul gives way, and he "told her all his heart" (16:17).; Jesus' soul stays sorrowful, and he prays "not as I will" (Mat 26:39; §7.3).; What follows the soul's extremity decides the outcome: a heart surrendered to another person, or a will surrendered to God.; The end of the sequence counts the dead: "the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life" (16:30). The narrator weighs Samson's life against his death, and the death outweighs it.

16086.text: What the sequences show [Claude reading]: the spear (10); "that he might kill him in the morning" (11); Michal: "If you do not escape with your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed" (11); [Claude reading] The oath by the Lord's life is kept for three verses. Victory, then the spirit, then the spear break it. This is the pattern of 1Sa 18:8–10 (Batch F §1.1) repeated after an oath.; The king's oath over a son's life (2Sa 14:11; context in §16.6).

16127.text: The noun elsewhere: "I always take pains to have a clear conscience [*without stumbling*] toward both God and man" (Act 24:16); "let not your heart be glad when he stumbles" (Pro 24:17; Batch F §8.3); "their silver and gold … was the stumbling block of their iniquity" (Eze 7:19)

16145.text: Philistines and Arabians (filed under against Jehoram): "the Lord stirred up against Jehoram the anger [*spirit*] of the Philistines" (2Ch 21:16) [T]

16154.text: 13.1 Spirit and the laying on of hands: "Take Joshua … a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him" (Num 27:18) [U]; "Joshua … was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. So the people of Israel obeyed him" (Deu 34:9) [X]; [Claude reading] The sequence across two books: Joshua already has "the Spirit" (Num 27:18).; The hands are laid on him.; He is "full of the spirit of wisdom" (Deu 34:9).; The people obey.; As in Num 11 and 2Ki 2 (Batch F §9.5), the spirit's presence is confirmed by others' response — here, obedience.; "men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2Pe 1:21) [D1]; "uphold me with a willing spirit" (Psa 51:12) — Batch F §5; "Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! Lift your hands to him for the lives of your children, who faint for hunger" (Lam 2:19)

16156.text: Other meetings: Aaron "is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart" (Exo 4:14); "the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart" (Pro 7:10)

16170.text: What answers the wish is seldom death. The answer is food (Elijah; Israel in Exo 16), a question (Jonah), or something to look at (Num 21).; It is granted only twice: to Samson, in one final act, and to Saul, by a hand that is then condemned.; To carry out another's death-wish is still to kill (2Sa 1:14–16).

16172.text: "To death" as the measure of the soul's distress: "his soul was vexed to death" (Judg 16:16) — Samson; see §3.6 revisit; "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Mat 26:38; Mar 14:34) — see §7.3; "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me" (Psa 55:4; Batch A); "my heart is wrung within me … In the street the sword bereaves; in the house it is like death" (Lam 1:20)

16174.text: 16.3 The heart and soul measured against death: "I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets" (Ecc 7:26). The context is the searcher's own heart: "I turned my heart to know … the foolishness that is madness" (7:25).; [Claude reading] One heart searching finds another heart as the trap. A heart set with snares is worse than death.; "His greed [*nephesh*] is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough" (Hab 2:5). It follows directly on "his soul is puffed up" (2:4; §5.5).; [Claude reading] Here the soul is compared with death as appetite. Both swallow and are never satisfied.

16184.text: The heart's condition as the cause of death — wisdom and sayings: "fools die for lack of sense [*heart*]" (Pro 10:21); "Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die" (Pro 19:16); "he who fails to find me injures himself [*his soul*]; all who hate me love death" (Pro 8:36; Batch F §3.1); "The godless in heart cherish anger … They die in youth" (Job 36:13–14); "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecc 9:3) → "a living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die" (9:4–5); "Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death" (Pro 19:18) [lexical: *nephesh*]; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity. They lie down alike in the dust" (Job 21:25–26). Here the soul's state at death makes no difference to the outcome. This is Job's counter to the wisdom sayings above.; "I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart" (Rev 2:23). The death is the evidence that the heart is searched.

16217.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: Life is held in the breath and the soul, and it is God's to give and gather.; "Living soul" is shared with the animals. God's breathing is what marks Gen 2:7.; One decision of God's heart could gather every breath back (Job 34:14–15).; In the flood narrative God's heart changes while man's heart does not (Gen 6:5–6 → 8:21).; *rûaḥ* moves across senses within a single passage, and the passage uses the movement: Eze 37: carrying Spirit → breath → winds → "my Spirit within you"; Judg 15: rushing Spirit → one's own spirit returning; Jon 4: an appointed wind that makes the soul wish to die; Strength and hardness are one word. *ḥāzaq* is courage, hardening and the nerve to kill, according to what the heart is set toward (§3.3). This mirrors the tender heart (Batch F §6): neither softness nor strength of heart has a fixed moral value.; Revisit (Batch H §7.4): more words of this kind — *nāṣar* (keep the heart / the "guarded" wily heart), *šāmar*, vengeance, fatness of soul and of heart, *šāgâ*, kinship-flesh.; The inner components give way in order. Samson (Judg 16): the soul vexed; the heart told; the strength gone; the Lord gone; The strength returns only when asked for, and joined to the soul's consent to die.; Jacob (Gen 45): heart numb → spirit revived by words and sight.; The soul is what one swears by and what one bargains for.; Oaths "as your soul lives" mark adherence at a cost (Elisha, the Shunammite, Uriah) or protection with fear (Zedekiah).; Souls are hunted for bread (Eze 13) and "captured" by the wise (Pro 11:30).; Nothing can be given in return for a soul (Mic 6:7–8; Mat 16:26).; Eating and drinking recur at inner thresholds, now in three registers: the merry heart (Batch F §7); the heart sustained by bread before it is made merry (Judg 19:5, 8); the soul that blesses after a meal and wine (Gen 27:25); Also: the sad heart at a feast that turns to prayer (Hannah, Nehemiah), and the wine-threshold refused (Uriah).; Enticement and stirring show how other agents reach the inner seat: God stirs human spirits (Cyrus, Pul, the remnant).; God sends an other-spirit to entice through prophets' mouths (1Ki 22).; God allures and speaks to the heart (Hos 2:14).; Desire, gods and false teachers entice hearts and souls.

16727.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Conscience is the NT's named moral-awareness faculty. It can be clear, pure, good, evil, defiled, seared, weak or wounded. It testifies (2Co 1:12; Rom 9:1) and is purified by Christ's blood (Heb 9:14). It is frequently paired with the heart (1Ti 1:5; Heb 10:22).; The OT does this work with the heart: "David's heart struck him" (2Sa 24:10); "my heart does not reproach me" (Job 27:6).; The Levitical "realizes his guilt" (Lev 5) describes the same moment without naming an organ.; The heart deceives itself and is the source of evil.; It deceives its owner: Jer 17:9; Obd 3; Isa 44:20.; Evil comes from it: Gen 6:5; Mat 15:19; Luk 6:45.; Its evil hides behind speech: Psa 28:3; 41:6; Pro 26:23–25.; Pride deceives the heart that holds it (Obd 3), linking M08 and M14.; Flesh carries on from Batch C (§11.5).; OT: flesh is the ritual body and meat — clean or unclean, holy or tainted.; NT Pauline: flesh is the seat of sin (Rom 7–8; Gal 5:19) and the ground of false boasting (Phili 3:3).; Positive NT uses remain: "holy … in his body of flesh" (Col 1:22); "bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).; Wind and breath are the image of moral emptiness: iniquity takes us away like wind (Isa 64:6); the wicked are chaff (Psa 1:4); "wind and lies" (Mic 2:11); idols with no breath (Jer 10:14); the *hevel* + *rûaḥ* refrain (Ecc); Only the messianic "breath of his lips" (Isa 11:4) and the breath that conveys the Holy Spirit (Joh 20:22) are active and effective.; Fringe worth keeping: *nephesh* = corpse as the defiling body (§8.2); the "high heart" that is pride or courage depending on direction (2Ch 17:6 vs 2Ch 32:25); the heart that strikes or does not reproach — pre-conscience (§3.3, §9.5); sin against one's own soul (§3.2); the servant's soul as guilt offering (§3.6); lies that kill and keep alive souls (Eze 13:19); the spirit of jealousy that comes whether or not the defilement is real (Num 5:14); false humility of the flesh (Col 2:18, 23); the thorn in the flesh against conceit (2Co 12:7); Eliab misreading David's heart (1Sa 17:28); "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" (2Ki 10:15)

16728.text: 0. Data notes (short): Pre-filter — "Lord of hosts" (H6635B, M72): 28 pairs in 22 verses. This is a divine title, not dominion as a relation. The group is reported in §1.9, not dropped.; Misleading tags (noted, and not read as the cluster's sense): "choirmaster" (H5329 "to conduct", M76): 10 psalm superscriptions (Psa 9:1, 11:1, 14:1, 36:1, 42:1, 45:1, 53:1, 57:1, 62:1, 69:1). The M47 word belongs to the psalm body. The heading has no bearing on it.; "hand: power" (H3027H, M72): 49 verses. Mostly the idiom "into the hand of" (Jeremiah's "into the hand of those who seek their life"; Joshua's conquest lists). It is read as agency, and only where the hand acts on an inner component (§1.1, §1.4).; Quantity words in M46: "abundance / greatness / multitude" of iniquity or idols (Jer 13:22; Hos 9:7; Eze 14:4), "numerous" (Deu 10:22), "to no avail" (Dan 11:27), "good for nothing" (Jer 13:10), "retinue" (1Ki 10:2). None of these is about wealth.; Words in M76 and M26 used in other senses: "pity" (Psa 69:20) — *nûd*, a sympathetic shaking of the head; "intoxicated" (Pro 5:20) — *šāgâ*, see §4.2; "appointed" (Jon 4:8) and "count on" (2Co 10:2); "heart" = "midst": "the heart of the seas" (Eze 27:27).; "spokes" (Eze 10:12) is tagged hand.; The death words are outside the M-codes (see the handoff §3), as in Batch G.

16738.text: 1.2 The heart that claims a throne: [Claude reading] Isa 14, Dan 8 and Rev 18 all use the same form: the heart speaks a claim to rule, and the fall follows. Deu 17 gives the only preventive, and it is a daily one: reading, so that the heart is not raised. Haman's inner sentence is the courtier's form of the same claim, and the reversal follows within the same scene.

16750.text: Esther — the soul reversed. Context read: Est 4:12–16; 5:6–14; 7:3–8.; Mordecai: "Do not think to yourself [*in your nephesh*] that in the king's palace you will escape" (4:13) → "if I perish, I perish" (4:16).; Then, at the wine: "let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request" (7:3).; The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking … Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther" (7:7).; [Claude reading] Within one banquet the *nephesh* asked for passes from Esther to Haman. Esther's inner reckoning ("do not think in your soul") is corrected first. Only then does she stake her life. See §7.6 for the wine-threshold.

16751.text: Ben-hadad and the prophet's parable. Context read: 1Ki 20:31–43.; "Perhaps he will spare your life" (31) → "Please, let me live" → "Does he still live? He is my brother" (32); The disguised prophet: "Guard this man; if … he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (39); "your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people" (42) → Ahab "went to his house vexed and sullen" (43; the same phrase as 21:4 — Batch F §7); [Claude reading] A life has a price in silver in the parable, but not in the verdict. Ahab spares one life by calling him "brother", and forfeits his own life for it. This bears on Batch G §5.4 (§R-V).

16752.text: The king's anger costs a life: "whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life" (Pro 20:2). "let my life be precious in your sight" (2Ki 1:13–14; see Batch C).

16755.text: 1.5 Rule turned inward: "he who rules his spirit [is better] than he who takes a city" (Pro 16:32) [H1]; "If the anger [*spirit*] of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness will lay great offenses to rest" (Ecc 10:4) → Batch F §9.5 ("holding the spirit back"); "let the peace of Christ rule [*umpire*] in your hearts" (Col 3:15); "having his desire under control [*authority over his own will*] … determined this in his heart" (1Co 7:37); "after it was sold, was it not at your disposal [*authority*]? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart?" (Act 5:4); "while applying my heart … when man had power over man to his hurt" (Ecc 8:9); God "does not give him power to enjoy them" (Ecc 6:2); "Let every soul be subject to the governing authorities" (Rom 13:1); [Claude reading] Words for rule and authority are applied to the self's own components: a man rules his spirit, peace rules the heart, a person has authority over his own will. Ananias shows the reverse: authority over what he owned, with the heart left unruled.

16767.text: Hardened against the Spirit's words: "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear … the words that the Lord of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets" (Zec 7:12) [D1]

16780.text: Wealth does not satisfy a heart set on a grievance. Context read: Est 5:9–14.; Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart", sees Mordecai, and is "filled with wrath" (5:9).; He "recounted … the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions" (5:11). Then: "Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai" (5:13).; The gallows follow (5:14).

16796.text: Moses' burden, then the Spirit shared. Context read: Num 11:10–17.; "why … you lay the burden of all this people on me?" (11); "Did I conceive all this people? … Carry them in your bosom" (12); "kill me at once … that I may not see my wretchedness" (15); "I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden … with you" (17) [D2]; [Claude reading] Despair under a burden (like Batch G §6) is answered by distributing the Spirit, not by removing the burden.

16801.text: The way follows the heart: "he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17); "Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9) → Batch F §7.4; "if … my heart has gone after my eyes" (Job 31:7)

16805.text: The heart blames God for the ruined way: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the Lord" (Pro 19:3)

16807.text: 4.1 Heart and way — which leads?: [Claude reading] The relation runs in both directions. The heart can lead the way (Pro 23:19), be dragged by the eyes (Job 31:7), or go its own way (Isa 57:17). The best state is one heart with one way (Jer 32:39), enlarged so that the way can be run (Psa 119:32). Eyes judge the way; God weighs the heart or spirit behind it (Pro 16:2; 21:2).

16840.text: Context read: Job 32:1–3.; "he was righteous in his own eyes" (1); "Elihu … burned with anger at Job because he justified himself [*his nephesh*] rather than God" (2); "also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong" (3)

16841.text: 6.2 The heart as judge of the self: "Faithless Israel has shown herself [*her nephesh*] more righteous than treacherous Judah" (Jer 3:11) — comparative justification; "I do not say this to condemn you, for … you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together" (2Co 7:3); [Claude reading] The heart can condemn the self (1Jo 3:20) or justify it (Job 32:2; Luk 16:15). In both cases the text places a higher court above it: "God is greater than our heart"; "God knows your hearts". 1Jo 3 is the gentler reading: the self-condemning heart is reassured, not overruled harshly. In 2Co 7:3 condemnation is set aside because the other person is held in the heart.

16847.text: 7. Cross-cutting observations for Batch H [Claude reading]: The most powerful heart is shown as the least its own. The king's heart is turned, filled, stirred, hardened and cut off by God (§1.1). When it claims a throne for itself, it falls (§1.2). Deu 17:20's daily reading is the one preventive.; Allegiance is a heart-matter, and it moves by attention and kinship. Absalom steals hearts by hearing their causes. David sways them back by "bone and flesh". Abimelech uses the same flesh-claim to incline hearts toward fratricide (§1.3).; The social relations of this batch supply the vocabulary for the self's relation to itself: rule: one rules one's spirit; peace rules the heart (§1.5); service: one serves from the heart, or serves sin with the flesh (§3.1); guarding: one keeps one's heart, soul and spirit (§5.1); judgment: the heart condemns or justifies the self (§6.2); Setting-words turned inward describe the inner seat as governed. This is the batch's main contribution.; More words with opposite value by circumstance (for synthesis item 3): *nāṣar*: keep the heart (Pro 4:23) / the "guarded" wily heart (Pro 7:10) (§5.1); *šāmar*: keep the law / God keeps the soul / enemies watch for the life (§5.2); vengeance: malice in the soul / redemption in God's heart / comfort to the anxious heart (§6.1); fatness: a satisfied soul / a dull heart (§2.3); *šāgâ*: unwitting error / self-accusation / intoxication (§4.2); the heart "lifted up": courage in the Lord's ways / pride (2Ch 17:6; already in Batch D); kinship-flesh: restoration (David) / fratricide (Abimelech) (§1.3); A life has a price in law and in narrative, but not before God (§2.2; §1.4). This qualifies Batch G §5.4.; The eating-and-drinking threshold, extended (Batch F §7): Esther's wine-banquets: Haman leaves "joyful and glad of heart" → wrath → gallows (Est 5:6–14). At the second banquet the king rises "from the wine-drinking" in wrath, and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8). The same banquet is the threshold for Esther's petition and for Haman's fall.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (Batch F §7.5).; The inner sentence before the feast: "My master is delayed" → eat, drink, get drunk → the master arrives (Luk 12:45–46; §3.2).

16848.text: 7. Cross-cutting observations for Batch H [Claude reading]: The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of … joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; David's heart reads kings rightly. Both flights to Achish begin in the heart (1Sa 21:12; 27:1). The second follows immediately on Saul's oath and confession (26:21–25) (§1.8).; Voices addressed to the soul — beyond self-address (for synthesis item 1): Others speak to my soul: "Flee like a bird" (Psa 11:1); God swears by his own soul (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14); God's soul is burdened (Isa 1:14) and avenges itself (Jer 5:9); Fringe worth keeping: the king's heart read by Joab (2Sa 14:1); bitterness of soul as the recruiting ground of a king (1Sa 22:2); the queen of Sheba's mind filled and spirit emptied (1Ki 10:2, 5); Haman's riches "worth nothing" to a heart fixed on Mordecai (Est 5:13); the soul's "burden" as its desire (Eze 24:25); Moses' despair answered by distributing the Spirit (Num 11); the watchman who delivers his own soul (Eze 33:9); Eli killed by the word "ark" (1Sa 4:18); Mary keeping what she did not understand (Luk 2:50–51); the sons of Sceva mastered by the spirit (Act 19:16); Simon's money exposing his heart (Act 8:21); the good intention set aside overnight (2Sa 7:3–5); "he who seeks my life seeks your life" (1Sa 22:23); Balaam's soul wishing for the death of the upright (Num 23:10)

The words overlap with Joh 12:25; the purpose differs.; On "lose / save": Mat 16:26 ("what shall a man give in return for his soul?") and Mic 6:7–8 (the firstborn refused as a price for "the sin of my soul") both refuse a price for the soul.

16932.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The merry heart is a threshold state. In every narrative it comes after eating and drinking and immediately before a decisive event, which others usually initiate. The good heart lowers guard. What enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder (Amnon); exposure and anger (Vashti, Ahasuerus); mockery turned to catastrophe (Samson); outrage (Gibeah); approach and redemption (Ruth); a dead heart the next morning (Nabal); God's claim on the soul (the rich fool); The heart's condition swings overnight. Nabal: merry heart → dead heart (1Sa 25:36–37). Ahasuerus: merry heart → burning anger (Est 1:10–12). The heart's state is not stable; wine sets it high, and news or refusal drops it.; 1Ki 21 joins spirit and heart. Ahab's spirit is vexed and he stops eating. Jezebel prescribes food and a good heart, secured by injustice. A spirit-state is "cured" by manufacturing a heart-state — the only place in the batch where one is treated through the other.; Positive merriment exists outside the narratives: "they … went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1Ki 8:66); "A joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "let your heart cheer you … But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9); When the heart is good because of God, no threshold event follows. When it is good from wine, one does.; Revisit (Batch G) — the threshold pattern extended: The step before the merry heart: "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5, 8). The father-in-law alternates *strengthen* (5, 8) and *merry* (6, 9). Each round delays departure (G §3.1).; The threshold engineered and refused: David "made him drunk" (2Sa 11:13). Uriah, who had sworn "as your soul lives, I will not do this thing" (11:11), still does not go home. The next morning: the death letter (11:14–15) (G §4).; The soul's version: "prepare for me delicious food … that my soul may bless you" (Gen 27:4). "He ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank" (27:25) → the irreversible blessing of the false firstborn → Esau's hatred "in his heart" (27:41; §8.2 below) (G §13.3).; The Samson sequence in full (Judg 16:15–30): soul vexed (16); heart told (17); strength and the Lord gone (19–20); the Philistines' merry hearts (25); strength asked for (28)

16933.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: "let my soul die" (30); The merry-heart threshold is the penultimate step (G §3.6).; The counter-case: the sad heart at a feast.; Hannah "would not eat … why is your heart sad?" → prays "after they had eaten and drunk" → is taken for drunk → "troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul" → face no longer sad (1Sa 1:7–18).; Nehemiah: "when wine was before him … Why is your face sad? … sadness of the heart" → prayer → request granted (Neh 2:1–5).; The sad heart at the feast is also a threshold, but what enters is prayer, and the outcome is a gift (G §8.2).; Revisit (Batch H §7.6) — the threshold pattern extended again: Esther's wine-banquets (Est 5:6–14; 7:3–8): "as they were drinking wine after the feast" (5:6) → Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart" (5:9) → sees Mordecai → wrath → "all this is worth nothing to me" (5:13) → the gallows (5:14).; At the second banquet Esther asks for her life (7:3). The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking" (7:7), and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8).; One banquet is the threshold for two outcomes: Esther's petition is granted; Haman falls.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (point 5).; The inner sentence comes first: "if that servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,' and begins … to eat and drink and get drunk" → the master comes "on a day when he does not expect him" (Luk 12:45–46; Mat 24:48–51).; The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16) — the threshold and death: Nabal's sequel: the heart dies in the morning (1Sa 25:37), and "about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (25:38). The dead heart comes before the dead man.

16936.text: Prior hatred as a legal criterion: "since he had not hated his neighbor in the past" (Deu 19:6) — the manslayer is protected; "if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait … he flees" (Deu 19:11) — the murderer is not; A past inner state decides guilt.

16945.text: 8.3 Joy at an enemy's fall — the heart is watched: [Claude reading] The inner response to another people's ruin is itself judged. Rejoicing "with all the malice of the soul" brings judgment (Eze 25). The prophetic heart grieves over the fall of an enemy nation (Isa 15; Jer 48). Pro 24:17–18 states the principle: God watches the heart's gladness at an enemy's stumbling.

16965.text: Anger: "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges [*rests*] in the heart of fools" (Ecc 7:9). The context Ecc 7:8 sets "the patient in spirit" against "the proud in spirit".

16968.text: Context 2Ki 2:9–15 — the resting spirit confirmed by others: "Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me" (9); "You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken … it shall be so" (10); Elijah goes up; Elisha sees, cries out and tears his clothes (11–12); Takes up the cloak, strikes the water: "Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?" The water parts (13–14); The sons of the prophets: "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (15); [Claude reading] The request (9) is granted on condition of seeing (10). Elisha's first act is a question to God, not a claim of power (14). The resting of the spirit is recognised by others from its effect (15), not asserted by its bearer. Num 11 has the same shape: others see and report (27).

16970.text: Holding the spirit back — the wise and the fool: "A fool gives full vent to his spirit [*temper*], but a wise man quietly holds it back" (Pro 29:11) [T]. "calmness will lay great offenses to rest" (Ecc 10:4) [T].

16981.text: 12.1 The heart's own purpose inside God's purpose: "But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few" (Isa 10:7); [Claude reading] Assyria is the Lord's rod (Isa 10:5), but its heart has its own intention. The instrument's heart does not share the purpose of the one who wields it. This underlies the judgment on the instrument that follows (10:12 — Batch D §9.1, "the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria").

16988.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch F [Claude reading]: Relating to others is most often a matter of the soul.; Souls are knit (1Sa 18:1).; A soul loves, seeks and fails (Song 3; 5).; Malice lives in the soul (Eze 25:6, 15).; Souls abhor each other, even God's soul and the people's (Lev 26).; One loves another "as one's own soul".; The heart is where hatred starts and is spoken (Lev 19:17; Gen 27:41). It is also where the response to another's fall is judged (Pro 24:17).; The human spirit registers bonds and bearing.; It is unsettled by a friend's absence and refreshed by a friend's arrival (2Co 2:13; 7:13; 1Co 16:18).; It is the manner of approach — gentleness (1Co 4:21).; It is what the wise hold back and the fool vents (Pro 29:11).; Sequences matter more than single verses. Reading before and after changed the picture in six places: 1Sa 18 (Jonathan and Saul); Lev 26 (reciprocal abhorrence broken by God); Psa 143 and Psa 51 (the crushing chains); Judg 19 and the other merry-heart narratives (threshold states); 2Co 2 → 7 (the spirit's rest through persons); 2Ki 2 (spirit transfer confirmed by others); Meaning shifts with circumstance in consistent ways: *crush*: by whom, and turned to whom (§5); *tender heart*: to what it yields (§6); *good heart*: from God or from wine (§7); *love / hate one's soul*: well-being vs clinging (§3); *hāgâ*: what the heart rehearses (§12.2); *nûaḥ*: what rests in or on the person (§9.5); Inner states spread between people: the fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8); heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42); a lowly heart gives rest to other souls (Mat 11:29); a congregation refreshes Titus's spirit (2Co 7:13); the prophet's heart takes in the people's doom (Jer 4:18–19); Other spirits relate to people as occupants of a house (Mat 12:43–45) and as seizures between people (1Sa 18:10; Judg 9:23 in Batch D). The divine Spirit rests upon people and is recognised by others (Num 11; 2Ki 2).; Fringe worth keeping: the knit soul beside the seizing spirit in one chapter (1Sa 18); the heart awake while the body lags (Song 5); God refusing to complete reciprocal abhorrence (Lev 26:44); Jezebel curing a vexed spirit by a manufactured good heart (1Ki 21); the prophet's heart for Moab set against Ammon's malice of soul (Isa 15; Jer 48; Eze 25); past hatred as a legal criterion (Deu 19)

17173.text: 10. Madness (M66): "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live" (Ecc 9:3); "The Lord will strike you with madness and blindness and confusion of mind [*heart*]" (Deu 28:28); "I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly … a striving after wind" (Ecc 1:17); "I turned my heart to know … the foolishness that is madness" (Ecc 7:25); "The prophet is a fool; the man of the spirit is mad" (Hos 9:7) [U]; [Claude reading] Madness is located in the heart (Ecc 9:3; Deu 28:28). The heart can also investigate madness (Ecc 1:17; 7:25). Hos 9:7 is the only verse linking madness to "spirit", and its spirit is not determinable.

17174.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch C [Claude reading]: The soul is the desiring self. In the OT, *nephesh* is the ordinary subject of "want / crave / long / thirst", from appetite for meat (Deu 12:20) to thirst for God (Psa 42:1–2). The same *nephesh* is the life that enemies seek (§7.5) and the life that is precious (§1.7). Desire and vitality are one word.; The heart is where orientation is set, held, divided or hardened. It plans, forms intentions, resolves, seeks, turns, is whole or not whole, and is stubborn or hardened. Many of these are expressed as setting / directing / inclining the heart (1Sa 7:3; Jos 24:23; 2Ch 19:3; 30:19). This extends Batch B's "attention = setting the heart" into will.; The human spirit carries energy and disposition, more than choice. It is "moved" to give (Exo 35:21), "fervent" (Rom 12:11), "willing" against weak flesh (Mat 26:41), patient or proud (Ecc 7:8), ruled (Pro 16:32), hardened with the heart (Deu 2:30), not faithful (Psa 78:8), and crushed or contrite (Psa 34:18; 51:17). Planning and choosing are rarely predicated of the human spirit [observation, not a count].; Heart and spirit are paired in the orientation verses (Exo 35:21; Deu 2:30; Psa 51:17; 78:8; Isa 57:15; Eze 11:19; 36:26). Heart and soul are paired in the "all your heart and all your soul" formula for seeking and returning (Deu 4:29; 1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 15:12).; Flesh changes role across the corpus.; OT: flesh longs and faints for God with the soul (Psa 63:1; 84:2). The "heart of flesh" is God's gift (Eze 36:26).; NT: flesh is the main subject of wrong desire (Gal 5:16–17; 1Jo 2:16), set against the Spirit and the soul (1Pe 2:11) and weak beside a willing spirit (Mat 26:41).; 2Co 3:3 ("tablets of fleshly hearts") keeps the OT positive use inside the NT.; God's Spirit relates to orientation as giver and as the one resisted.; Giver: good Spirit leading (Psa 143:10), patience (Gal 5:22), hope (Rom 5:5; 15:13), received on repentance (Act 2:38).; Resisted: rebelled against and grieved (Isa 63:10), disregarded (1Th 4:8), bypassed in plans (Isa 30:1).; The Spirit also desires against the flesh (Gal 5:17) and wills (1Co 12:11).
