18877.text: Hiding from God: In each scene where a person hides from God, something of God is perceived first: a sound (Genesis 3:10), God naming himself (Exodus 3:6), "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).; Adam hid because he knew he was naked (Genesis 3:10).; Moses "hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God" (Exodus 3:6), and no wrong is named.; At the end, people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us'", for "who can stand?" (Revelation 6:16–17).; Job names the one condition on which he will not hide: "Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me" (Job 13:20–21). In his words, it is the dread that makes a person hide.; None of it works. "Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jeremiah 23:24). "There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves" (Job 34:22). Isaiah names what the attempt does: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay" (Isaiah 29:15–16).; That nothing is hidden from God is the same fact for everyone, and it falls very differently.; For the one who suffers it is comfort: "O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you" (Psalm 38:9).; For the one being made it is wonder: "My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret" (Psalm 139:15), and the psalmist answers, "my soul knows it very well" (139:14).; For the one who has done wrong it is judgement: "I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore" (Hosea 5:3).

18889.text: The hidden trap: In the Psalms a purpose is hidden in order to catch someone. "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" (Psalm 64:5). The next verse says where the purpose was hidden first: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (64:6).; The one it is set for prays out of his weakness. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psalm 142:3). "No one cares for my soul" (142:4). It is worse when it comes from those he had prayed for: "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them" (Jeremiah 18:20).; And the trap turns. "In the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught" (Psalm 9:15). The soul the pit was dug for (Psalm 35:7) is the soul that rejoices: "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord" (35:9). The one taken "out of the net they have hidden for me" says, "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:4–5).

18890.text: Longing to be hidden: Job in his pain wishes he had been hidden from life itself, cursing the night that did not "hide trouble from my eyes" (Job 3:10). Later the same wish becomes a hope: "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!" (Job 14:13; section 10.3).

18891.text: Who hides whom. God hiding a person is safety. God hiding his face from a person is dismay. The two are four verses apart in one psalm (Psalm 27:5, 9; 10.9).

18925.text: *satar* H5641, hide (75 no-seat) | Psa 143:7 "my spirit fails! Hide not your face"; Psa 88:14 soul; Psa 104:29 "they are dismayed … breath"; Psa 10:11 heart | God hiding his face. The seat is the human recipient's: Psa 13:1 (13:2 "sorrow in my heart"); Psa 30:7 "you hid your face; I was dismayed"; Psa 44:24; 69:17; 102:2; Isa 8:17 ("I will wait … and I will hope in him"); Isa 54:8; 59:2; 64:7; Mic 3:4; Deu 31:17 | Physical hiding (David 1Sa 20, 23, 26; Jeremiah and Baruch Jer 36): outward, with inner being behind the act at most. God concealing (Pro 25:2; Deu 29:29): divine subject

18935.text: Books: Isaiah is high because of H8213 "bring low" (Isa 2, 5, 25, 26) and the Sennacherib account (Isa 37). Mark is the mute spirit and the silencing words.

18949.text: G0880 *aphōnos*: the lamb "silent" before its shearer (Act 8:32, Isa 53:7) versus "mute idols" (1Co 12:2) versus the "speechless donkey" (2Pe 2:16) versus languages "without meaning" (1Co 14:10).

18965.text: C, mute and silence (23 verses), is not part of #2171. It meets M07 three times only, each a neighbouring verse with another subject: an idol "speechless" (Hab 2:18) two verses from "you will have your fill of shame" (2:16); the muzzled ox (Deu 25:4) next to the brother not to be "degraded" (25:3); Balaam's donkey (2Pe 2:16) near "accursed children" (2:14). Its own family is the silence words of M33 Rest & Peace (§5).

18978.text: h. Old Testament "the Spirit" without a marker, where the prophet's own spirit is also possible: Eze 2:2; 3:24 ("the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet") — D3.; Num 27:18 ("a man in whom is the Spirit").; 1Ch 28:12 ("all that he had in mind" = "by the spirit" [lexical]).; Hos 9:7 ("the man of the spirit").

18984.text: #1979 (the M47 check). 28 B verses are shared with M47, checked by word as for M64 (#1989): 11 are already cited and carried.; 8 are read in §2 for the first time: Eph 6:12, Ecc 8:9, Judg 9:2, Act 8:19, Jude 8, Rom 13:1, Jer 51:46 and Jer 30:21.; 4 go forward: Ecc 10:4, Act 5:4, Mar 1:27 and Luk 4:36.; 4 are God's character (13.1): Mat 10:1, Mar 6:7, Joh 17:2 and Psa 103:22.; 1 goes to the other spirits (13.3): Act 19:16.

18993.text: The person rules. *"he who rules his spirit"* (Pro 16:32); *"you must rule over it"* (Gen 4:7); *"having his desire under control"* (1Cor 7:37); *"I will not be dominated by anything"* (1Cor 6:12).

19000.text: Already carried: Lev 25:43 and Neh 5:15 (10.10 *The fear of God and the weak*); Isa 14:6 (10.10 *Anger between people*)

19017.text: The passage, before: men are to pray *"without anger or quarreling"* (2:8), and women to dress *"with modesty and self-control"* (2:9). *"Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness"* (2:11).

19019.text: The passage. Vashti refused to come (1:12; cited in 10.1, 10.13 and Ch 11). The counsel was that the noble women *"will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty"* (1:18). The decree was to have this result: *"all women will give honor to their husbands"* (1:20). *"This advice pleased the king"* (1:21).

19020.text: Reading: The rule of each house is made a matter of royal law.; The motive given is fear of contempt and wrath (1:18), and the aim is honour (1:20). Honour, an inner act, is commanded by decree.

19028.text: The inner ground of harsh rule: feeding oneself (Eze 34:2), a lack of understanding and love of gain (Pro 28:16), anger (Isa 14:6).

19038.text: The passage. Dathan and Abiram refuse twice: *"We will not come up"* (16:12, 14). Moses before this, to Korah: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (16:10). After: *"Moses was very angry and said to the Lord, 'Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them'"* (16:15).

19047.text: The passage. *"he is God's servant for your good"* (13:4). *"Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience"* (13:5; in Ch 8).

19054.text: Paul's own account: *"I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth"* (26:9); *"after receiving authority from the chief priests … I cast my vote against them"* (26:10); *"in raging fury against them I persecuted them"* (26:11); *"with the authority and commission of the chief priests"* (26:12); *"It is hard for you to kick against the goads"* (26:14)

19055.text: Roles: "authority" (M72) is received from men, and it is the means.; The characteristics are the conviction (26:9) and the raging fury (26:11). They carry no M72 word.

19092.text: He rules over all.; *"you rule over all"* (1Ch 29:12); *"You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations"* (2Ch 20:6, in prayer); *"he rules over the nations"* (Psa 22:28); *"his kingdom rules over all"* (Psa 103:19); *"Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven"* (Job 25:2); *"You rule the raging of the sea"* (Psa 89:9); *"who rules by his might forever, whose eyes keep watch on the nations — let not the rebellious exalt themselves"* (Psa 66:7)

19093.text: His rule is to be known: *"that they may know that God rules over Jacob"* (Psa 59:13; OT-16).

19157.text: The passage (15:26–30): Samuel: "you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you from being king"; (15:26).; Saul seizes the skirt of Samuel's robe "and it tore" (15:27). Samuel turns the tear into the word; of 15:28.; Then "the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret" (15:29).; Saul answers: "I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people" (15:30).

19159.text: Saul's "yet honor me now before the elders" (15:30) is honour sought from people straight; after confessing to God. It is not a fear or M72 act. It belongs to the strand that reads honour; (M22), and should be marked forward there, not woven now.

19162.text: Ezra 8. The hand brings him the men he needed (8:18). He will not ask the king for soldiers; because he has said, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him" (8:22). 8:21–22 are in; 10.14.

19167.text: 10.12 *Fear*, "What changes it", or 10.9: Ezra 7:28, courage taken *because* God's hand is on; him. Ezra 8:22 already shows Ezra choosing not to lean on the king's soldiers. 7:28 gives the inner; ground.

19171.text: 13.1 *Ruling*: "His reign, and the nations' rage" (Rev 11:17–18) has God's reign with wrath.; Isa 52:7–9 is the other face: his reign is good news, joined to peace, salvation and comfort. This; sits with "The ruler to come", where "His rule comes with peace".

19187.text: 0.1 The seat-sense mapping (new in v3): Each phenomenon now ends with a Seat block. It records three things.; Whose seat it is: the bearer's own: the person who undergoes the phenomenon; the other party's: someone else in the scene (God, a second person, an interpreter); the offender's: the one whose wrong produces the phenomenon (e.g. Isa 57:17); none; The seat-sense check: whether the seat word is used in a genuine inner-being sense. It fails where the word means something else: wind, meat, flesh as food, bodily life only, or the divine Spirit speaking. The spurious links were first set out in v1 §0.; Where the seat arrives outside the verse: in the next verse, or at the head of the passage or discourse.

19188.text: What it does. It puts a covering between the self and God: "among the trees of the garden" (Gen 3:8); "Moses hid his face" (Exo 3:6); "enter into the rock and hide in the dust" (Isa 2:10); "in the caves and among the rocks … Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne" (Rev 6:15–16)

19189.text: Where it comes from. In every case a perception of God comes first: "I heard the sound of you in the garden" (Gen 3:10); God names himself: "I am the God of your father" (Exo 3:6); "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isa 2:10); "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Rev 6:16); Inside the person, what meets that perception differs: Adam: knowledge of exposure. "The eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked" (Gen 3:7), and so "I was afraid, because I was naked" (3:10).; Moses: "he was afraid to look at God" (Exo 3:6), with no transgression stated.; The kings, the great, "slave and free": "who can stand?" (Rev 6:17).

19190.text: How it co-exists. It is always with fear (Gen 3:10; Exo 3:6), terror (Isa 2:10), or wrath felt as unbearable (Rev 6:16–17). In Adam, self-knowledge ("naked") comes between perception and fear. Job 13:20–22 turns the phenomenon inside out. Job names the conditions under which he will *not* hide: "withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me. Then call, and I will answer". Job shows that hiding is what dread produces. Remove the dread and the person can face God and speak.

19191.text: What it leads to. The same act has three outcomes: Being sought and questioned: "Where are you?" (Gen 3:9), then Adam's answer and his blame of the woman (3:12); Being addressed further: God goes on to speak to the hidden-faced Moses, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people" (Exo 3:7); Despair of standing at all (Rev 6:17)

19203.text: God hiding the person: "hide me in the shadow of your wings" (Psa 17:8); "he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble" (Psa 27:5); "you hide them from the plots of men; you store them … from the strife of tongues" (Psa 31:20); "Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked" (Psa 64:2); "You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue" (Job 5:21); "the Lord hid them" (Jer 36:26); "in the shadow of his hand he hid me … in his quiver he hid me away" (Isa 49:2): hidden for later use, not only for safety; "enter your chambers … hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isa 26:20): God's own people hidden from God's own fury; "perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3): conditional, after "seek humility"; "your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Col 3:3), after "Set your minds on things that are above" (3:2)

19207.text: Seat.; In the verse: none of the 23 names a seat.; Outside the verse — new in v3. For Rahab, the one human hider who explains herself, the seat arrives in her own confession: "our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the Lord your God, he is God" (Jos 2:11). The seat is the hider's own, and genuine. It is the collective heart of Jericho that melted. [Claude reading] What turns Rahab to shelter the spies is not the melting itself, which all Jericho shares, but the confession she draws from it. The seat is where the fear sits. The act of hiding comes from the confession.; Isa 26:20 → 26:18 "wind" ("we have given birth to wind") is *ruach* as wind. Spurious.; Psa 17:8 → 17:9 "my deadly enemies who surround me". The seat word is inside the English "deadly": *nephesh*, the life the enemies are against. Life-sense only. It names what is at stake in the petition "hide me", as in §2 (Psa 54:4).; Whose seat, God as hider: none is named. The sheltered person's inner state is carried by the petition ("hide me") and the trust, not by a seat word.

19209.text: How it shifts. Job 14:13 moves the same wish into hope: "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!" Being hidden is no longer non-existence. It is being kept by God through the wrath, and then remembered.

19211.text: Where it comes from, as the verses themselves state: The human's turning or sin: "because of all the evil that they have done, because they have turned to other gods" (Deu 31:18); "a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness" (Deu 32:20); "your iniquities have made a separation … your sins have hidden his face from you" (Isa 59:2); "he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17): the seat named is the offender's; "because they have made their deeds evil" (Mic 3:4); "they dealt so treacherously with me" (Eze 39:23); "their uncleanness and their transgressions" (39:24); "all their evil" (Jer 33:5); Momentary anger: "In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion" (Isa 54:8).; No reason given, only "why?" and "how long?": Psa 13:1; 44:24; 88:14; 89:46; Job 13:24.

19212.text: What it does in the human: Dismay: "you hid your face; I was dismayed" (Psa 30:7); "When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die" (Psa 104:29); The spirit failing: "My spirit fails! Hide not your face from me, lest I be like those who go down to the pit" (Psa 143:7); Being cast away: "why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face" (Psa 88:14); Feeling forgotten: "Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psa 13:1). The seat follows at once: "How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day?" (13:2); The body pressed down: "Why do you hide your face? … For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground" (Psa 44:24–25); Melting: "you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities" (Isa 64:7). The previous verse: "We all fade like a leaf" (64:6); Being counted an enemy: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24); "Will you frighten a driven leaf?" (13:25); A collective conclusion: "Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?" (Deu 31:17); Complaint: "My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God" (Isa 40:27). The answer: "He does not faint or grow weary … He gives power to the faint" (40:28–29); Banishment and the fear that follows it: Cain, "from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive … whoever finds me will kill me" (Gen 4:14), after "My punishment is greater than I can bear" (4:13). Being hidden from God's face is followed at once by fear of man.

19213.text: How it co-exists.; Petition is the most common companion: "Hide not your face from me" (Psa 27:9; 69:17 "for I am in distress"; 102:2 "in the day of my distress"; 143:7).; Petition reversed: "Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities" (Psa 51:9), then "Create in me a clean heart" (51:10). The penitent asks God to hide his face from the sin, not from the self: the same act, wished in the opposite direction.; A false inference: the wicked "says in his heart, 'God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it'" (Psa 10:11). He reads hiddenness as licence.; Its denial as resolution: "he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him" (Psa 22:24).; Waiting and hope through it: "I will wait for the Lord, who is hiding his face … and I will hope in him" (Isa 8:17). "Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior" (Isa 45:15) holds hiddenness and saving together. Job 34:29 (Elihu): "When he hides his face, who can behold him".

19215.text: What it leads to at the end. "I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my Spirit" (Eze 39:29). "With everlasting love I will have compassion" (Isa 54:8).

19216.text: Seat. This is the phenomenon where the seat is densest. There are six links in the verse itself, and in nine more passages a seat arrives in the next verse or close by: Psa 13, 22, 27, 44, 51, 69, 89 and 102, and Isa 54.; In the verse, the bearer's own (genuine): Psa 143:7 "My spirit fails! Hide not your face". Batch A v3 §6 (and §7 Faintness).; Psa 88:14 "why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face". Batch C v3 §9.5 ("Cast off"). New in v3: the two questions are parallel, so the hidden face and the rejected soul are one experience seen from two sides, God's act and the human's undergoing of it.; Psa 104:29 "they are dismayed … you take away their breath". Batch A v3 §6 . Seat-sense: *ruach* here is life-breath (H7307H "spirit: breath"), the breath that keeps the creature alive, not an inner faculty. The inner state is carried by "dismayed". The pairing A §6 drew still holds: hidden face with breath withdrawn, dismay with death.; In the verse, the offender's (genuine): Psa 10:11 "He says in his heart, 'God has forgotten, he has hidden his face'". Batch A v3 §6 . The heart is where the false inference is spoken: the wicked tells himself that the hidden face means no one sees.; Isa 57:17 "I hid my face and was angry, but he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart". Batch H v1 §4.1 ("the heart … go[es] its own way"). New in v3: the verse sets two movements against each other. God hides his face; the offender does not turn but keeps to his own heart's way. The hidden face here is not felt at all. That is the opposite of Psa 30:7 and 143:7, where it is felt at once.; In the verse, the other party's (divine): Eze 39:29 "I will not hide my face anymore … when I pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel". Batch A v3 §6 [D1]. The Spirit is God's. The human side is the receiving: the end of hiddenness lands on the house of Israel as a Spirit poured out on them.; In the next verse or the passage (bearer's own, genuine): Psa 13:1 → 13:2 "counsel in my soul … sorrow in my heart all the day" (v1 §2, *satar* row).; Psa 44:24 → 44:25 "our soul is bowed down to the dust" (v2).

19217.text: Psa 51:9 → 51:10 "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me". New in v3: when God is asked to hide his face *from the sin*, the next request places the remedy in the heart and spirit. The seat is where the cleansing is to happen. The requests go on: "Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me" (51:11), then "uphold me with a willing spirit" (51:12). The face hidden from the sin (51:9) is set against the presence not withdrawn from the person (51:11). Between them stand two spirits: God's, which is not to be taken away, and the human's, which is to be renewed and made willing.; New in v3: Psa 102:2 ("Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress") → 102:4 "My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread". The distress of 102:2 is a withered heart, and it reaches the body: the sufferer forgets to eat. It is the same movement as Psa 44:25 ("our belly clings to the ground").; New in v3: Psa 27:9 ← 27:8 "You have said, 'Seek my face.' My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek.'" The heart seeks the face one verse before it asks that the face not be hidden. The petition "Hide not your face" (27:9) is the voice of a heart already turned toward the face. What hiddenness would cut off is the heart's own seeking.; New in v3: Psa 69:17 → 69:20 "Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none". The "distress" of 69:17 is named three verses later as a broken heart that finds no comforter. The hidden face of 69:17 and the absent human pity of 69:20 are the same lack, felt from God and from people. In between, the petition names the soul: "Draw near to my soul, redeem me" (69:18). The opposite of the hidden face is God drawing near to the soul.; New in v3, the resolution in the heart: Psa 22:24 ("he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard") → 22:26 "The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the Lord! May your hearts live forever!" When the face is not hidden, the outcome lands in hearts that live. It is the reverse of the withered heart that forgets to eat (Psa 102:4): here the afflicted eat, and the hearts live.

19218.text: Life-sense, in the passage: Psa 89:46 ("How long, O Lord? Will you hide yourself forever?") → 89:48 "What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" *Nephesh* here is the life facing death. The hidden face is set against human mortality. This is a pointer to Batch G v3 §16.4 ("The soul delivered from death"), not read further here.; New in v3: Isa 54:8 ← 54:6 "the Lord has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off". The momentary hiding of 54:8 is borne in a grieved spirit (the bearer's own, Zion's). The image is marital: the hidden face is felt as desertion.; Spurious context links: Isa 64:7 ← 64:6 "our iniquities, like the wind, take us away" (*ruach* as wind); Mic 3:4 ← 3:2–3 "flesh" (the flesh torn from the people). Neither is an inner seat.; What the map shows. Every genuine seat in this phenomenon falls on the human side. Three forms: The sufferer's spirit, soul or heart is where the hiddenness is felt: failing, cast away, sorrowing, bowed down, broken, grieved.; The offender's heart is where it is misread or ignored: "God has forgotten" (Psa 10:11); "the way of his own heart" (Isa 57:17).; God's Spirit is where it ends: poured out (Eze 39:29).

19257.text: Where it comes from. In all five verses, from another party: a father's provoking: "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); false prophets' lies: "you have disheartened the righteous falsely, although I have not grieved him" (Eze 13:22). God did not do the grieving; the lie did.; an oppressor: "The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might" (Psa 10:10), while "He says in his heart, 'God has forgotten'" (10:11); a persecutor who "pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death" (Psa 109:16), who "loved to curse" (109:17); military defeat: "ships of Kittim shall come against him" (Dan 11:30)

19258.text: What it does and leads to.; The crushed "sink down, and fall" (Psa 10:10).; In Dan 11:30 losing heart turns into rage and action: "he shall be afraid [disheartened] and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant". Disheartenment feeds aggression against a third party.; God's answer to the lie: "I will deliver my people out of your hand" (Eze 13:23).

19259.text: Seat.; Inside the word or phrase, the victim's own (genuine): Eze 13:22 "you have disheartened the righteous". The Hebrew includes *lev*, the heart, in the phrase. Batch A v3 §6 ("Disheartened by others").; Psa 109:16 "the brokenhearted" (*nikh'eh levav*). Batch G v3 §16.1 ("A broken heart is the prey of the pursuer"); Batch D v2 §10.3 and R6 (poverty and lowliness entangled).; Col 3:21 *athumeō*, "without *thumos*" (v1 §1.3). Not an M47 word, but the inner place is inside the verb.; New in v3, what the map shows: in all three cases the seat named is the victim's, and the cause is another person's act. Losing heart is the one M20 phenomenon where the seat word always sits with the one acted upon.; In the passage, the aggressor's heart (genuine): Psa 10:10 → 10:11 "He says in his heart" (v1 §1.3; the same verse is FH §5, Batch A v3 §6 ). The oppressor's heart speaks while the victim is seen only from outside.; New in v3: Dan 11:30 ← 11:27 "as for the two kings, their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table". The king who is disheartened in 11:30 is one of the two whose heart was already bent on evil three verses earlier. The losing of heart feeds an aggression that was already in the heart. The rage of 11:30 has a prior seat. The next step names that seat's object: "he shall return to his land with great wealth, but his heart shall be set against the holy covenant" (11:28). The act of 11:30, "take action against the holy covenant", is the act of a heart set on it two verses earlier. Losing heart does not create the target. It releases a hostility the heart already held.; Different party, next verse: Col 3:21 → 3:22 "with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord" is addressed to bondservants, the next household group. It does not bear on the children's discouragement (v1 §1.3).

19275.text: Seat.; In the verse, the victim's own (genuine): Psa 142:3 "When my spirit faints within me … they have hidden a trap for me". Batch A v3 §7 (Faintness & Despair, M24). → 142:4 "no one cares for my soul" (v2).; In the verse, the victim's life (life-sense): Psa 35:7 "without cause they dug a pit for my life". *Nephesh* here is the life aimed at, in its life sense. It passes the check as life, not as an inner faculty. New in v3: this verse was not read in the M47 batches. It is the same use as Batch G v3 §5.3 ("Hunting souls").; In the next verse, the trapper's (genuine): Psa 64:5 → 64:6 "the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (v2). The heart is where the trap is first hidden, before the net is hidden in the path. New in v3, a second instance: Psa 140:5 ("The arrogant have hidden a trap for me") follows "who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually" (140:2). The trappers' heart is again where the plan starts.; Life-sense, in the passage: Jer 18:22 ("they have dug a pit to take me") comes two verses after "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them" (18:20). *Nephesh* is the life aimed at, as in Psa 35:7. New in v3: the verse adds what makes the hidden trap bitter. It is set by those the victim once interceded for. Good repaid with evil, as in Psa 55:12–13 (§2 g), where the betrayer is the familiar friend.; In the next verse, the victim's soul after the reversal — new in v3: Psa 35:8 ("let the net that he hid ensnare him") → 35:9 "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord, exulting in his salvation". The soul the pit was dug for (35:7) is the soul that rejoices when the trap turns on its maker (35:9). The seat is the same in the threat and in the rescue.; In the next verses, the victim's own — new in v3: Psa 31:4 → 31:5 "Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O Lord, faithful God", and → 31:7 "you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul". The one taken out of the hidden net commits his spirit into God's hand. The next verses then say that the soul's distress has been known by God. Being known (§6) answers the concealment of the trap. Batch E v2 §1.7 reads Psa 31:5 as the spirit committed at death. Here the committal comes in the middle of danger, not at death.

19276.text: What the map shows. This phenomenon has three seats in three hands: the trapper's heart (the hiding place of the intent), the victim's spirit (fainting, then committed), and God's knowing of the victim's soul.

19301.text: Dan 11:27–30: hearts bent on evil (v3) → disheartened → withdraw → enraged → action against the covenant

19303.text: Two phenomena face each other in one psalm: "he will hide me in his shelter" (Psa 27:5) and "Hide not your face from me" (27:9). The same verb gives safety (§3) and dread (§5), depending on whether God hides the person or hides himself from the person. v3 adds that the heart between them, "My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek'" (27:8), is seeking the face.

19369.text: Co-existence in one psalm, Psa 27: "he will hide me in his shelter" (27:5) and "Hide not your face from me" (27:9). Being hidden by God and God hiding from me are asked for side by side (see §5).

19416.text: 1.7 It takes in what people do against him, without excusing them: *"this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men"* (Act 2:23). The plan and the guilt are stated in one sentence.; The church prays Psalm 2, *"Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain?"* (Act 4:25). They say those gathered against Jesus came *"to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place"* (4:28).; Their next words are a request for themselves: *"grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness"* (4:29).; Pointer, from outside the 31: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Gen 50:20). The same verb is used for both.

19484.text: H3045 *yādaʿ* "know" (M15) has six faces: the ground of choosing: Isa 7:15–16; paired with choosing: Job 34; the purpose of being chosen: Isa 43:10; a response: 1Sa 20:30; a contrast: Isa 45:4; God making himself known, an operation: Num 16:5, Eze 20:5

19494.text: Celebrating. *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21). The celebrating had stopped at Uzzah's death, when David was angry, afraid and unwilling (6:8–10). It came back when he heard of the Lord's blessing (6:12).

19502.text: Put on. *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (Col 3:12). It comes after *"Set your minds on things that are above"* (3:2) and after putting away *"anger, wrath, malice"* (3:8). What is put on is turned toward others: *"forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (3:13); *"above all these put on love"* (3:14); *"let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts"* (3:15).

19526.text: Michal's contempt (2Sa 6:16) and Moses in the breach (Psa 106:23). These are kept for §2c.

19581.text: Led to: *"He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity"* (v15).; *"He also allured you out of distress into a broad place"* (v16).; *"Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing"* (v18).

19607.text: Psalm 106:5: "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation": Psalm 106 follows 105 and tells the same history from the other side. I read the two side by side because they stand together; neither refers to the other.; The speaker asks to be included: *"Remember me, O Lord, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them, that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance"* (v4–5). He does not claim the chosen ones' gladness. He asks to look upon it and to share it. "Gladness" here (H8057) is the same word as David's *"rejoicing"* in 2 Samuel 6:12.; He then confesses at once: *"Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness"* (v6). The rest of the psalm is the chosen people's inner failure, named act by act: *"did not consider your wondrous works; they did not remember the abundance of your steadfast love"* (v7); *"Then they believed his words; they sang his praise. But they soon forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel"* (v12–13); *"they had a wanton craving in the wilderness"* (v14); *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (v16); *"They forgot God, their Savior"* (v21); *"Then they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise"* (v24); *"they were rebellious in their purposes"* (v43); "Despised" in v24 is H3988A, the same word as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. The chosen people refused what they were given. "Faith" in v24 is H0539, the same word as *"believed"* in v12. The psalm has them believing, then forgetting, then without faith.; One of the chosen acts for the rest: *"had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath"* (v23).; The psalm's turn is God's remembering, as in Psalm 105: *"he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant"* (v44–45). It ends with the chosen asking again for the joy of v5: *"gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise"* (v47).

19613.text: Being chosen is not a guarantee. This is stated in the verses, not inferred: the condition put on Solomon, and the *"cast you off forever"* (1Ch 28:7, 9); the chosen people's forgetting, craving, jealousy and unbelief, and their despising the land (Psa 106:7–43); the chosen people weary of God, and not calling on him (Isa 43:22–24); In Psalm 106:24 the chosen *"despised"* (H3988A) what was given. This is the same word as the refusing in §2a.

19616.text: The chosen still go through anger, fear and refusal. David was angry, afraid and unwilling between the two celebrations (2Sa 6:8–10). His own heart's wish to build was refused, though he was chosen (1Ch 28:2–4).

19617.text: Moses in the breach (Psa 106:23). One chosen man stands before God for the rest. This is already cited in the narrative. Whether it belongs with "together" in the §2a account, or with 2c ("in others, around the choosing"), is left until 2c is read.

19623.text: Judges 20:34: "but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them": The chosen men are 10,000 troops: *"there came against Gibeah 10,000 chosen men out of all Israel, and the battle was hard"*. The not-knowing belongs to the other side. The passage follows it through: Benjamin thinks *"They are routed before us, as at the first"* (v32); Israel draws them away because *"they trusted the men in ambush"* (v36); then the smoke rises, *"and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster was close upon them"* (v41).; The not-knowing is not bound to the choosing. "Chosen" names picked troops. The HIB/qualifier file has this as "none", and the reading agrees. Under rule 72 it was routed C.

19624.text: 1 Samuel 20:30: "do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame": The chapter is the covenant between Jonathan and David, tested at Saul's table. Before the meal it says what binds the two men: *"Whatever you say, I will do for you"* (v4); *"you have brought your servant into a covenant of the Lord with you"* (v8); *"And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (v17); David knows Saul's mind before Jonathan does: *"Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he thinks, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved'"* (v3). Jonathan will not believe it: *"Far from it! … my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me"* (v2). The test is set by Saul's anger: *"if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him"* (v7).; At the table: *"Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, 'You son of a perverse, rebellious woman, do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother's nakedness?'"* (v30).; Saul names the choice and calls it shame. He gives the reason in the next verse: *"For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die"* (v31). What Saul fears for is the kingdom of his house.; When Jonathan asks *"Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"* (v32), Saul turns his spear on his own son (v33). Now Jonathan knows: *"So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death"* (v33).; Jonathan's own anger follows: *"And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (v34). His anger is not for himself, though the spear was thrown at him. It is grief for David.; The chapter ends with the two men weeping together and with the oath: *"we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord, saying, 'The Lord shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever'"* (v42).

19631.text: Psalm 106:23: "had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath": The verse comes in the psalm's account of the calf: *"They made a calf in Horeb and worshiped a metal image. They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass. They forgot God, their Savior"* (v19–21). *"Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them"* (v23).; "Chosen one" is *bāḥîr* (H0972). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the moment he stands between God's wrath and the people. The ones he stands for are those who *"forgot God"*.; Psalm 106 names Moses three times, and each time he is set beside the people: *"When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord"* (v16); *"Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him"* (v23); *"They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (v32–33); The people were jealous of him. He stood for them. They made his spirit bitter, and it cost him. The psalm sets the three side by side and does not comment on them.; The psalm gives one more man who stands: *"Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed"* (v30). Phinehas is not called chosen.

19632.text: For OT-62 (anger and will together): The wrath in v23 is God's (*ḥēmāh*, H2534). Under rule 72 that part goes to Ch 13. The narrative already gives this event from Exodus 32 in 10.13 ("Moses stands between the anger and the people").; What v23 adds to 10.13 is the word "chosen". The man who stands in the breach is named by his being chosen.; Psalm 106:32–33, already cited in 10.13 ("Speech that must come out"), is the other side: the chosen man's own spirit embittered by the same people.

19633.text: Where it belongs (kept open from §2b). §2b asked whether this goes with "Choosing together" or with §2c. Read in its psalm, the inner acts of others around Moses are the jealousy (v16) and the embittering (v32–33). In v23 itself the act is the chosen man's: he stands for others before God. I read it as belonging with "Being chosen" in 10.7, as what a chosen man does for others. It is not a case of choosing together. This is for the researcher to rule.

19634.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: The chosen man stands for the others, before God, when they have forgotten God.; The same others are jealous of him (v16) and embitter his spirit (v32–33).

19639.text: Isaiah 58:5: "Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?": Here the inner act is what is weighed by God's choosing. The chapter opens on people who look devout: *"Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness … they delight to draw near to God"* (v2); *"'Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?'"* (v3); The answer is about what is going on alongside the fast: *"Behold, in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers. Behold, you fast only to quarrel and to fight and to hit with a wicked fist"* (v3–4).; Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?"* (v5).; "Humble himself" in v5 is *ʿānâ* (*to afflict*; H6031B) with the soul (H5315I), the same phrase as *"humbled ourselves"* in v3. The self-humbling of the soul is what they offered. God asks whether that is what he chooses.; What he does choose is turned outward: *"Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry … and not to hide yourself from your own flesh?"* (v6–7).; "Delight" in v2 (twice) is *ḥāpēṣ* (H2654A). It is the same word as *"chose that in which I did not delight"* in Isaiah 66:4, read in §2a. In v3 *"your own pleasure"* is the noun from the same root (H2656).

19642.text: What others do around a choice, in these verses: grumble against the chosen man, and God counts it as against himself (Num 16:11; 17:5, 10); seek more than they were given, and are jealous (Num 16:10; Psa 106:16); name a choice as shame, and are angry at what it costs them (1Sa 20:30–31); despise the chosen in the heart, by the eyes of people (2Sa 6:16, 20); despise and abhor the chosen servant (Isa 49:7); conclude from the chosen people's ruin that God rejected them, and despise them in their own sight (Jer 33:24); ask to share the joy of the chosen (Psa 106:5); not know God, and still be called and equipped for the sake of the chosen (Isa 45:4–5); offer an inner act, the humbling of the soul, that God's choosing weighs and does not accept (Isa 58:3–5)

19650.text: OT-62. Two of its seven verses are read here (1Sa 20:30, Psa 106:23). The other five are outside the choose set. OT-62 stays open for them.

19651.text: Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good": The setting is a king’s heart in fear. Syria and Ephraim are marching on Jerusalem, and *"the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind"* (v2). The Lord sends Isaiah with a word for that heart: *"Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint"* (v4); the threat *"shall not stand"* (v7); then the condition: *"If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all"* (v9). Both "firm" words are the one verb (H0539), so standing firm and being kept firm are the same word.; Then the Lord makes Ahaz an offer: *"Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven"* (v11). Ahaz refuses, in pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). The answer shows what that refusal was: *"Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"* (v13). Ahaz’s refusal was a choice. He chose not to take hold of what the Lord held out.; The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides: refusing the evil (H3988A); choosing the good (H0977); Refusing is not a step before the choice. It is the choice seen from the other side. Both rest on a knowing: *"when he knows how"*. The verse marks the moment a person can tell evil from good and turn from the one to the other.; The verse ties the eating to that knowing: he eats *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The oracle itself says what curds and honey are. *"In that day … because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey"* (v21–22). It is the food of those left in the land after the Lord has swept it with *"the king of Assyria"*: vineyards turned to *"briers and thorns"*, hills *"where cattle are let loose"* (v23–25). The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats with those who are left, and eats from abundance, in a land stripped of what it had.

19653.text: Isaiah 1:29 — "the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen": The oracle opens as a lawsuit: *"Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth"* (v2). The charge goes to the inner being: *"Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me"* (v2); *"The ox knows its owner … but Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (v3); *"The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint"* (v5); Their worship goes on, and the Lord refuses it: *"I do not delight in the blood of bulls"* (v11); *"your appointed feasts my soul hates"* (v14); *"even though you make many prayers, I will not listen"* (v15).; Then the choice is laid before them, in the same two-sided shape as Isa 7:15: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"* (v16–17); *"Come now, let us reason together"*, with the offer that sins *"like scarlet"* shall be *"as white as snow"* (v18); the two outcomes: *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (v19–20); Being willing, and refusing (here H3985, a different word from Isa 7), are the two sides of the choice. Eating, and being eaten, are its two outcomes.; The oracle ends with those who did not take the offer. v29–31 is figurative speech, and the figure is the point: *"they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"*; *"you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"*; *"the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark, and both of them shall burn together"*; The things they desired and chose become the picture of what they themselves become. They chose oaks and gardens, and they become a withering oak and a garden with no water. The choice comes back as an image of the chooser. The last line goes further: the strong man’s own *"work"* is the spark that sets him alight. What he made burns him, *"with none to quench them"*.; Shame comes first in the verse: *"ashamed"*, *"blush"* (H0954, H2659). The chooser is ashamed of the very thing that was desired and chosen. What drew the desire becomes the cause of the shame.

19656.text: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations": The Lord sees beneath the choosing: *"For I know their works and their thoughts"* (v18).; The tremblers are promised the opposite outcome: *"You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice"* (v14).

19684.text: Proverbs 3:31 — "Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways": The chapter is a father's teaching to a son, and it is about the heart: *"let your heart keep my commandments"* (v1); *"Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding"* (v5); *"Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord, and turn away from evil"* (v7); The father's ground is love: *"the Lord reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights"* (v12).; The verse forbids two things, and they are in order: *"Do not envy a man of violence"*: the pull, inside. Envy (H7065) is wanting what he has.; *"and do not choose any of his ways"*: the choice that would follow from it.; The command reaches back past the choice to the envy that would draw it. Proverbs describes the same man elsewhere, in a separate saying: *"A man of violence entices his neighbor and leads him in a way that is not good"* (16:29). The violent man draws others into his way.; The reason given is the Lord’s own stance: *"for the devious person is an abomination to the Lord, but the upright are in his confidence"* (v32). "Confidence" is H5475, the same word as *"The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him"* (Psa 25:14). The one who does not choose the violent man's ways is brought into the Lord’s confidence. The sayings that follow set the outcomes side by side: *"The Lord’s curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous"* (v33); *"The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace"* (v35).

19698.text: Narrative: 10 verses are cited.; Deu 30:19 in Ch 2 and 10.7; Job 7:15 and Jer 8:3 in Ch 2 ("Wanting to die"); Pro 1:29 in 10.2; Isa 66:4 in 10.12; Act 10:41 in Ch 2; new in v2: Psa 106:23 in 10.13 ("Pleading, and standing in the breach"); Isa 42:1 in Ch 9; Luk 10:42 in 10.1 ("What anxiety does"); Phili 1:22 in Ch 7; The other 222 are uncited. 10.7 *Choosing and setting direction* carries only Deu 30:19 from these words.

19724.text: The chosen one stands between: "had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them" (Psa 106:23). This is an OT-62 verse (anger face 2J).

19742.text: 3.9 Choosing a king or a side (4): "your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the Lord will not answer you in that day" (1Sa 8:18); "behold the king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked; behold, the Lord has set a king over you" (1Sa 12:13). Both the people's choosing and the Lord's setting are stated.; Loyalty: "whom the Lord and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain" (2Sa 16:18).; Choosing a friend draws anger: "Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan … do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame" (1Sa 20:30). This is an OT-62 verse (anger face 3O).

19782.text: Face: The chosen one stands between (v2); Who: God's chosen; Circumstance in the verses: "Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach"; Verses: Psa 106:23

19880.text: They read it in suffering. Elihu: *"this you have chosen rather than affliction"*, seen in wrath and scoffing (Job 36:18, 21).

19882.text: Choices weighed by another: The book does not let these evaluations have the last word. Job is the one the Lord calls *"a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil"* (1:8). Of Eliphaz and his friends the Lord says *"you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has"* (42:7); Elihu is not named.; The choice Elihu pressed is made, in his own verb, but only when Job sees the Lord: *"now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent"* (42:5–6).

19926.text: 3.8 Isa 10:12–15, in 10.13 *Those who carry it out*: Extend the Assyria bullet: > … (Isaiah 10:5, 7). He boasts, *"By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom"* (10:13), and the Lord *"will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes"* (10:12). *"Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it …?"* (10:15).

19939.text: Turned toward it from far off: For those far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of prayer. Solomon's prayer gives the hardest case, the people in captivity because they sinned: *"for there is no one who does not sin"* (1Ki 8:46). The inner turning comes in steps: *"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive"* (8:47); *"and repent and plead with you … saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'"* (8:47); *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies … and pray to you toward their land, … the city that you have chosen"* (8:48); "Turn" and "repent" are the one verb, *šûb*. The turning happens in the enemy's land. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is turned toward what God chose. Solomon prays it before the one who knows hearts: *"for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind"* (8:39). He also asks God to do the turning: *"that he may incline our hearts to him"* (8:58).; Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb. He asks God to remember his word to Moses: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Neh 1:9). Here the return is to God himself, and the place is where he brings those who return. Nehemiah's own part comes first: he *"sat down and wept and mourned for days"* (1:4), and confessed *"Even I and my father's house have sinned"* (1:6).

19941.text: Anger at what a choice costs. Saul to Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1Sa 20:30). Saul calls the choice shame and gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). His anger is for his house. It goes from insult to a death sentence to a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan's choice was made in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His own anger answers his father's, and it is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). The choice holds, sealed by an oath *"in the name of the Lord"* (20:42).

19952.text: With the chosen, and for them: The chosen also stand for the others. *"Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath"* (Psa 106:23). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the moment he stands for people who *"forgot God"* (106:21). The same psalm says those people were jealous of him (106:16), and that later *"they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (106:33). The psalm sets these side by side and does not comment.

19964.text: OT-62: 1Sa 20:30 and Psa 106:23 are read. Five OT-62 verses outside the choose set are not.

20013.text: One case where planning does not seem to come first: Act 5:33, *"they were enraged and wanted to kill them"*. Here G1011 renders the wish that follows rage, rather than a plan laid in advance. I read this as worth noting beside 10.13 Anger; it is not placed.

20031.text: 10.10 Relating to others, new section *Plotting against another* | Planned in the heart (Psa 140:2; Zec 7:10; 8:17). Done together (Psa 31:13; Jer 48:2; Joh 11:53; 12:10–11; Eze 11:2; Dan 11:25, 27; Jer 49:30). Aimed at the quiet and the weak (Psa 10:2; 35:20; 37:12; Eze 38:10–11). Hidden behind something friendly (Neh 6:2–3; 1Sa 18:25). Accusing the other of a plan (Neh 6:6, 8–9). The one plotted against: not knowing (Jer 11:19–20); praying to be guarded (Psa 140:4, 8; 35:4); trusting (Psa 31:14–15); another pleading (Est 8:3; 9:24); another stopping it (Act 27:42–43). Named and checked (Pro 24:8–9; 30:32–33; Deu 19:19–20) | New section

20035.text: 10.13 Anger, *What it does next* | The plot with gnashing teeth (Psa 37:12); rage that wants to kill at once, which is not a plan (Act 5:33–35) | Widened

20128.text: The epistle openings and requests (*"I want you to know"*, Phi 1:12; Tit 3:8; Jude 5; 1Ti 2:8; 5:14; 2Jo 12; Phm 13; 3Jo 10) mostly use the word as a stated wish in teaching. Their bearing on setting direction is slight, but each still needs to be read.

20137.text: God's "not willing" (route A): *"The Lord was unwilling to destroy you"* (Deu 10:10); *"the Lord was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant"* (2Ki 8:19); *"the Lord would not pardon"* (2Ki 24:4); *"The Lord will not be willing to forgive him"* (Deu 29:20); His unwillingness goes both ways, and the verses give his reasons: covenant, promise and the blood shed.

20143.text: 5. If you want this woven: Read the 99 verses in their passages, the method used for the plan set.; Route them under rule 72. By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).; A home in 10.7 would be a section on willing, next to *Planning* and *Holding a choice*. The working note already reserves "Will and resolve" for there.; Placed already (in the narrative for another reason, #1987): Deu 1:26; 2:30; 1Sa 31:4; Psa 51:12; Pro 6:35; Dan 5:19; Act 25:20; 1Ti 2:8. Each still needs reading for its will word.

20154.text: A refusal that costs the one who makes it: Asahel would not turn aside, and he died (2Sa 2:21–23).; The man who *"does not wish to take his brother's wife"*, and *"persists, saying, 'I do not wish to take her'"*, is publicly shamed (Deu 25:7–9).; Saul and the people *"spared Agag and the best of the sheep … and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction"* (1Sa 15:9). The refusal was selective. They destroyed what they did not value and kept what they did. God's word follows: *"he has turned back from following me"* (15:11), and *"Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night"* (15:11).

20157.text: Jealousy: *"For jealousy makes a man furious … He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts"* (Pro 6:34–35).

20164.text: What the refusal goes with. In these passages the "no" to God is placed beside something the people chose or planned instead: *"But you were unwilling, and you said, 'No! We will flee upon horses'"* (Isa 30:15–16). The refusal is said in their own words, together with their own plan. The chapter opened with *"stubborn children … who carry out a plan, but not mine"* (30:1). They told the prophets, *"Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things"* (30:10).; *"Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels"* (Psa 81:11–12).; *"Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices"* (Pro 1:29–31).; *"None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on"* (Eze 20:8).; *"a hard forehead and a stubborn heart"* (Eze 3:7).

20186.text: Paul's wishes for the churches are mostly stated wishes in teaching. Their passages give each one a reason: *"I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling"* (1Ti 2:8); *"I would have younger widows marry … for some have already strayed after Satan"* (1Ti 5:14–15); *"I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works"* (Tit 3:8); *"I want you to know … what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel"* (Phi 1:12); *"I would rather not use paper and ink … talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete"* (2Jo 12); *"I want to remind you"* (Jude 5)

20199.text: Against the self-blessing stubborn heart: of the one who *"blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'"* (Deu 29:19), *"The Lord will not be willing to forgive him"* (29:20).

20215.text: Grief (2Sa 12:17) and jealousy (Pro 6:34–35) fix the will in place. For 10.1 and 10.13.

20218.text: *ʾāḇâ* | refusing God (Isa 30:15); refusing sin (Pro 1:10); refusing to harm the anointed (1Sa 26:23); refusing a gift for others' sake (2Sa 23:17); refusing a plea by force (2Sa 13:14); refusing in grief (2Sa 12:17); God not willing to destroy (2Ki 8:19); God not willing to forgive (Deu 29:20) | What is refused, and for whose sake. The passages give the reason each time: faith, fear, grief, honour, force, covenant, love, a stubborn heart

20223.text: Already in the narrative for another reason (#1987): Deu 1:26; 2:30; 1Sa 31:4; Psa 51:12; Pro 6:35; Dan 5:19; Act 25:20; 1Ti 2:8; Act 27:43 (as a plan verse in 10.10). Each is now read for its will word above.

20224.text: A (other beings) — 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9; Luk 22:42.; Also B: Deu 10:10 (Moses' intercession), Deu 29:20 (the self-blessing heart), Dan 4:25 and 4:32 (the king's learning), Dan 5:21, Luk 22:42.

20303.text: The frame the book sets: Before any friend speaks, the book says who Job is, twice: the narrator: *"that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil"* (1:1); the Lord: *"there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil"* (1:8); Job's choosing is already named there, in its refusing side: he *"turned away from evil"*.; At the end the book gives a verdict on the friends: *"the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite"*: *"My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has"* (42:7). The verdict is about how they spoke *of God*. Elihu is not named in it, either way.; So every evaluation of Job's choices in these speeches is made by someone the book does not let have the last word.

20304.text: Job 15:5 — Eliphaz: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty": Eliphaz weighs Job by his words. He opens with *"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge"* (v2), and charges *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4). Then he names the choice: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5). He reads it this way: something inside, iniquity, teaches the mouth; the mouth then chooses a crafty tongue; From that he gives the verdict: *"Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you"* (v6).; He takes his evaluation further inside. He moves from the mouth to the heart, eyes and spirit: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?"* (v12–13). For Eliphaz, the words show what the heart has chosen.; His grounds for judging are age and tradition: *"Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father"* (v10); *"what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers"* (v18); His picture of the outcome is the wicked man's end (v20–35).; Set against the book's frame, his charge *"you are doing away with the fear of God"* (v4) runs against the narrator's and the Lord's *"one who feared God"* (1:1, 8). The Lord's verdict in 42:7 is on how Eliphaz spoke of God, not directly on this charge. Still, the man Eliphaz says has chosen the tongue of the crafty is the one the Lord twice calls *"my servant Job"* (42:7–8).

20305.text: Job 34:4 — Elihu: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good": Elihu is angry with both sides. He *"burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God"*, and at the friends *"because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong"* (32:2–3).; He calls the listeners to weigh Job's case together, and calls that weighing a choosing: *"Hear my words, you wise men"* … *"for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food"*; *"Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good"* (v2–4). The choosing here is not of a course of life. It is a judgement: picking out what is right in the case before them.; The picture is tasting. The ear tests (H0974) as the palate tastes (H2938). Then *"let us know among ourselves what is good"* uses the same words as Barzillai's *"Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not"* (2Sa 19:35): know (H3045), between (H0996), good (H2896). Barzillai said the palate's knowing had gone with age. Elihu uses the palate as the picture for weighing words.; What they are to weigh is Job's own claim. Elihu quotes it: *"I am in the right, and God has taken away my right"* (v5). He judges it at once: *"What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water"*, *"who travels in company with evildoers"* (v7–8). His ground is God's justice: *"far be it from God that he should do wickedness"* (v10); *"his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps"* (v21).

20310.text: Job 36:21 — Elihu: "this you have chosen rather than affliction": Elihu speaks *"on God’s behalf"* (v2), and his speech is about what affliction is for: *"if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction, then he declares to them their work … He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity"* (v8–10); *"If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity … But if they do not listen, they perish"* (v11–12); *"He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity"* (v15); In Elihu's account, affliction is how God opens the ear.; Then he turns to Job, and what he sees in him is inward: *"you are full of the judgment on the wicked"* (v17); *"Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing"* (v18); *"Do not long for the night"* (v20); His evaluation: *"Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (v21). The choice he sees is a preference, as in Proverbs 16:16 (*"rather than"*). Of the two things before Job, affliction (H6040, the word in v15) and iniquity (H0205), Elihu says Job has taken iniquity rather than accept the affliction as the opening of his ear. The warning *"Take care"* treats the choice as still able to be turned.; He ends by pointing to God: *"who is a teacher like him?"* (v22). "Teacher" here is H4175, from the same root as *"instruct"* in Psalm 25:8, 12 (H3384).

20358.text: Zec 7:10: the hardened hearts and the anger (7:12) are quoted in Ch 4, 10.2 and 10.13.

20440.text: Face: God's purpose; Verses: Jer 23:20; 30:24; 51:11; Job 42:2; Who thinks: God; Joined with / aimed at: "the intents of his heart"; cannot be thwarted

20476.text: 6.1 What the full pull adds: The mind has its own desires: "the desires of the flesh and the mind" (Ephesians 2:3).; Thoughts come from the heart or mind, but the condition of that source is itself shaped by what is written on it, what blinds it, and what guards it. The new-covenant verses describe God changing the source itself, not only the thoughts it produces.

20477.text: 4. One word covers both inner reasoning and outward dispute. *Dialogismos* is rendered "thoughts" (Mark 7:21), but also "quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8), "disputing" (Philippians 2:14) and "opinions" (Romans 14:1). The same activity happens inside a person as an inner conversation and between people as argument.

20488.text: 5. God is a thinker too, and his thinking has the last word. The same vocabulary is used of God: *maḥăšāvāh*: Jer 29:11; Ps 33:11; 40:5; 92:5; Isa 55:8–9; *ḥāšav*: Jer 18:11; 2 Sam 14:14; Lam 2:8; "the Lord takes thought for me" (Ps 40:17); "that you think of him" (Ps 144:3); *mᵊzimmāh*: "the intents of his heart" (Jer 23:20); "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2); In Gen 50:20 there are two opposite intentions about one event, expressed with the same verb: "you meant evil … God meant it for good." Human plans are real, but "it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Prov 19:21; also Prov 16:9; Ps 33:10–11; Job 5:12).

20531.text: Face: The sufferer's reading of God's reckoning; Verses: Job 13:24; 19:11; 33:10; Psa 44:22; What differs: Who: the one in pain. "Why do you … count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). "He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary" (19:11); Why (basis): From inside suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity. Job 42:7 says Job spoke rightly; this reading is still not God's own word about Job (R; crosses into the anger strand)

20544.text: God's purpose is carried by his anger: "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jer 23:20; 30:24). The word for discretion and for evil device is here God's *intent*, and his anger serves it. Understanding comes only afterwards. This is a link to the anger strand.

20553.text: Face: Devising and plotting; Verses: Pro 24:2; Psa 38:12; 2:1; Isa 59:3, 13; What differs: Fixed on violence or treachery, "all day long"; "the nations rage and the peoples plot" (Psa 2:1): plotting stands beside rage

20561.text: *śᵉʿippîm* | Divided opinions · thoughts that answer back · night thoughts claimed as revelation | 1Ki 18:21 · Job 20:2 · Job 4:13 | Haste makes thoughts answer back (Job 20:2, S). Eliphaz's night vision (4:13–17) yields a teaching that God later says was not right (42:7). A night thought claimed as revelation is not proved by being nocturnal (R; contrast Daniel)

20563.text: *ʿaštût* | Thought shaped by ease | Job 12:5 | "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (S). Comfort is a circumstance that changes thought's character. Compare Amo 6:1–5 and "the nations that are at ease" (Zec 1:15, anger strand)

20565.text: *dialogizomai / dialogismos* | Honest troubled reasoning · hardened anxious reasoning · inner questioning seen by Jesus · reasoning together into murder · self-talk of the rich man · quarrel, dispute, opinions · argument about greatness · futile thinking · evil thoughts from the heart · partiality: "judges with evil thoughts" · thoughts revealed by the child set for a sign | Luk 1:29 · Mar 8:16–17; Mat 16:7–8 · Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 5:21–22; 6:8; 9:47 · Luk 20:14; Mat 21:25 · Luk 12:17 · 1Ti 2:8 ("without anger or quarreling"); Phili 2:14; Rom 14:1 · Luk 9:46 · Rom 1:21; 1Co 3:20 · Mar 7:21; Mat 15:19 · Jam 2:4 · Luk 2:35 | Inner reasoning becomes outward quarrel when it is shared and set on one's own standing (Luk 9:46; Rom 14:1) (R). The heart state decides honest or hardened (Luk 1:29 against Mar 8:17, S). In 1Ti 2:8 the quarrel word stands beside anger, a link to the anger strand

20566.text: *dianoia* | The mind given wholly to love God · the mind hostile · the mind darkened because of hardness of heart · the mind's desires, "children of wrath" · proud in the thoughts of their hearts · laws written on minds · minds prepared · a sincere mind stirred · understanding given | Mat 22:37; Mar 12:30; Luk 10:27 · Col 1:21 · Eph 4:18 · Eph 2:3 · Luk 1:51 · Heb 8:10; 10:16 · 1Pe 1:13 · 2Pe 3:1 · 1Jo 5:20 | Eph 4:18 states the causal direction: "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart." The heart's state changes the mind's character (S). Eph 2:3 links the mind's desires to wrath (anger strand)

20578.text: *mᵊzimmāh* | 10.3; 11 §4 | Third face: God's intents, carried by his anger (Jer 23:20)

20579.text: Links to the anger strand, recorded here and carried to the M02 strand ledger: Pro 14:17; Jer 23:20 / 30:24; Psa 2:1; Job 19:11; 1Ti 2:8; Eph 2:3; 1Sa 18:8 → 18:25; Zec 1:15; Psa 106:31 (Phinehas).

21283.text: Quiet is the inner calm and stillness of a person or God: a chosen or given settledness, or its refusal, that the verse commands, praises, laments the lack of, or promises.

21286.text: Quiet, negated, gives unrest: the sea of fear that cannot be calm, and the fool's raging so that no calm is left.

21296.text: Being silent is a person's, or God's, holding back of speech for a reason the verse shows: submission, fear, shame, awe, wisdom, obedience, waiting, or failure to speak up; or the refusal of it (anguish, praise, the watchmen's duty).

21301.text: Call is a purposeful act of the inner being turned to God: calling or crying out to the Lord, or on his name, in need, trust, praise or worship, or refusing to.

21305.text: Call is here the outward use of the Lord's name over others (a formula spoken over a person or thing); it is the outward act and bears on them, with no inner operation of the speaker named.

21311.text: Called here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21313.text: Called is here the outward act of summoning, addressing or sending for another person or thing; it bears on the other's response but names no inner-being operation of the one who calls.

21323.text: Calling is here the cry or call of a person to another in need or appeal: a purposeful voicing of the person's own need, longing or request.

21350.text: Deal is God's own act of dealing with a person or people according to what they are or have done, or according to his own faithfulness or love; it bears on them and is the outward act upon them.

21351.text: Deal is here the outward act of dealing with a person in hatred, fury, violence or by what they deserve, named by another word of the verse; it bears on the one dealt with and names no inner operation of its own.

21357.text: Dealt is here the use of, or resort to, a thing or another party, the stance toward it named by another word of the verse; the outward act bears on that stance.

21368.text: Offered is here an offering made to a party other than the Lord (an idol, a demon, the dead or a man); it is the outward act of worship, and its devotion is named by other words of the verse, if at all.

21378.text: Fresh is here God's act of making new or renewing toward a person (his mercies, his oil, his creation, his pressure); it bears on the person's inner state, named by another word of the verse, and is the outward act upon them.

21386.text: Old here states an age, an old age or an age class (years old, an old man, young and old, the older brother); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21399.text: Oldest here states an age, an old age or an age class (years old, an old man, young and old, the older brother); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.
